sections.title: Sets before formulas
sections.text: The intersection $A\cap B$ contains inputs allowed by both restrictions; the union $A\cup B$ allows either. The interval $[a,b)$ includes a and excludes $b$. A function assigns exactly one output to every member of its domain. Its codomain is the declared target set; its range consists of outputs actually attained.

sections.title: Set laws preserve membership
sections.text: For subsets of one universe, union and intersection are each commutative: $A\cup B=B\cup A$ and $A\cap B=B\cap A$. They are each associative: $A\cup(B\cup C)=(A\cup B)\cup C$ and likewise for $\cap$. Distribution works in both directions: $A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)$ and $A\cup(B\cap C)=(A\cup B)\cap(A\cup C)$. Check these by translating membership into “or” and “and”; changing parentheses never changes which member passes the test.

sections.title: Derive the domain
sections.text: For $f(x)=\sqrt{x-1}/(x-2)$, the root requires $x\geq 1$ and the denominator requires $x\ne 2$. Intersecting gives $[1,2)\cup (2,\infty )$. Declaring only $[3,4]$ as the domain defines a different, restricted function. A circle as a relation fails the function test where one input has two output heights.

exercise.prompt: Let $f:[-2,2]\to\mathbb R$ be $f(x)=x^2$. Identify domain, codomain and range. Can the same rule define a function into $[1,4]$?
exercise.hint: Check the output at $x=0$; then show that every value in your proposed range is attained.
exercise.solution: The domain is $[-2,2]$, codomain $\mathbb{R}$, and range $[0,4]$. Every $y$ in $[0,4]$ is attained at $x=\sqrt{y}$. The proposed codomain $[1,4]$ fails because $f(0)=0$ lies outside it.
rubric: Separate declared inputs from allowed outputs.
Prove both inclusion and attainment for the range.
Use an explicit input to refute the proposed codomain.

contentBlocks.title: Specify the set and its universe
items: A set contains distinct elements. List a small set, such as $S=\{1,3,5\}$, or describe it, such as $I=\{n\in\mathbb Z:n>0\}$. Membership $x\in S$ is a statement about one object.
Write $A\subseteq B$ only when every element of $A$ belongs to $B$. The empty set is a subset of every set; disjoint sets have empty intersection.
Fix a universe $U$ before taking complements: $A^{c}=U\setminus A$. A different $U$ can change the complement.

contentBlocks.title: Read operations as logical tests
contentBlocks.tex: x\in A\cup B\iff(x\in A\lor x\in B),\qquad x\in A\cap B\iff(x\in A\land x\in B),\qquad x\in A^c\iff(x\in U\land x\notin A)
contentBlocks.note: The “or” in a union includes elements in both sets. A complement is always relative to the chosen universe.

contentBlocks.title: Work one finite universe
contentBlocks.strategy: Test membership before writing each result; use an explicit witness to reject a subset claim.

steps.label: Subset and disjointness
steps.text: Every member of $A$ lies in $B$, so $A\subseteq B$. The sets are not disjoint because $1$ belongs to both.

steps.label: Union and intersection
steps.text: The shared members are $1$ and $3$; every member of either set is $1$, $2$, or $3$.

steps.label: Complement
steps.text: Subtract the members of $A$ from the specified universe, not from all integers.

contentBlocks.result: $2\in B$ but $2\notin A$, so $B\nsubseteq A$ even though $A\subseteq B$.
contentBlocks.verification: The complement changes if the universe changes: with $U^{\prime}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$, it also contains $5$.

contentBlocks.title: Why the distributive law holds
contentBlocks.strategy: Show the same arbitrary element passes both membership tests.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $A,B,C$ be subsets of the same universe.

steps.label: Expand the left side
steps.text: $x\in A\cap(B\cup C)$ means $x\in A$ and at least one of $x\in B$ or $x\in C$.
steps.equation: x\in A\cap(B\cup C)\iff (x\in A)\land((x\in B)\lor(x\in C))

steps.label: Distribute the and
steps.text: This is equivalent to $x$ lying in both $A,B$ or in both $A,C$.

contentBlocks.result: $A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)$ by equality of members.
contentBlocks.verification: Replacing $(A\cap C)$ with $C$ is invalid: elements of $C$ outside $A$ would be added.

contentBlocks.title: Decide whether a rule assigns exactly one output to every declared input.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: In $R$, each of the three inputs appears once and every output belongs to $E$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: In $S$, input $0$ has two outputs, $0$ and $2$; the rule is ambiguous at that input.

contentBlocks.result: $R$ defines a function $D\to E$; $S$ does not.
contentBlocks.verification: Merely listing an output for every input is insufficient when one input has two outputs.

contentBlocks.title: Translate a complete verbal rule into a numerical table and formula.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.
contentBlocks.setup: On $D=\{-2,0,3\}$, the rule is “square the input, then add one.”

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: Applying the same operation to each input gives $f(-2)=5$, $f(0)=1$, and $f(3)=10$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: The table $(-2,5),(0,1),(3,10)$ and formula $f(x)=x^2+1$ on $D$ encode the same function.

contentBlocks.result: A table covering all of this finite $D$ is complete; a table missing $3$ is not.
contentBlocks.verification: A finite sample table does not define the rule on all real inputs unless the domain is restricted.

contentBlocks.title: Read graph points as ordered pairs and distinguish input from output.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: Substitute each permitted input: $f(-1)=-1$, $f(0)=1$, $f(2)=5$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Plot only $(-1,-1),(0,1),(2,5)$ because the declared domain has three points.

contentBlocks.result: The graph is a three-point set, not the full line $y=2x+1$.
contentBlocks.verification: The formula and domain jointly determine the graph.

contentBlocks.title: Apply the vertical line test and select a single-valued branch.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: At $x=2$, $y^2=4$, so the vertical line hits $(2,2)$ and $(2,-2)$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Selecting $y=\sqrt{x+2}$ retains one output for each $x\ge-2$; the negative branch also defines a separate function.

contentBlocks.result: The whole sideways parabola fails the test, while either branch passes.
contentBlocks.verification: A horizontal line may meet a function graph twice; that is irrelevant to the vertical line test.

contentBlocks.title: Simplify a difference quotient before taking any limit.
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the given rule and its domain before simplifying.

steps.label: Set up
steps.text: Expanding gives $f(a+h)=2a^2+4ah+2h^2-5a-5h+1$.

steps.label: Derive
steps.text: Subtracting $f(a)$ leaves $4ah+2h^2-5h=h(4a+2h-5)$; cancel only because $h\ne0$.

contentBlocks.result: The quotient is $4a+2h-5$.
contentBlocks.verification: The expression at $h=0$ is still undefined in its original quotient form.

exercises.outcome: Translate a described set to a roster and decide membership.
exercises.prompt: In $U=\{-2,-1,0,1,2,3\}$, let $S=\{n\in U:n\text{ is odd}\}$. Enumerate $S$. Decide whether $0\in S$ and $3\in S$, and explain why writing $\{-1,1,3,3\}$ gives the same set.
exercises.hint: Test every member of the finite universe against “odd”. A set records membership, not repetition.
exercises.solution: The odd members of $U$ are $-1,1,3$, so $S=\{-1,1,3\}$. We have $0\notin S$ and $3\in S$. Repeating $3$ in a roster adds no new element.
rubric: Enumerate exactly the odd members of the stated universe.
Use membership symbols correctly for $0$ and $3$.
Explain that repeated entries do not change a set.

exercises.outcome: Compute set operations and a relative complement, and decide subset claims by a witness.
exercises.prompt: Let $U=\{0,1,2,3,4\}$, $A=\{0,2,4\}$, and $B=\{2,3\}$. Find $A\cap B$, $A\cup B$, $A^c$ relative to $U$, and $(A\cup B)^c$. Is $B\subseteq A$? Justify. Are $A$ and $B$ disjoint?
exercises.hint: For each element of $U$, mark membership in $A$ and $B$. A single counterexample settles a false subset claim.
exercises.solution: The only common element is $2$, so $A\cap B=\{2\}$. The union is $\{0,2,3,4\}$. Relative to $U$, $A^c=\{1,3\}$ and $(A\cup B)^c=\{1\}$. The subset claim fails because $3\in B$ but $3\notin A$. They are not disjoint because $2\in A\cap B$.
rubric: Use the stated $U$ for both complements.
Include $3$ in the union but not the intersection.
Give the member $3$ as a witness against $B\subseteq A$.
Use the shared member $2$ to reject disjointness.
exercises.solutionTex: A\cap B=\{2\},\quad A\cup B=\{0,2,3,4\},\quad A^c=\{1,3\},\quad(A\cup B)^c=\{1\}

exercises.outcome: Prove a set law by element membership and reject a tempting false variant.
exercises.prompt: Prove $A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)$ for subsets of one universe. Is $A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup C$ always true? Give a counterexample if not.
exercises.hint: Start with an arbitrary $x$ and translate $\cap$ to “and” and $\cup$ to “or”. For the second claim, try an element of $C$ that is outside $A$.
exercises.solution: For any $x$, membership in the left side means $(x\in A)\land((x\in B)\lor(x\in C))$. Distributing gives $((x\in A)\land(x\in B))\lor((x\in A)\land(x\in C))$, exactly membership in the right side. For the false variant, take $A=\{1\}$, $B=\varnothing$, $C=\{2\}$ in $U=\{1,2\}$: the left side is empty but the proposed right side is $\{2\}$.
rubric: Prove both directions through an arbitrary member or an equivalent biconditional.
Keep $A$ in both intersection terms.
Give a concrete universe and contrasting results for the false variant.
exercises.solutionTex: x\in A\cap(B\cup C)\iff (x\in A\cap B)\lor(x\in A\cap C)

exercises.outcome: Use commutativity and associativity to rearrange a union without changing members.
exercises.prompt: For arbitrary sets $A,B,C$, justify $(A\cup B)\cup C=B\cup(A\cup C)$ by naming each law or by testing an arbitrary member. Does the same rearrangement hold with every $\cup$ replaced by $\cap$?
exercises.hint: First change the grouping; then swap $A$ and $B$. Both operations are available for union and intersection.
exercises.solution: Associativity gives $(A\cup B)\cup C=A\cup(B\cup C)$. Commutativity of the outer union gives $(B\cup C)\cup A$, and associativity/commutativity yield $B\cup(A\cup C)$. More directly, both sides contain exactly the members in at least one of $A,B,C$. The all-intersection statement also holds, because intersection is associative and commutative; both sides contain exactly the members in all three sets.
rubric: Name or demonstrate both associative and commutative steps.
Apply the same membership reasoning to intersection.
Do not invoke distributivity for a pure rearrangement.

exercises.outcome: Decide whether a rule assigns exactly one output to every declared input.
exercises.prompt: Let $D=\{-1,0,1\}$ and $E=\{0,1,2\}$. Does $T=\{(-1,1),(0,0)\}$ define a function $D\to E$? What if its declared domain is $\{-1,0\}$?
exercises.hint: Check both existence and uniqueness for every declared input.
exercises.solution: $T$ fails on $D$ because $1$ has no output. On domain $\{-1,0\}$ it is a function into $E$, with outputs $1$ and $0$.
rubric: Use the stated domain or branch condition before computing.
Give a reason that distinguishes the answer from a nearby incorrect claim.

exercises.prompt: On $D=\{-1,0,2\}$, turn “twice the input minus three” into a complete table and formula.
exercises.hint: Evaluate the verbal rule at every member of $D$.
rubric: Use the stated domain or branch condition before computing.

exercises.outcome: Read graph points as ordered pairs and distinguish input from output.
exercises.prompt: List the graph of $g(x)=x^2$ on $D=\{-2,1\}$ and decide whether $(0,0)$ belongs.
exercises.hint: A point is present only if its first coordinate is in $D$.
exercises.solution: The graph is $\{(-2,4),(1,1)\}$. Although the formula gives $0$ at zero, $(0,0)$ is absent because $0\notin D$.

Give a reason that distinguishes the answer from a nearby incorrect claim.

exercises.outcome: Apply the vertical line test and select a single-valued branch.
exercises.prompt: Does $x=y^2-9$ define $y$ as a function of $x$? State a branch and domain that does.
exercises.hint: Use a permitted input with two heights.
exercises.solution: At $x=0$, $y=3$ or $y=-3$, so the relation fails. The branch $y=\sqrt{x+9}$ on $[-9,\infty)$ is a function.
rubric: Use the stated domain or branch condition before computing.
Give a reason that distinguishes the answer from a nearby incorrect claim.

exercises.outcome: Simplify a difference quotient before taking any limit.
exercises.prompt: For $g(x)=3x^2+x$, simplify $[g(a+h)-g(a)]/h$ for $h\ne0$.
exercises.hint: Expand before canceling.
exercises.solution: $g(a+h)-g(a)=6ah+3h^2+h$, so the quotient is $6a+3h+1$.
rubric: Apply the correct rule and domain restriction.
Show the decisive calculation or interval argument.

sections.title: Classify with the domain
sections.text: Even means $f(-x)=f(x)$, odd means $f(-x)=-f(x)$, and either requires a domain symmetric about zero. Restricting $x^{2}$ to $[0,2]$ removes evenness under this convention. Increasing means $x_{1}<x_{2}$ implies $f(x_{1})\leq f(x_{2})$; strict increase replaces $\leq$ with $<$. The function $x^{3}$ is strictly increasing although its derivative vanishes at zero.

sections.title: Families and junctions
sections.text: Polynomials have real natural domains; rational functions exclude denominator zeros. Exponentials are positive, logarithms require positive inputs, and trigonometric domains depend on the function: $\tan$ excludes $\pi /2+k\pi$. For a piecewise function, inspect each formula on its assigned interval and compare both limiting heights with the actual junction value. The identity $|x|=-x$ for $x<0$ and $x$ for $x\geq 0$ makes its corner explicit.

exercise.prompt: Is $f(x)=x^3$ on $[-1,2]$ odd, strictly increasing, both, or neither?
exercise.hint: Test domain symmetry independently of the algebraic identity.
exercise.solution: It is strictly increasing, since $x_{1}^{3}<x_{2}^{3}$ whenever $x_{1}<x_{2}$. It is not odd under the symmetric-domain convention: 2 belongs to the domain but $-2$ does not.
rubric: State the domain convention.
Distinguish strict monotonicity from a derivative being everywhere positive.

contentBlocks.title: Choose the active piece at a boundary and mark open and closed graph endpoints.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: The first rule owns $-1$, so $f(-1)=2$ and the line has a filled point $(-1,2)$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: The second rule approaches height $1$ at $-1$ but excludes that input, so draw an open point $(-1,1)$.

contentBlocks.result: The graph has a jump at $-1$; the two nearby heights do not change the assigned value.
contentBlocks.verification: Using both formulas at the boundary would violate the single-output rule.

contentBlocks.title: Convert absolute value and ReLU to piecewise rules and compare their negative inputs.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: For $x<0$, $a(x)=-x>0$ but $r(x)=0$; for $x\ge0$, both equal $x$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: At $x=0$, both branches meet at the filled origin; the absolute-value graph has a rising left ray, while ReLU has a flat left ray.

contentBlocks.result: $a(-2)=2$ and $r(-2)=0$; identical right halves do not make the functions identical.
contentBlocks.verification: Distance from zero explains $|x|$, while maximum with zero explains ReLU.

contentBlocks.title: Use a leaky ReLU parameter to determine branch slope and junction value.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: The negative branch has slope $0.1$ and includes $L(0)=0$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: The positive branch has slope $1$; unlike ReLU, $L(-2)=-0.2$ rather than zero.

contentBlocks.result: Both rays join at the origin but have different slopes.
contentBlocks.verification: A small positive left slope does not make the negative branch flat.

contentBlocks.title: Interpret a rational-indicator piecewise rule on its dense input classes.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: The rational input $1/2$ gives $q(1/2)=1$; the irrational input $\sqrt2$ gives $q(\sqrt2)=0$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Both input classes occur arbitrarily near every real $x$, so the graph has points on both height lines in every horizontal interval.

contentBlocks.result: The graph is not a solid horizontal line at either height.
contentBlocks.verification: A small sampled table cannot reveal every point of this graph.

contentBlocks.title: Classify a function as even, odd, or neither by substituting the negative input.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: Compute $p(-x)=-x^3+x^2$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: This is neither $p(x)=x^3+x^2$ nor $-p(x)=-x^3-x^2$ for all $x$.

contentBlocks.result: $p$ is neither even nor odd.
contentBlocks.verification: Checking one convenient input cannot prove parity; an identity for all inputs is required.

contentBlocks.title: Decompose a function on a symmetric domain into unique even and odd parts.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $f$ be defined on a domain symmetric about zero.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: Set $e(x)=[f(x)+f(-x)]/2$ and $o(x)=[f(x)-f(-x)]/2$. Substitution shows $e(-x)=e(x)$ and $o(-x)=-o(x)$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Adding gives $e(x)+o(x)=f(x)$; subtracting any two decompositions shows the even and odd differences must both be zero.

contentBlocks.result: These formulas give the unique parity decomposition.
contentBlocks.verification: The construction needs $-x$ in the domain whenever $x$ is in it.

contentBlocks.title: Test strict increase or decrease using every ordered input pair on an interval.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: For $0\le x_1<x_2$, $x_2^2-x_1^2=(x_2-x_1)(x_2+x_1)>0$; hence strict increase holds on $[0,3]$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: On $[-3,3]$, inputs $-2<-1$ give $4>1$, while $1<2$ give $1<4$; neither single direction holds throughout.

contentBlocks.result: State the interval with the monotonicity claim.
contentBlocks.verification: A rising segment of a graph does not certify a whole larger interval.

contentBlocks.title: Derive the range of a decreasing function from endpoint and limiting behavior.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: The radical requires $x\ge-1$. For $x_1<x_2$ in this domain, the denominator grows strictly, so the positive reciprocal decreases.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: At $x=-1$, $f=1$; as $x\to\infty$, the denominator grows without bound and $f\to0$ without reaching zero.

contentBlocks.result: $\operatorname{range}(f)=(0,1]$.
contentBlocks.verification: A limit at infinity is not an attained endpoint.

contentBlocks.title: Distinguish polynomial degree from a general power function and give natural domains.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: The leading nonzero term of $P$ has exponent 4; all exponents are nonnegative integers, so $P$ is a degree-four polynomial on $\mathbb R$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: The rule $r(x)=\sqrt{x}$ is a power function with exponent $1/2$ and real domain $[0,\infty)$; it is not a polynomial.

contentBlocks.result: A power function need not be a polynomial.
contentBlocks.verification: A written high-degree term with zero coefficient does not set polynomial degree.

contentBlocks.title: Classify rational and algebraic rules and retain restrictions after simplification.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: For $r$, denominator zero excludes $x=1$ even though cancellation gives $x+1$ elsewhere.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: The rule $a$ is algebraic; its square root needs $x\ge-2$ and its denominator excludes $1$.

contentBlocks.result: $\operatorname{Dom}(r)=\mathbb R\setminus\{1\}$ and $\operatorname{Dom}(a)=[-2,1)\cup(1,\infty)$.
contentBlocks.verification: Simplifying a formula does not silently fill a hole in its original domain.

contentBlocks.title: Distinguish bounded periodic sine and cosine from reciprocal trigonometric domain gaps.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: Sine is defined for every real input, repeats after $2\pi$, and stays in $[-1,1]$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: The reciprocal requires $\sin x\ne0$, so $c$ excludes $k\pi$ for integer $k$; its magnitude is at least one.

contentBlocks.result: $s$ has range $[-1,1]$; $c$ has range $(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)$.
contentBlocks.verification: Periodicity does not imply boundedness or a full real domain.

contentBlocks.title: Use the base to distinguish increasing and decreasing exponentials while keeping positive range.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: Both pass through $(0,1)$ and remain positive; $f(1)=2$ while $g(1)=1/2$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Because $g(x)=2^{-x}$, it reflects $f$ across the vertical axis and decreases as $x$ grows.

contentBlocks.result: Both have domain $\mathbb R$ and range $(0,\infty)$; zero is never attained.
contentBlocks.verification: A base below one reverses direction without making outputs negative.

contentBlocks.title: Use exponential inverse relation to determine logarithm domain and range.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: Rewrite as $x=2^y$: this requires $x>0$ and permits every real $y$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Since $2^0=1$ and $2^3=8$, the log graph contains $(1,0)$ and $(8,3)$; it reflects $y=2^x$ across $y=x$.

contentBlocks.result: $\operatorname{Dom}(\log_2)=(0,\infty)$ and its range is $\mathbb R$.
contentBlocks.verification: A logarithm base must be positive and different from one to define an inverse; the source omits the latter condition.

contentBlocks.title: Classify mixed function formulas by construction and natural domain.
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the given rule and its domain before simplifying.

steps.label: Set up
steps.text: The variable is the exponent in $5^x$, so it is exponential; the variable is the base in $x^5$, so it is both a power function and polynomial.

steps.label: Derive
steps.text: The root-containing quotient is algebraic with $x\ge0$ and $x\ne1$; the last expression is a degree-four polynomial on $\mathbb R$.

contentBlocks.result: The family name follows the construction, and domain restrictions still apply.
contentBlocks.verification: A formula can belong to more than one family, as $x^5$ does.

exercises.prompt: Is $g(x)=-x^2$ strictly decreasing on $[0,4]$? Is it decreasing on $[-4,4]$?

exercises.solution: On $[0,4]$, $x_1<x_2$ implies $-x_1^2>-x_2^2$, so yes. On $[-4,4]$, $-2<-1$ gives $-4<-1$, contradicting decrease.
rubric: Use the stated domain or branch condition before computing.
Give a reason that distinguishes the answer from a nearby incorrect claim.

exercises.outcome: Derive the range of a decreasing function from endpoint and limiting behavior.
exercises.prompt: Find the domain and range of $h(x)=1/(2+\sqrt{x})$.
exercises.hint: Use the smallest input and the unattained lower limit.
exercises.solution: The domain is $[0,\infty)$; $h$ decreases from $h(0)=1/2$ toward but never to $0$, so its range is $(0,1/2]$.
rubric: Use the stated domain or branch condition before computing.
Give a reason that distinguishes the answer from a nearby incorrect claim.

exercises.outcome: Distinguish polynomial degree from a general power function and give natural domains.
exercises.prompt: Classify $Q(x)=0x^5+2x^2-1$ and $s(x)=x^{-1}$; state degrees or natural domains.
exercises.hint: Discard zero leading coefficients and check negative exponents.
exercises.solution: $Q$ is a degree-two polynomial on $\mathbb R$; $s$ is a power function $1/x$ with domain $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, not a polynomial.

exercises.outcome: Classify rational and algebraic rules and retain restrictions after simplification.
exercises.prompt: Classify $u(x)=1/(x^2-4)$ and find its domain; is $v(x)=\sqrt{x-5}$ rational?
exercises.hint: Factor the denominator; roots permit algebraic functions beyond rational ratios.
exercises.solution: $u$ is rational with domain $\mathbb R\setminus\{-2,2\}$. $v$ is algebraic with domain $[5,\infty)$ but is not rational.
rubric: Use the stated domain or branch condition before computing.

exercises.outcome: Distinguish bounded periodic sine and cosine from reciprocal trigonometric domain gaps.
exercises.prompt: Find the excluded inputs and range of $u(x)=1/\cos x$.
exercises.hint: Cosine zeros occur at odd half-turns; reciprocals of values in $[-1,1]\setminus\{0\}$ have magnitude at least one.
exercises.solution: $u$ excludes $\pi/2+k\pi$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$ and has range $(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)$.
rubric: Use the stated domain or branch condition before computing.
Give a reason that distinguishes the answer from a nearby incorrect claim.

exercises.outcome: Use the base to distinguish increasing and decreasing exponentials while keeping positive range.
exercises.prompt: Find $h(-1)$ and $h(0)$ for $h(x)=3^x$ and state its range.

exercises.solution: $h(-1)=1/3$, $h(0)=1$, and the range is $(0,\infty)$.

exercises.outcome: Use exponential inverse relation to determine logarithm domain and range.

exercises.hint: Translate to an exponential equation.

exercises.outcome: Classify mixed function formulas by construction and natural domain.
exercises.prompt: Classify $2^x$, $x^{-2}$, and $3x^2-1$; give natural domains.
exercises.hint: Ask whether the variable sits in the exponent or base and whether a denominator can vanish.
exercises.solution: $2^x$ is exponential on $\mathbb R$; $x^{-2}=1/x^2$ is a power and rational function on $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$; $3x^2-1$ is a degree-two polynomial on $\mathbb R$.

sections.title: Track a point
sections.text: For $g(x)=a f(b(x-h))+k$ with $b\ne 0$, a point $(u,f(u))$ maps to $(h+u/b,k+a f(u))$. A negative $b$ reflects the input direction; a negative a reflects output heights. If $b=0$ and $f(0)$ exists, $g$ is constant a $f(0)+k$; the inverse point mapping is unavailable.

sections.title: Order changes the domain
sections.text: For $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $g(x)=x-1$, $f\circ g$ has domain $[1,\infty )$ and value $\sqrt{x-1}$. The reverse composition $g\circ f$ has domain $[0,\infty )$ and value $\sqrt{x}-1$. In each case require the inner input to exist and the inner output to belong to the outer domain.

exercise.prompt: If $(2,3)$ lies on $f$, where does it move under $g(x)=-2 f(-3(x-1))+4$?
exercise.hint: Solve $-3(x-1)=2$ before changing the output.
exercise.solution: The input is $x=1-2/3=1/3$; the output is $-2\cdot 3+4=-2$. The new point is $(1/3,-2)$.
rubric: Invert the input transformation.
Apply output scaling and translation in order.

contentBlocks.title: Track vertical and horizontal shifts by mapping a known graph point.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: To reuse input $2$, solve $x-4=2$, giving new input $x=6$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Add five to the old output: $g(6)=f(2)+5=8$.

contentBlocks.result: The known point moves to $(6,8)$; the graph moves right four and up five.
contentBlocks.verification: The minus inside the input corresponds to a right shift, unlike the plus outside.

contentBlocks.title: Track point coordinates under horizontal and vertical scaling and reflection.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: Set $-x/2=2$, so $x=-4$: input reversal and stretch act before evaluation.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Scale and reflect the height: $g(-4)=-2f(2)=-6$.

contentBlocks.result: The point becomes $(-4,-6)$.
contentBlocks.verification: The argument scale acts inversely on the input coordinate; the outer factor acts directly on height.

contentBlocks.title: Derive domains of sum, product, and quotient from both input domains and zeros of the divisor.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: Both are defined exactly when $x\ge1$, so $f+g$ and $fg$ have domain $[1,\infty)$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: For $f/g$, also remove $x=3$ because $g(3)=0$; for $g/f$, remove $x=1$ because $f(1)=0$.

contentBlocks.result: $\operatorname{Dom}(f/g)=[1,3)\cup(3,\infty)$ and $\operatorname{Dom}(g/f)=(1,\infty)$.
contentBlocks.verification: Quotient domains depend on which function is below the fraction bar.

contentBlocks.title: Calculate composite values and reject inner outputs outside the outer domain.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: The inner function requires $x\ne0$. The outer function rejects input $-2$, so solve $g(x)=-2$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Multiplying by nonzero $x$ gives $(x+1)^2=0$, hence $x=-1$ must also be removed.

contentBlocks.result: $\operatorname{Dom}(f\circ g)=\mathbb R\setminus\{-1,0\}$.
contentBlocks.verification: Simplifying the composed fraction must not restore an originally forbidden input.

contentBlocks.title: Evaluate nested composition from the innermost function outward.
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable condition, compute explicitly, and contrast the tempting incorrect reading.

steps.label: Determine
steps.text: For any real $x$, the first application produces either $0$ or $1$.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: Both outputs lie in $[-1,1]$, so the second application gives $1$; a third application gives $f(1)=1$.

contentBlocks.result: $f(f(f(x)))=1$ for every real $x$.
contentBlocks.verification: The middle expression becomes constant even though the first application is not constant.

contentBlocks.title: Compose a sign rule with sine using zeros and sign intervals.
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the given rule and its domain before simplifying.

steps.label: Set up
steps.text: Sine is zero at $k\pi$, so $q(k\pi)=0$ for every integer $k$.

steps.label: Derive
steps.text: On $(2k\pi,(2k+1)\pi)$ sine is positive, giving height 1; on $((2k+1)\pi,(2k+2)\pi)$ it is negative, giving height -1.

contentBlocks.result: The graph alternates horizontal open intervals at heights 1 and -1, with isolated zeros at integer multiples of $\pi$.
contentBlocks.verification: The zero points must be included; the sign function does not assign them a side value.

contentBlocks.title: Derive product-to-sum and half-angle identities from addition formulas.
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the given rule and its domain before simplifying.

steps.label: Set up
steps.text: Subtract the minus case from the plus case: $\sin(\alpha+\beta)-\sin(\alpha-\beta)=2\cos\alpha\sin\beta$.

steps.label: Derive
steps.text: Set $\beta=\alpha$ in $\cos(\alpha-\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\beta$ and $\cos(\alpha+\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\beta$; subtract to get $1-\cos(2\alpha)=2\sin^2\alpha$.

contentBlocks.result: Thus $\cos\alpha\sin\beta=[\sin(\alpha+\beta)-\sin(\alpha-\beta)]/2$ and $\sin^2\alpha=[1-\cos(2\alpha)]/2$.
contentBlocks.verification: The two formulas come from different pairings; reversing subtraction changes the sign.

contentBlocks.title: Derive hyperbolic product and square identities from supplied addition formulas.
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the given rule and its domain before simplifying.

steps.label: Set up
steps.text: Add plus and minus formulas; the $\sinh\alpha\sinh\beta$ terms cancel, giving $2\cosh\alpha\cosh\beta$.

steps.label: Derive
steps.text: Set $\beta=\alpha$ and subtract $\cosh(0)=1$ from $\cosh(2\alpha)$ to obtain $2\sinh^2\alpha$.

contentBlocks.result: Hence $\cosh\alpha\cosh\beta=[\cosh(\alpha+\beta)+\cosh(\alpha-\beta)]/2$ and $\sinh^2\alpha=[\cosh(2\alpha)-1]/2$.
contentBlocks.verification: The hyperbolic square identity has a minus one, unlike the trigonometric sine-square identity.

exercises.outcome: Track vertical and horizontal shifts by mapping a known graph point.
exercises.prompt: Suppose $(1,-2)$ lies on $f$. Where does it move under $h(x)=f(x+3)-4$?
exercises.hint: Solve $x+3=1$ before changing height.
exercises.solution: The new input is $-2$ and output is $-6$, so the point moves to $(-2,-6)$.
rubric: Use the stated domain or branch condition before computing.

exercises.outcome: Track point coordinates under horizontal and vertical scaling and reflection.
exercises.prompt: Suppose $(3,-1)$ lies on $f$. Map this point under $h(x)=3f(2x)$ and state the graph changes.
exercises.hint: Solve $2x=3$ and multiply output by three.
exercises.solution: The point moves to $(3/2,-3)$: horizontal shrink by two, vertical stretch by three.
rubric: Use the stated domain or branch condition before computing.
Give a reason that distinguishes the answer from a nearby incorrect claim.

exercises.outcome: Derive domains of sum, product, and quotient from both input domains and zeros of the divisor.
exercises.prompt: For $u(x)=\sqrt{x+2}$ and $v(x)=x$, find domains of $uv$ and $u/v$.
exercises.hint: Intersect input domains, then exclude divisor zeros only for the quotient.
exercises.solution: $uv$ has domain $[-2,\infty)$; $u/v$ has domain $[-2,0)\cup(0,\infty)$.
rubric: Use the stated domain or branch condition before computing.
Give a reason that distinguishes the answer from a nearby incorrect claim.

exercises.outcome: Calculate composite values and reject inner outputs outside the outer domain.
exercises.prompt: For $p(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $q(x)=x-4$, find domains of $p\circ q$ and $q\circ p$.
exercises.hint: Test the inner domain, then the outer domain.
exercises.solution: $p(q(x))=\sqrt{x-4}$ needs $x\ge4$; $q(p(x))=\sqrt{x}-4$ needs $x\ge0$.
rubric: Use the stated domain or branch condition before computing.
Give a reason that distinguishes the answer from a nearby incorrect claim.

exercises.outcome: Evaluate nested composition from the innermost function outward.
exercises.prompt: Let $r(x)=0$ when $x<0$ and $r(x)=2$ when $x\ge0$. Find $r(r(x))$ for all real $x$.
exercises.hint: Track the possible first outputs before applying the rule again.
exercises.solution: The first output is $0$ or $2$, both nonnegative, so $r(r(x))=2$ for all real $x.
rubric: Use the stated domain or branch condition before computing.
Give a reason that distinguishes the answer from a nearby incorrect claim.

exercises.outcome: Compose a sign rule with sine using zeros and sign intervals.
exercises.prompt: With $\operatorname{sgn}(t)=-1,0,1$ according as $t<0,t=0,t>0$, find $\operatorname{sgn}(\cos x)$ on $(0,2\pi)$ and at $x=\pi/2,3\pi/2$.
exercises.hint: Track cosine signs and its zeros.
exercises.solution: It is 1 on $(0,\pi/2)\cup(3\pi/2,2\pi)$, -1 on $(\pi/2,3\pi/2)$, and 0 at the two endpoints $\pi/2,3\pi/2$.
rubric: Apply the correct rule and domain restriction.
