exercises.outcome: Derive product-to-sum and half-angle identities from addition formulas.
exercises.prompt: Given $\sin(\alpha\pm\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta\pm\cos\alpha\sin\beta$, derive $\sin\alpha\cos\beta=[\sin(\alpha+\beta)+\sin(\alpha-\beta)]/2$.
exercises.hint: Add the two sine formulas.
exercises.solution: Adding cancels the $\cos\alpha\sin\beta$ terms and gives $2\sin\alpha\cos\beta$; divide by two.
rubric: Apply the correct rule and domain restriction.
Show the decisive calculation or interval argument.

exercises.outcome: Derive hyperbolic product and square identities from supplied addition formulas.
exercises.prompt: Given $\cosh(\alpha\pm\beta)=\cosh\alpha\cosh\beta\pm\sinh\alpha\sinh\beta$, derive $\sinh\alpha\sinh\beta=[\cosh(\alpha+\beta)-\cosh(\alpha-\beta)]/2$.
exercises.hint: Subtract the two supplied cosh formulas.
exercises.solution: Subtraction cancels the $\cosh\alpha\cosh\beta$ terms and leaves $2\sinh\alpha\sinh\beta$; divide by two.
rubric: Apply the correct rule and domain restriction.
Show the decisive calculation or interval argument.

contentBlocks.title: When a two-sided limit exists
contentBlocks.statement: A finite $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ exists if and only if the left and right limits both exist as finite numbers and equal $L$.
hypotheses: The domain has inputs approaching $a$ from both sides.
Each side is considered on a punctured neighbourhood; $f(a)$ does not enter the limit.
prerequisites: the left- and right-hand approach described in this lesson

contentBlocks.title: Why the two directions hold
contentBlocks.strategy: Restrict an approach to each side, then combine the two near-input conditions. The later precise-limits lesson gives the formal epsilon-delta version.
contentBlocks.setup: Assume inputs of the domain approach $a$ from both sides.

steps.label: Only if
steps.text: If outputs approach $L$ for every sufficiently near input, they also approach $L$ when we restrict inputs to either side.

steps.label: If
steps.text: Each side can bring outputs as close to $L$ as wanted. Use the smaller of the two allowable input distances; every sufficiently near input lies on one of those sides.

contentBlocks.result: Both directions give the stated equivalence for a finite limit.
contentBlocks.verification: The argument never uses the value at $a$ and needs approach points on both sides.

contentBlocks.title: Equal sides, missing point value
contentBlocks.strategy: Simplify only where the function is defined, then take each side's limit.

steps.label: Simplify
steps.text: For $x\ne1$, factor and cancel $x-1$; this says nothing about $f(1)$.

steps.label: Compare sides
steps.text: The simplified expression approaches 2 from below and above 1.

contentBlocks.result: The two-sided limit is 2 even though $f(1)$ is undefined.
contentBlocks.verification: Setting $f(1)=7$ changes continuity, not either one-sided limit.

contentBlocks.title: Unequal sides, no two-sided limit
contentBlocks.strategy: Evaluate the branch used on each side before asking about the value at the join.

steps.label: Approach from left
steps.text: The left branch approaches 1.

steps.label: Approach from right
steps.text: The right branch approaches 0.

contentBlocks.result: The limits disagree, so $\lim_{x\to0}g(x)$ does not exist.
contentBlocks.verification: Along $x=-1/n$, values tend to 1; along $x=1/n$, values tend to 0. Changing $g(0)$ cannot reconcile them.

contentBlocks.title: A secant uses two distinct points
contentBlocks.text: For $P=(a,f(a))$ and $Q=(x,f(x))$ with $x\ne a$, the secant slope is $m_{PQ}=[f(x)-f(a)]/(x-a)$. If these slopes approach one finite value as $x\to a$, that limit is the tangent slope. The quotient is not evaluated at $x=a$.

contentBlocks.title: A velocity uses shrinking nonzero intervals
contentBlocks.text: For one-dimensional position $s(t)$, average velocity on a nonzero interval of length $h$ is $[s(t+h)-s(t)]/h$. Instantaneous velocity at $t$ is its finite limit as $h\to0$, if that limit exists; the sign depends on the chosen position direction.

contentBlocks.title: A tangent slope is a limit of secants
contentBlocks.strategy: Keep the nearby point distinct from the target, simplify the secant slope, then take the limit from both sides.
contentBlocks.setup: MH1100 Lecture 02 Example 1: find the tangent to $y=x^2$ at $P=(1,1)$ using $Q=(x,x^2)$ with $x\ne1$.

steps.label: Form a secant
steps.text: The slope is $m_{PQ}=(x^2-1)/(x-1)$ for $x\ne1$; it is undefined when $Q=P$.

steps.label: Let the point approach
steps.text: As $x\to1$ from either side, $m_{PQ}=x+1\to2$. The tangent slope is the limit of these secant slopes, not the value of the original quotient at $x=1$.

steps.label: Use the base point
steps.text: The line through $(1,1)$ with slope $2$ is $y-1=2(x-1)$.

contentBlocks.result: The tangent is $y=2x-1$.
contentBlocks.verification: For $Q=(1.5,2.25)$ the source secant slope is $2.5$; on the left, $Q=(0.5,0.25)$ gives $1.5$. Both approach $2$ as $Q\to P$.

contentBlocks.title: Average velocities approach one instantaneous rate
contentBlocks.strategy: Form a nonzero-time average rate, simplify it exactly, then let the interval shrink.
contentBlocks.setup: MH1100 Lecture 02 Example 3 models downward distance by $s(t)=4.9t^2$ metres. Find velocity after $5$ seconds.

steps.label: Average over a short interval
steps.text: For nonzero $\tau$, use the interval from $5$ to $5+\tau$ seconds.

steps.label: Shrink the interval
steps.text: The two-sided limit as $\tau\to0$ is $49$ metres per second; the quotient at $\tau=0$ is never evaluated.

contentBlocks.result: The velocity is $49\,\mathrm{m/s}$ downward because $s$ measures downward distance.
contentBlocks.verification: For $\tau=0.1$, average velocity is $49.49\,\mathrm{m/s}$; for $\tau=-0.1$, it is $48.51\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Both approach $49\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

contentBlocks.title: Precise left and right limits
contentBlocks.statement: $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=L$ means every $\varepsilon>0$ admits $\delta>0$ such that $a-\delta<x<a$ implies $|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon$. For $\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=L$, require $a<x<a+\delta$ instead.
hypotheses: The inputs must lie in the domain on the named side of $a$.
The target point $a$ is excluded; the opposite side is not constrained.

contentBlocks.title: Source example: prove a right-hand square-root limit
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the right-side condition to convert the input distance into a bound on the square root.

steps.label: Choose $\delta$
steps.text: Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\varepsilon^2+4\varepsilon$. If $0<x-4<\delta$, then $4<x<4+\delta=(2+\varepsilon)^2$.

steps.label: Bound the output error
steps.text: Taking square roots gives $2<\sqrt{x}<2+\varepsilon$, hence the right-side output error is less than $\varepsilon$.

contentBlocks.result: $\lim_{x\to4^+}\sqrt{x}=2$.
contentBlocks.verification: The proof uses $x>4$ throughout; it makes no claim about inputs from the left.

sections.title: Four different failures
sections.text: A removable hole has equal finite one-sided limits but no matching point value. A jump has unequal one-sided limits. The function $1/x^{2}$ tends to $+\infty$ at zero, which is not a finite limit. The bounded function $\sin(1/x)$ oscillates: inputs approaching zero can give outputs 1 or $-1$.

sections.title: A rate with units
sections.text: If position is $s(t)=t^{2}$ metres with $t$ in seconds, average velocity over $[2,2+h]$ is $((2+h)^{2}-4)/h=4+h$ metres per second. As $h$ tends to zero from either side, velocity tends to 4 $m/s$. The $h=0$ quotient is undefined; its limit supplies the instantaneous rate.

exercise.prompt: For $f(x)=x+1$ when $x\ne 1$ and $f(1)=7$, find the limit at 1. Which point value makes $f$ continuous?
exercise.hint: The punctured neighborhood contains no information about $f(1)$.
exercise.solution: Both one-sided limits are 2. Setting $f(1)=2$ restores continuity. Changing only $f(1)$ cannot repair a jump with unequal one-sided limits.
rubric: Distinguish the limit from $f(1)$.
Explain why one-point repair needs a pre-existing finite limit.

exercises.outcome: Decide whether a two-sided limit exists when one one-sided limit fails.
exercises.prompt: Let $h(x)=x+2$ for $x<0$, $h(x)=\sin(1/x)$ for $x>0$, and $h(0)=2$. Does $\lim_{x\to0}h(x)$ exist? Explain using both sides, not only a plot or $h(0)$.
exercises.hint: The left limit is 2. On the right, find two positive sequences tending to zero whose sine values differ.
exercises.solution: From the left, $x+2\to2$. On the right, $x_n=1/(\pi/2+2\pi n)$ gives $h(x_n)=1$ and $y_n=1/(3\pi/2+2\pi n)$ gives $h(y_n)=-1$. Both sequences approach zero from the right, so the right-hand limit does not exist. Therefore the two-sided limit does not exist; $h(0)=2$ is irrelevant.
rubric: State the left-hand limit and identify that the right-hand limit fails to exist.
Give two right-side sequences with distinct limiting outputs or an equivalent proof of oscillation.
Do not use the point value as evidence for a punctured limit.

exercises.outcome: Derive a tangent equation from a secant-slope limit for a new curve.
exercises.prompt: Use secants through $P=(1,1)$ on $y=x^3$ to find its tangent equation. State where the secant quotient is defined and why its limit gives the slope.
exercises.hint: For $Q=(x,x^3)$ with $x\ne1$, factor $x^3-1=(x-1)(x^2+x+1)$.
exercises.solution: For $x\ne1$, the secant slope is $(x^3-1)/(x-1)=x^2+x+1$. Its limit as $x\to1$ is $3$ although the original quotient is undefined at $1$. The tangent through $(1,1)$ is $y-1=3(x-1)$, or $y=3x-2$.
rubric: Define the secant for a distinct nearby point.
Simplify only for the punctured domain and take its limit.
Use the limiting slope and the correct base point.

exercises.outcome: Obtain instantaneous velocity from shrinking average rates for a new position function.
exercises.prompt: For position $s(t)=t^3$ metres with $t\ge0$, find the average velocity on $[2,2+h]$ and the instantaneous velocity at $t=2$. Explain why $h=0$ is excluded from the quotient.
exercises.hint: Expand $(2+h)^3-8$ before dividing by nonzero $h$.
exercises.solution: For $h\ne0$ with $2+h\ge0$, the average velocity is $[(2+h)^3-8]/h=12+6h+h^2$ metres per second. Its limit as $h\to0$ is $12\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The quotient at $h=0$ would divide by zero; only its nearby values define the instantaneous rate.
rubric: Use displacement divided by a nonzero elapsed time.
Expand and simplify the average-rate expression correctly.
Take the limit with units and distinguish it from evaluation at zero.

exercises.outcome: Use a left-only input condition to prove a finite one-sided limit.
exercises.prompt: Prove $\lim_{x\to4^-}\sqrt{x+5}=3$ with a valid $\delta$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.
exercises.hint: First require $|x-4|<1$, then rationalize $3-\sqrt{x+5}$.
exercises.solution: Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\min\{1,3\varepsilon\}$. If $0<4-x<\delta$, then $x>3$ and $\sqrt{x+5}>0$. Thus $0<3-\sqrt{x+5}=(4-x)/(3+\sqrt{x+5})<(4-x)/3<\delta/3\leq\varepsilon$.
rubric: Use the left-sided input condition $0<4-x$.
Keep $x$ in the real domain of the square root.
Rationalize with a positive denominator.
Choose $\delta$ to enforce both the local bound and $\varepsilon$ tolerance.

contentBlocks.title: One infinite side is enough
contentBlocks.statement: The line $x=a$ is a vertical asymptote of $y=f(x)$ if at least one of $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)$ or $\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)$ is $+\infty$ or $-\infty$. A two-sided infinite limit also suffices.
hypotheses: Approach $a$ through points in the domain on the side being claimed.
Show values eventually exceed every positive bound or fall below every negative bound on that side; a zero denominator alone is not enough.

contentBlocks.title: Check tangent on each side
contentBlocks.strategy: Find candidate denominator zeros, then determine numerator and denominator signs separately on each side.

steps.label: Numerator
steps.text: $\sin x$ stays positive near $\pi/2$ and tends to $1$.

steps.label: Denominator
steps.text: $\cos x$ tends to zero through positive values on the left and negative values on the right.

contentBlocks.result: $x=\pi/2$ is a vertical asymptote; the two sides need not share one sign.
contentBlocks.verification: Translation by $\pi$ repeats this sign pattern at $x=\pi/2+n\pi$ for every integer $n$.

contentBlocks.title: Infinity describes eventual bounds
contentBlocks.text: For a function defined on both sides of $a$ near but possibly not at $a$, $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=+\infty$ means that every threshold $M>0$ is exceeded whenever $0<|x-a|<\delta$ for some $\delta>0$. For $-\infty$, every value is below $-M$ in such a deleted neighborhood. These are not finite real limits: $\infty$ is not a number. A one-sided statement restricts the inputs to the named side.

contentBlocks.title: Prove both infinite signs by a threshold
contentBlocks.strategy: Solve the output inequality for the input distance, keeping the puncture and both sides.

steps.label: Choose a distance
steps.text: Given any $M>0$, choose $\delta=M^{-1/2}$. If $0<|x-2|<\delta$, then $1/(x-2)^2>M$.

steps.label: Reverse the sign
steps.text: For the same punctured neighborhood, $f_-(x)=-f_+(x)<-M$. The condition covers both sides of $2$.

contentBlocks.result: These functions diverge with specified signs; neither has a finite real limit at $2$.
contentBlocks.verification: The proof handles every $M>0$ and every allowed $x$ sufficiently close to $2$; a clipped graph or selected samples would not establish either claim.

contentBlocks.title: Positive infinite limits use thresholds
contentBlocks.statement: $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=+\infty$ means that for every $M>0$ there is a $\delta>0$ such that every allowed $x$ with $0<|x-a|<\delta$ satisfies $f(x)>M$.
hypotheses: The inequality must hold for every allowed input in the deleted neighborhood, not only selected samples.
The notation $+\infty$ describes arbitrarily large values; it is not a finite real limit.

contentBlocks.title: Source example: prove reciprocal squares grow without bound
contentBlocks.strategy: Solve the threshold inequality for the distance to the target.

steps.label: Choose a threshold radius
steps.text: Let $M>0$ be arbitrary and choose $\delta=1/\sqrt{M}$.

steps.label: Verify the threshold
steps.text: If $0<|x|<\delta$, then $x^2<1/M$. Taking reciprocals of positive quantities gives $1/x^2>M$.

contentBlocks.result: $\lim_{x\to0}1/x^2=+\infty$.
contentBlocks.verification: The bound holds on both sides and for every positive $M$. A denominator zero alone would not establish this inequality.

contentBlocks.title: Negative infinite limits use lower thresholds
contentBlocks.statement: $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=-\infty$ means that for every negative number $N$ there is a $\delta>0$ such that every allowed $x$ with $0<|x-a|<\delta$ satisfies $f(x)<N$. For a one-sided limit, restrict $x$ to that side.
hypotheses: The threshold $N$ is negative and is chosen before $\delta$.
The inequality must hold for every domain input in the specified deleted neighborhood.

contentBlocks.title: Source exercise: prove the right-hand logarithm limit
contentBlocks.strategy: Invert the logarithm inequality while preserving the positive-side domain.

steps.label: Choose $\delta$ from the negative threshold
steps.text: Given any negative $N$, choose $\delta=e^N>0$.

steps.label: Check every right-side input
steps.text: If $0<x<\delta$, the logarithm is increasing, so $\ln x<\ln(e^N)=N$.

contentBlocks.result: $\lim_{x\to0^+}\ln x=-\infty$.
contentBlocks.verification: Only $x>0$ is in the claimed approach; there is no two-sided logarithm domain near zero.

sections.title: Quantifiers and signs
sections.text: A right-hand limit of $+\infty$ at a means: for each $M>0$ there exists $\delta >0$ such that $0<x-a<\delta$ implies $f(x)>M$. Replace $f(x)>M$ by $f(x)<-M$ for $-\infty$. For $1/x$, the right limit at zero is $+\infty$ and the left limit is $-\infty$; for $1/x^{2}$ both are $+\infty$.

sections.title: Unbounded is weaker
sections.text: A denominator zero can be removable: $(x^{2}-1)/(x-1)$ has limit 2 at 1. The function $\sin(1/x)/x$ is unbounded near zero but does not tend to either infinity: along $x=1/(n\pi )$ its value is zero. A graph clipped at a finite height cannot certify an infinite limit.

exercise.prompt: Prove that $1/x^2$ tends to $+\infty$ as $x\to 0$.
exercise.hint: Given $M$, choose $\delta$ so that $\delta^{2}=1/M$.
exercise.solution: For $M>0$ choose $\delta =1/\sqrt{M}$. If $0<|x|<\delta$, then $x^{2}<1/M$, hence $1/x^{2}>M$. This works on both sides.
rubric: Choose $\delta$ after $M$.
Keep the puncture $0<|x|$.
Reverse the reciprocal inequality correctly.

exercises.outcome: Use one-sided signs to certify a vertical asymptote rather than relying on a zero denominator.
exercises.prompt: For $f(x)=(x+1)/(x^2-4)$, determine the left and right behaviour at $x=2$. Is $x=2$ a vertical asymptote?
exercises.hint: Factor $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$. Near 2, the numerator and $x+2$ are positive; only $x-2$ changes sign.
exercises.solution: As $x\to2^-$, $(x-2)<0$ tends to zero while $(x+1)/(x+2)\to3/4>0$, so $f(x)\to-\infty$. As $x\to2^+$, the same positive factor is divided by a positive number tending to zero, so $f(x)\to+\infty$. Either one-sided result certifies the vertical asymptote $x=2$.
rubric: Factor and identify the signs of all nonzero factors near 2.
Give the correct sign of each one-sided infinite limit.
Apply the one-sided asymptote definition explicitly.

exercises.outcome: Prove a negative infinite limit with a bound valid throughout a deleted neighborhood.
exercises.prompt: For $g(x)=-(x+3)^2/(x+1)^2$ with $x\ne-1$, prove $\lim_{x\to-1}g(x)=-\infty$ using the threshold definition. Give a valid $\delta$ for any $M>0$.
exercises.solution: Given $M>0$, take $\delta=\min\{1,M^{-1/2}\}$. When $0<|x+1|<\delta$, we have $x\in(-2,0)$ and $x+3>1$, so $g(x)=-(x+3)^2/(x+1)^2<-1/(x+1)^2<-M$. This holds on both sides of $-1$, proving the negative infinite limit. It does not assert a finite real limit.
rubric: State an arbitrary positive threshold and a valid positive distance.
Bound the numerator and denominator throughout the deleted neighborhood.
Use the eventual negative inequality on both sides, without treating infinity as a number.

exercises.outcome: Construct a positive threshold radius for a shifted reciprocal square.
exercises.prompt: Prove $\lim_{x\to3}1/(x-3)^2=+\infty$ using the threshold definition.
exercises.hint: Given $M>0$, solve $1/(x-3)^2>M$ for $|x-3|$.
exercises.solution: Given $M>0$, choose $\delta=M^{-1/2}$. If $0<|x-3|<\delta$, then $(x-3)^2<1/M$, hence $1/(x-3)^2>M$. The condition covers both sides.
rubric: Quantify over every $M>0$.
Choose $\delta$ as a positive distance.
Keep $x=3$ excluded.
Reverse the positive reciprocal inequality correctly.

exercises.outcome: Prove a right-hand negative infinite limit with a threshold valid throughout the side-neighborhood.
exercises.prompt: Prove $\lim_{x\to0^+}\ln(2x)=-\infty$ using a negative threshold $N$.
exercises.hint: Choose $\delta$ so that $2\delta=e^N$.
exercises.solution: Given any negative $N$, choose $\delta=e^N/2>0$. If $0<x<\delta$, then $0<2x<e^N$, so monotonicity of $\ln$ gives $\ln(2x)<N$.
rubric: Use arbitrary negative $N$ and choose $\delta$ afterward.
Restrict inputs to the positive side.
Use the monotonicity of $\ln$ and state a strict threshold inequality.

contentBlocks.title: Read nearby graph values, then use laws
contentBlocks.statement: Read the left and right approaches of each graphed function before applying a limit law. Filled or open markers at the target do not replace nearby limits.
hypotheses: Component limits must exist for a two-sided sum-law calculation.
If one side differs, compute the composite one-sided limits before claiming a two-sided answer.

contentBlocks.title: A point marker and a graph jump have different effects
contentBlocks.strategy: Read each nearby branch, then combine side limits.
contentBlocks.setup: Lecture pages 4–5 ask about $\lim(f(x)+g(x))$ from two graphs.

steps.label: Page 4 at $-1$
steps.text: The blue $f$ branch tends to 0 despite its filled marker at $-2$; black $g$ tends to $-1$. The sum law gives $-1$.

steps.label: Page 5 at 0
steps.text: The blue $f$ branch tends to 1 from the left and 2 from the right; black $g$ tends to 0 on each side despite its filled marker at $-1$. The sum tends to 1 from the left and 2 from the right.

contentBlocks.result: The page 4 sum limit is $-1$; the page 5 two-sided sum limit does not exist.
contentBlocks.verification: A changed point value cannot change a limit; a jump in nearby values can.

contentBlocks.title: Build limits from finite pieces
contentBlocks.statement: If $f\to L$ and $g\to M$ as $x\to a$, then $f+g\to L+M$, $f-g\to L-M$, $cf\to cL$, and $fg\to LM$. Constant and identity functions tend to $c$ and $a$; repeated products give $f^n\to L^n$ for positive integers $n$.
hypotheses: Both component limits exist as finite real numbers.
The difference law follows by combining the sum and constant-multiple laws; the power law follows by repeated products.

contentBlocks.title: Justify each polynomial step
contentBlocks.strategy: Check the limit-law hypotheses before each calculation.

steps.label: Simple functions
steps.text: $x\to3$ and the constant $4\to4$. First use the power law to get $x^2\to9$.

steps.label: Combine
steps.text: $2x^2\to18$ and $-3x\to-9$ by constant multiples; finite sum limits give $18-9+4$.

contentBlocks.result: The limit is $13$.
contentBlocks.verification: Direct substitution agrees because this polynomial is defined at 3. The source polynomial at page 19 uses 5 and has value 39; this is a guide-created contrast.

contentBlocks.title: Check denominators and even roots
contentBlocks.statement: If $f\to L$ and $g\to M\ne0$, then $f/g\to L/M$. If $f\to L$, then its positive-integer $n$th root tends to $\sqrt[n]{L}$ where defined; the lecture requires $L>0$ for even $n$.
hypotheses: The quotient denominator has a nonzero limit and is defined near the target.
For even roots, the lecture assumes a strictly positive inner limit; an odd root needs no sign restriction.

contentBlocks.title: Use a nonzero denominator and a positive radicand
contentBlocks.strategy: Check the limit-law hypotheses before each calculation.

steps.label: Quotient
steps.text: $2x^2-3x+4\to39$ and $5-3x\to-10\ne0$, so the quotient tends to $-39/10$.

steps.label: Even root
steps.text: $x+5\to9>0$, so the square-root law gives $\sqrt9=3$.

contentBlocks.result: The two limits are $-39/10$ and $3$.
contentBlocks.verification: At a zero limiting denominator the quotient law is unavailable; the root example is guide-created and uses the source page 12 law.

contentBlocks.title: Apply laws on each side separately
contentBlocks.statement: The finite limit laws hold for one-sided limits. A two-sided limit exists exactly when the left and right finite limits exist and agree.
hypotheses: Check both sides separately when a component has different one-sided limits.
A missing component limit prevents direct use of a two-sided law; it alone does not determine the composite limit.

contentBlocks.title: A jump survives multiplication by a nonzero limit
contentBlocks.strategy: Check the limit-law hypotheses before each calculation.
contentBlocks.setup: At $x\to1$, suppose $f\to2$, while $g\to-2$ from the left and $g\to-1$ from the right, as in the lecture graph example.

steps.label: Left
steps.text: $fg\to2(-2)=-4$ using the left-hand product law.

steps.label: Right
steps.text: $fg\to2(-1)=-2$ using the right-hand product law.

contentBlocks.result: Because $-4\ne-2$, the two-sided product limit does not exist.
contentBlocks.verification: A vanishing multiplier can erase a jump, so failure of a component limit is not by itself a product failure.

contentBlocks.title: Substitute only inside the domain
contentBlocks.statement: A polynomial has $\lim_{x\to a}P(x)=P(a)$. A rational function $P/Q$ has $\lim_{x\to a}P(x)/Q(x)=P(a)/Q(a)$ when $Q(a)\ne0$.
hypotheses: The target is in the function domain.
For a rational function, its denominator at the target is nonzero.

contentBlocks.title: A hole changes which method applies
contentBlocks.strategy: Check the limit-law hypotheses before each calculation.

steps.label: Eligible
steps.text: $x+1\to2\ne0$, so direct substitution gives $2/2=1$.

steps.label: Ineligible
steps.text: $x-1\to0$, so direct substitution and the quotient law do not apply. On $x\ne1$, factor and use the replacement law to get $x+1\to2$.

contentBlocks.result: The limits are $1$ and $2$, by different justifications.
contentBlocks.verification: The second expression is undefined at 1 even though its finite limit exists.

contentBlocks.title: Compare both approaches
contentBlocks.statement: A two-sided finite limit at $a$ exists with value $L$ if and only if its left and right limits both exist with value $L$.
hypotheses: Approach through allowed domain points on both sides of $a$.
The value at $a$ does not repair unequal one-sided limits.

contentBlocks.title: Resolve an absolute-value quotient by sign
contentBlocks.strategy: Check the limit-law hypotheses before each calculation.

steps.label: Right
steps.text: For $x>0$, $|x|/x=1$, so the right limit is 1.

steps.label: Left
steps.text: For $x<0$, $|x|/x=-1$, so the left limit is -1.

contentBlocks.result: The two-sided limit does not exist.
contentBlocks.verification: In contrast, $|x|\to0$ from both sides; a quotient can turn a removable point issue into a jump.

contentBlocks.title: Pass a near-point inequality to limits
contentBlocks.statement: If $f(x)\le g(x)$ throughout some deleted neighborhood of $a$ and both finite limits exist, then $\lim f\le\lim g$.
hypotheses: The pointwise order holds for every sufficiently near allowed input, except possibly at $a$.
Both limits exist as finite real numbers.

contentBlocks.title: Strict nearby order need not give strict limit order
contentBlocks.strategy: Check the limit-law hypotheses before each calculation.
contentBlocks.setup: For $x\ne0$, compare $0<x^2$ as $x\to0$; the weak inequality $0\le x^2$ is valid throughout the deleted neighborhood.

steps.label: Limits
steps.text: The constant zero tends to zero and $x^2\to0$ by the power law.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.text: The order theorem yields $0\le0$, not $0<0$.

contentBlocks.result: Near-point order is preserved weakly at the limit.
contentBlocks.verification: This guide-created failure case guards against replacing $\le$ with $<$ in the conclusion.

contentBlocks.title: Bound sine and cosine by arc length
contentBlocks.statement: For radian $\theta$ near zero, the unit-circle chord from $(1,0)$ to $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ has squared length $\sin^2\theta+(1-\cos\theta)^2\le\theta^2$. Thus $|\sin\theta|\le|\theta|$ and $|1-\cos\theta|\le|\theta|$.
hypotheses: Radian arc length on the unit circle is $|\theta|$.
The chord is no longer than the corresponding local arc; both squared terms are nonnegative.

contentBlocks.title: Establish elementary trigonometric limits without derivatives
contentBlocks.strategy: Check the limit-law hypotheses before each calculation.

steps.label: Sine
steps.text: $-|\theta|\le\sin\theta\le|\theta|$, and both bounds tend to zero.

steps.label: Cosine
steps.text: $-|\theta|\le1-\cos\theta\le|\theta|$, so $1-\cos\theta\to0$ and $\cos\theta\to1$.

contentBlocks.result: $\lim_{\theta\to0}\sin\theta=0$ and $\lim_{\theta\to0}\cos\theta=1$.
contentBlocks.verification: The argument uses radian arc length, not the later derivative of sine.

contentBlocks.title: Replace values away from the target
contentBlocks.statement: If $f(x)=g(x)$ for every allowed $x$ sufficiently near but unequal to $a$, then $f$ and $g$ have the same limit at $a$ whenever either limit exists; if one has no limit, neither does the other.
hypotheses: Both expressions must be defined and equal throughout a common deleted neighborhood of $a$.
The values $f(a)$ and $g(a)$ may differ or be undefined.
prerequisites: a limit depends on nearby input values, not the point value

contentBlocks.title: Cancel only where the expression exists
contentBlocks.strategy: Factor first; establish equality on the deleted domain before applying direct substitution to the replacement.
contentBlocks.setup: Evaluate $\lim_{x\to1}(x^2-1)/(x-1)$; the original quotient is undefined at $x=1$.

steps.label: Factor and restrict
steps.text: For $x\ne1$, the numerator is $(x-1)(x+1)$, so the quotient equals $x+1$ on a deleted neighborhood.

steps.label: Take the replacement limit
steps.text: The replacement law transfers the finite limit of $x+1$ to the original quotient.

contentBlocks.result: $\lim_{x\to1}(x^2-1)/(x-1)=2$ even though the original point value is absent.
contentBlocks.verification: A denominator tending to zero does not prove an infinite limit; here the numerator shares the vanishing factor.

contentBlocks.title: Solve the lecture common-factor exercise
contentBlocks.strategy: Factor both polynomials and cancel only where the original denominator is nonzero.

steps.label: Use the replacement limit
steps.text: The replacement denominator tends to $-2\ne0$, so its quotient limit is $(-3)/(-2)$.

contentBlocks.result: The source exercise limit is $3/2$.
contentBlocks.verification: The original quotient is undefined at $x=-2$; the cancellation asserts equality only for nearby $x\ne-2$.

contentBlocks.title: Solve the lecture radical exercise
contentBlocks.strategy: Multiply by a nonzero conjugate and cancel the shared square only away from zero.

steps.label: Rationalize
steps.text: For $t\ne0$, the quotient equals $t^2/[t^2(\sqrt{t^2+400}+20)]=1/(\sqrt{t^2+400}+20)$.

steps.label: Check the new denominator
steps.text: As $t\to0$, the square-root term tends to $20$, so the new denominator tends to $40\ne0$.

contentBlocks.result: The source exercise limit is $1/40$.
contentBlocks.verification: The conjugate is positive, and the cancellation is made only for $t\ne0$.

contentBlocks.title: Check both bounds and their common limit
contentBlocks.statement: If $f(x)\le g(x)\le h(x)$ throughout a deleted neighborhood of $a$, and both outer limits exist and equal the same finite $L$, then $\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=L$.
hypotheses: The inequalities hold for every sufficiently near allowed input, except possibly at $a$.
Both outer functions have finite limits and those limits agree.
prerequisites: finite limits and order of real numbers

contentBlocks.title: Trap an oscillating factor
contentBlocks.strategy: Bound the oscillating factor uniformly; then check each outer function's limit.

steps.label: Build the bounds
steps.text: Since $|\sin(1/x)|\le1$, multiplication gives a bound valid on both sides of zero.

steps.label: Check outer limits
steps.text: Both $-|x|$ and $|x|$ tend to zero, so the squeeze theorem applies although $\sin(1/x)$ itself has no limit.

contentBlocks.result: $\lim_{x\to0}x\sin(1/x)=0$.
contentBlocks.verification: The inequalities hold for every nonzero $x$ near zero; no value at zero is required.

contentBlocks.title: A vanishing absolute value forces the function to vanish
contentBlocks.statement: If $\lim_{x\to a}|f(x)|=0$, then $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=0$, because $-|f(x)|\le f(x)\le|f(x)|$ on the deleted domain.
hypotheses: $|f(x)|$ is defined near $a$ and has the finite limit zero.
Both pointwise bounds hold for every sufficiently near allowed input.

contentBlocks.title: Use magnitude when sign keeps changing
contentBlocks.strategy: Squeeze directly by the known magnitude.

steps.label: Apply the derived rule
steps.text: $-|f(x)|\le f(x)\le|f(x)|$; both outer limits are zero.

contentBlocks.result: $\lim_{x\to0}x\cos(1/x)=0$.
contentBlocks.verification: The oscillating cosine factor has no limit, but its bounded magnitude does not obstruct this proof.

contentBlocks.title: Triangle inequality for a sum error
contentBlocks.statement: For real numbers $u$ and $v$, $|u+v|\leq|u|+|v|$. In the sum-law proof, use $u=f(x)-L$ and $v=g(x)-M$.
hypotheses: $u$ and $v$ are real values at an allowed input $x$.

contentBlocks.title: Sum law for finite limits
contentBlocks.statement: If $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ and $\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=M$ both exist as finite limits, then $\lim_{x\to a}(f(x)+g(x))=L+M$.
hypotheses: Both component limits exist and are finite at the same target $a$.
Use inputs in a common deleted neighborhood contained in both domains.

contentBlocks.title: Source proof: split $\varepsilon$ and take the smaller radius
contentBlocks.strategy: Use half the output tolerance for each summand and intersect their input neighborhoods.
contentBlocks.setup: Lecture 04 proves the sum law for arbitrary finite component limits $L$ and $M$ at $a$.

steps.label: Allocate the error tolerance
steps.text: Given $\varepsilon>0$, the two component limits give positive radii $\delta_1$ and $\delta_2$ so each component error is less than $\varepsilon/2$.

steps.label: Use one input radius
steps.text: Choose $\delta=\min\{\delta_1,\delta_2\}$. A punctured input within $\delta$ satisfies both component bounds.

steps.label: Apply the triangle inequality
steps.text: Bound the total output error by the sum of the two component errors.

contentBlocks.result: $\lim_{x\to a}(f(x)+g(x))=L+M$.
contentBlocks.verification: Both finite-limit hypotheses are used. The minimum radius guarantees both implications; adding the radii would not do so.

supplementalBlocks.title: Prove the basic trigonometric limit in radians
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Compare areas of an inscribed triangle, a unit-circle sector, and a tangent triangle, then squeeze the ratio.
supplementalBlocks.setup: Take $0<x<\pi/2$ radians in a unit circle. The three areas are $\sin x/2$, $x/2$, and $\tan x/2$.

steps.label: Area order
steps.text: The inscribed triangle lies inside the sector, which lies inside the tangent triangle.
steps.usesHypothesis: Radian sector area is $x/2$; $0<x<\pi/2$ keeps all areas positive.

steps.label: Divide safely
steps.text: Since $\sin x>0$, divide and rearrange to trap the quotient.
steps.usesHypothesis: $x$ and $\sin x$ are nonzero in this punctured interval.

steps.label: Both sides
steps.text: The lecture chord estimate gives $|1-\cos x|\le|x|$, hence $\cos x\to1$ without a derivative. Squeeze from the right; since $\sin(-x)/(-x)=\sin x/x$, the left limit agrees.

supplementalBlocks.result: $\lim_{x\to0}\sin x/x=1$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The angle is in radians; the derivative of sine is not used. The chord estimate supplies the otherwise missing cosine limit.
prerequisites: trig-chord-bound: $|1-\cos x|\le|x|$ gives $\cos x\to1$ by squeeze

supplementalBlocks.title: Rationalize before applying limit laws
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Replace a $0/0$ expression by an equal expression on the deleted domain.

steps.label: Conjugate
steps.text: Multiply numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{1+h}+1$.

steps.label: Pass to the limit
steps.text: The new denominator tends to 2, so its limit is nonzero.

supplementalBlocks.result: The limit is $1/2$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The original expression is undefined at $h=0$; equality only on a deleted neighborhood suffices for the limit.

exercises.outcome: Read side limits and ignore point markers before applying the sum law.
exercises.prompt: Near $a$, a graph has $f(x)\to2$ on both sides, but $f(a)=9$. A second graph has $g(x)\to-1$ from the left and $g(x)\to3$ from the right, with $g(a)=0$. Does $f+g$ have a two-sided limit?
exercises.hint: Compute the sum limit on each side; do not use the point markers.
exercises.solution: The left sum limit is $2+(-1)=1$, while the right sum limit is $2+3=5$. They differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist. Neither $f(a)=9$ nor $g(a)=0$ changes these nearby limits.
rubric: Read the two side limits of each component.
Compute both sum limits using one-sided laws.
Ignore point values and conclude nonexistence.

exercises.outcome: Derive a zero limit from a vanishing magnitude.
exercises.prompt: Suppose $|h(x)|\le(x-3)^2$ whenever $0<|x-3|<1$. Prove $\lim_{x\to3}h(x)=0$ and explain why the sign of $h$ is irrelevant.
exercises.hint: First bound $|h|$ between zero and $(x-3)^2$.
exercises.solution: The inequalities $0\le|h(x)|\le(x-3)^2$ hold throughout the deleted neighborhood, and both outer limits equal zero. Thus $|h(x)|\to0$. Since $-|h(x)|\le h(x)\le|h(x)|$, squeeze gives $h(x)\to0$. No sign condition on $h$ is needed.
rubric: Check the bound on the deleted domain.
Prove the magnitude tends to zero.
Apply the absolute-zero rule without assuming a sign.

exercises.outcome: Combine finite limits and derive a difference.
exercises.prompt: Suppose $f(x)\to2$ and $g(x)\to-3$ as $x\to a$. Find $\lim(3f^2-g)$ and explain the laws used.
exercises.hint: Use the positive-integer power law, a constant multiple, then the difference law.
exercises.solution: Since $f^2\to4$, $3f^2\to12$ and $g\to-3$; therefore $3f^2-g\to12-(-3)=15$. The difference law follows from sum and constant multiple laws.
rubric: Identify both finite component limits.
Apply power and constant-multiple laws before the difference.
Explain why the result is 15.

exercises.outcome: Check quotient and even-root hypotheses.
exercises.prompt: Evaluate $\lim_{x\to2}\sqrt{x+7}/(x+1)$ and explain why the same quotient argument fails for denominator $x-2$.
exercises.hint: Check the radicand limit and both denominator limits.
exercises.solution: As $x\to2$, $x+7\to9>0$ and $x+1\to3\ne0$. Hence the root tends to 3 and the quotient tends to 1. For $x-2$, the denominator limit is zero, so the quotient law makes no conclusion.
rubric: Check the even-root hypothesis.
Check the nonzero limiting denominator.
Distinguish an unavailable law from a conclusion about existence.

exercises.outcome: Decide a product using one-sided laws.
exercises.prompt: Let $f(x)\to-3$ on both sides of 0, while $g(x)\to1$ from the left and $g(x)\to2$ from the right. Does $fg$ have a two-sided limit? Contrast with replacing $f$ by $x$.
exercises.hint: Calculate the two product limits separately.
exercises.solution: The left product limit is $-3$ and the right is $-6$, so $fg$ has no two-sided limit. If $f(x)=x$ and $g$ stays bounded near 0, both products tend to zero; a missing limit for $g$ alone does not decide the product.
rubric: Use one-sided product laws.
Compare the two resulting limits.
Explain why a zero multiplier changes the inference.

exercises.outcome: Choose substitution only when eligible.
exercises.prompt: Evaluate $\lim_{x\to2}(x^2+2)/(x+3)$ and say why substituting into $(x^2-4)/(x-2)$ at 2 is invalid.
exercises.hint: Check each denominator at 2.
exercises.solution: The first rational function is defined at 2, and its denominator equals 5, so direct substitution gives $6/5$. The second denominator is zero at 2; factor and replace on $x\ne2$ if its limit is needed, obtaining 4.
rubric: State domain eligibility.
Compute the first quotient limit.
Do not use direct substitution at the hole.

exercises.outcome: Compare both sides of an absolute-value quotient.
exercises.prompt: Find $\lim_{x\to0}|x|/|2x|$ and contrast with $\lim_{x\to0}|x|/x$.
exercises.hint: Simplify separately where $x\ne0$, then compare sides.
exercises.solution: For every nonzero $x$, $|x|/|2x|=1/2$, so both one-sided limits equal $1/2$ and the two-sided limit exists. For $|x|/x$, the right and left limits are 1 and -1, so no two-sided limit exists.
rubric: Respect the deleted domain.
Check both one-sided results.
Explain the contrast with $|x|/x$.

exercises.outcome: Use weak order correctly.
exercises.prompt: Suppose $u(x)\le v(x)$ for all $0<|x-a|<\delta$ and both limits exist, with $u(x)\to4$. What can you conclude about $\lim v$? Can you conclude it is greater than 4?
exercises.hint: Use the order theorem and test equality with $v=u$.
exercises.solution: The order theorem gives $\lim v\ge4$. Equality is possible: take $u(x)=4$ and $v(x)=4+(x-a)^2$; their limits both equal 4 although $u<v$ for $x\ne a$.
rubric: State the near-point and existence hypotheses.
Conclude a weak inequality.
Give an equality counterexample to a strict claim.

exercises.outcome: Use arc bounds to prove a related limit.
exercises.prompt: Using $|1-\cos\theta|\le|\theta|$ in radians, prove $\lim_{\theta\to0}(1-\cos\theta)=0$ and explain why this bound does not by itself evaluate $(1-\cos\theta)/\theta^2$.
exercises.hint: Squeeze the first expression; then inspect the bound after division by $\theta^2$.
exercises.solution: The bounds $-|\theta|\le1-\cos\theta\le|\theta|$ have common limit zero, so squeeze gives the first limit. Dividing the absolute-value bound by $\theta^2$ gives $|(1-\cos\theta)/\theta^2|\le1/|\theta|$, which does not tend to zero or a finite value. A sharper identity is required.
rubric: State the radian bound and common outer limit.
Conclude by squeeze.
Explain why the weakened quotient bound is inconclusive.

exercises.outcome: Use equality on a deleted neighborhood to transfer a finite limit despite a changed point value.
exercises.prompt: Let $f(x)=(x^2-4)/(x-2)$ for $x\ne2$, but set $f(2)=7$. Find $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)$ and explain why neither cancellation at $x=2$ nor $f(2)$ gives the limit.
exercises.hint: Factor for $x\ne2$; compare the resulting function on the deleted neighborhood.
exercises.solution: For every $x\ne2$ near 2, $f(x)=(x-2)(x+2)/(x-2)=x+2$. The replacement law gives $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)=\lim_{x\to2}(x+2)=4$. Cancellation was only valid when $x\ne2$, and the separately assigned value $f(2)=7$ does not affect the limit.
rubric: State the deleted-domain equality rather than asserting equality at 2.
Use the replacement law and evaluate the replacement limit.
Distinguish the limit from the assigned point value.

exercises.outcome: Verify a pair of shared finite bounds before applying squeeze to a new oscillatory expression.
exercises.prompt: Find $\lim_{x\to0}x^2(1+\sin(1/x))$ and state the bounds that justify your answer for every nonzero nearby $x$.
exercises.hint: Use $-1\le\sin(1/x)\le1$ and note $x^2\ge0$.
exercises.solution: For $x\ne0$, $0\le1+\sin(1/x)\le2$, so $0\le x^2(1+\sin(1/x))\le2x^2$. Both outer functions tend to zero at 0, and the inequalities hold throughout the punctured neighborhood. The squeeze theorem gives limit zero without assigning a limit to $\sin(1/x)$.
rubric: Give both bounds and justify multiplication by nonnegative $x^2$.
Show both outer limits are the same finite number.
Conclude by the squeeze theorem, without inventing a sine limit.

exercises.outcome: Use the proved sine limit and an identity to justify a new trigonometric limit.
exercises.prompt: Prove $\lim_{x\to0}(1-\cos x)/x^2=1/2$ in radians; name every nonzero denominator you introduce.
exercises.hint: Use $1-\cos x=\sin^2x/(1+\cos x)$ near zero.
exercises.solution: For nonzero $x$ sufficiently close to zero, $1+\cos x>0$. Then $(1-\cos x)/x^2=(\sin x/x)^2/(1+\cos x)$. The proved sine limit is $1$ and $\cos x\to1$, yielding $1/2$.
rubric: Use an identity valid near zero.
Check $x\ne 0$ and $1+\cos x\ne 0$.
Apply the sine limit in radians.

exercises.outcome: Rationalize a root limit while preserving its deleted domain.
exercises.prompt: Evaluate $\lim_{h\to0}(\sqrt{4+h}-2)/h$ and state where the original quotient is defined.
exercises.hint: Multiply by the conjugate before taking the limit.
exercises.solution: For $h\geq -4$ and $h\ne 0$, the quotient equals $1/(\sqrt{4+h}+2)$. Its denominator tends to 4, so the limit is $1/4$.
rubric: State $h\geq -4$ and $h\ne 0$.
Cancel only in the deleted domain.
Evaluate the nonzero limiting denominator.

exercises.outcome: Prove a new finite sum limit by splitting $\varepsilon$ and intersecting the component radii.
exercises.prompt: Use the sum-law proof to show $\lim_{x\to1}(2x+x^2)=3$. For the two terms, you may use $\delta_1=\varepsilon/4$ and $\delta_2=\min\{1,\varepsilon/6\}$.
exercises.hint: For $|x-1|<1$, we have $0<x<2$ and $|x+1|<3$. Choose $\delta=\min\{\delta_1,\delta_2\}$.
exercises.solution: If $0<|x-1|<\delta_1$, then $|2x-2|=2|x-1|<2\delta_1=\varepsilon/2$. If $0<|x-1|<\delta_2$, then $0<x<2$ and $|x^2-1|=|x-1||x+1|<3|x-1|<3\delta_2\leq\varepsilon/2$. With $\delta=\min\{\delta_1,\delta_2\}$ both bounds hold, so $|(2x+x^2)-3|\leq|2x-2|+|x^2-1|<\varepsilon$.
rubric: Show both component limits or their $\varepsilon/2$ bounds.
Keep the local restriction for the quadratic factor.
Choose the minimum of the radii.
Use the triangle inequality and conclude a strict total error below $\varepsilon$.

sections.title: Eligibility before arithmetic
sections.text: The sum and product laws require the component finite limits to exist; the quotient law additionally requires a nonzero denominator limit. A quotient $0/0$ calls for another argument. Cancellation is valid in a punctured neighborhood even if the original expression is undefined at the target.

sections.title: Build an estimate
sections.text: Since $|\sin(1/x)|\le1$, $|x\sin(1/x)|\le|x|$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, taking $\delta=\varepsilon$ bounds the output error for every nonzero $|x|<\delta$. This establishes a limit without requiring the oscillating factor to have one.

exercise.prompt: Find $\lim_{x\to0}x^2\cos(1/x)$, justifying the estimate.
exercise.hint: Bound the absolute value by a non-oscillating function.
exercise.solution: The absolute value is at most $x^{2}$. For $\varepsilon >0$ use $\delta =\sqrt{\varepsilon }$. Then $0<|x|<\delta$ implies $|x^{2}\cos(1/x)|<\varepsilon$, so the limit is zero.
rubric: Use a bound valid for every nearby input.
Do not assign a limit to $\cos(1/x)$.

sections.title: The order matters
sections.text: The statement is: for every $\varepsilon >0$ there exists $\delta >0$ such that every allowed $x$ with $0<|x-a|<\delta$ satisfies $|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon$. The chosen $\delta$ may depend on $\varepsilon$ and a, but not on the particular $x$. Its negation has some $\varepsilon_{0}>0$ for which every $\delta >0$ admits a violating input.

sections.title: A new guide example: nonlinear estimate
sections.text: Added guide example, not a calculation from Lecture 04: to prove $x^{2}\to4$ as $x\to2$, factor $|x^{2}-4|=|x-2||x+2|$. First require $|x-2|<1$, giving $|x+2|<5$. Then choose $\delta=\min(1,\varepsilon/5)$. The same $\delta$ enforces both the local bound and the requested output tolerance.

exercise.prompt: Give a valid $\delta$ for proving $3x+2\to 5$ as $x\to 1$, and explain why it works.
exercise.hint: Express output error as a multiple of input error.
exercise.solution: Since $|(3x+2)-5|=3|x-1|$, choose $\delta =\varepsilon /3$. Every $0<|x-1|<\delta$ gives output error less than $\varepsilon$.
rubric: State that $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary and positive.
Choose $\delta$ independently of $x$.
Use strict inequalities consistently.

contentBlocks.title: The precise finite-limit definition
contentBlocks.statement: $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ means: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a $\delta>0$ such that every allowed $x$ with $0<|x-a|<\delta$ satisfies $|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon$. Choose $\delta$ after $\varepsilon$; the same $\delta$ must work for all such $x$.
hypotheses: The domain contains an open interval around $a$, though $f(a)$ may be undefined.
The input condition is punctured: $x=a$ is excluded from the implication.
prerequisites: absolute value as distance on the real line

contentBlocks.title: Source example: prove the identity limit
contentBlocks.strategy: Choose a radius that makes the input error itself smaller than the requested output error.
contentBlocks.setup: Lecture 04 asks for an $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ proof that $\lim_{x\to a}x=a$.

steps.label: Choose the radius
steps.text: Given any $\varepsilon>0$, set $\delta=\varepsilon$. This choice uses only the requested tolerance.

steps.label: Check every nearby input
steps.text: If $0<|x-a|<\delta$, then $|x-a|<\varepsilon$, which is exactly the required output bound.

contentBlocks.result: $\lim_{x\to a}x=a$.
contentBlocks.verification: The radius is fixed before $x$ is chosen. Any positive $\delta\leq\varepsilon$ also works; the value at $x=a$ is not used.

contentBlocks.title: Source example: choose $\delta$ for an affine limit
contentBlocks.strategy: Solve the output-error inequality for the input distance, then verify the resulting radius.

steps.label: Relate the two errors
steps.text: Factor the output difference so its size is a constant multiple of the input distance.

steps.label: Choose and verify $\delta$
steps.text: Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\varepsilon/4$. Every $x$ with $0<|x-3|<\delta$ then has output error below $\varepsilon$.

contentBlocks.verification: The same radius works for every allowed $x$. The proof uses strict inequalities and does not depend on the value assigned at $x=3$.

contentBlocks.title: The quantifiers for a failed limit
contentBlocks.text: To disprove a proposed finite limit $L$, it is enough to find one fixed $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that every $\delta>0$ admits an allowed $x$ with $0<|x-a|<\delta$ and $|f(x)-L|\geq\varepsilon_0$. To disprove existence, this argument must work for every candidate $L$.

contentBlocks.title: Guide example: use a fixed $\varepsilon$ to rule out every limit
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the gap between the two side values to choose one $\varepsilon$ that defeats every candidate limit.
contentBlocks.setup: Added guide example based on Lecture 04’s nonexistence question: let $g(x)=1$ for $x<0$ and $g(x)=0$ for $x>0$; set $g(0)$ arbitrarily.

steps.label: Fix the output tolerance
steps.text: For any proposed $L$, the triangle inequality gives $1\leq|1-L|+|L|$, so at least one of the two side values is at least $1/2$ from $L$. Set $\varepsilon_0=1/3$.

steps.label: Defeat every input radius
steps.text: For any $\delta>0$, choose $x=-\delta/2$ or $x=\delta/2$ on a side whose value is at least $1/2$ from $L$. Then $0<|x|<\delta$ but $|g(x)-L|\geq1/2>\varepsilon_0$.

contentBlocks.result: No real $L$ is a limit of $g$ at $0$.
contentBlocks.verification: This follows the negated quantifier order: choose $\varepsilon$ first, then defeat each $\delta$. The assigned value $g(0)$ does not enter.

contentBlocks.title: The same definition in interval form
contentBlocks.statement: The finite-limit condition is equivalent to $f(((a-\delta,a+\delta)\setminus\{a\})\cap\operatorname{dom}f)\subset(L-\varepsilon,L+\varepsilon)$. The input interval is punctured at $a$, and every output lies in the open tolerance interval.
hypotheses: The input interval is restricted to the domain of $f$.
The point $a$ is omitted even when $f(a)$ is defined.
prerequisites: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition of a finite limit

contentBlocks.title: Guide example: read the $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ intervals
contentBlocks.strategy: Translate the absolute-value bounds into open intervals and check the image inclusion.
contentBlocks.setup: For the added guide example $f(x)=2x+1$, consider $x\to a$ with target value $2a+1$.

steps.label: Choose $\delta$
steps.text: Given $\varepsilon>0$, use $\delta=\varepsilon/2$. The allowed input interval is $(a-\delta,a+\delta)$ with $a$ removed.

steps.label: Map the interval
steps.text: For every input in that punctured interval, the output differs from $2a+1$ by less than $\varepsilon$.

contentBlocks.result: $f((a-\delta,a+\delta)\setminus\{a\})\subset(2a+1-\varepsilon,2a+1+\varepsilon)$.
contentBlocks.verification: The set inclusion is precisely the quantified definition in interval language; no output condition is asserted at $x=a$.

contentBlocks.title: Source example: bound an oscillating factor
contentBlocks.strategy: Replace a complicated factor by a uniform bound, then solve the remaining inequality for $\delta$.

steps.label: Bound the factor
steps.text: Since $0\leq\sin^2(2024x)\leq1$, the bracket lies between 1 and 2 for every $x$.

steps.label: Choose $\delta$
steps.text: Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=(\varepsilon/2)^{1/2023}$. If $0<|x|<\delta$, the bound is strictly below $\varepsilon$.

contentBlocks.verification: The bound holds for every nonzero $x$ near $0$, even though the oscillating factor need not have a limit.

contentBlocks.title: Bound locally before choosing $\delta$
contentBlocks.text: When factoring $|f(x)-L|$, first restrict $x$ to a small neighborhood where the remaining factor has a fixed bound. Then choose $\delta$ small enough to meet both the neighborhood restriction and the $\varepsilon$ requirement.

contentBlocks.title: Source example: estimate a cubic difference
contentBlocks.strategy: Factor the difference, locally bound the other factor, and combine both input restrictions with a minimum.

steps.label: Factor the output error
steps.text: The factor $x^2+3x+9$ is unbounded on all of $\mathbb R$, so first impose $|x-3|<1$. This gives $2<x<4$ and hence $x^2+3x+9<37$.

steps.label: Satisfy both restrictions
steps.text: Given $\varepsilon>0$, set $\delta=\min\{1,\varepsilon/37\}$. Then the local bound and the $\varepsilon$ bound hold together.

contentBlocks.verification: A global constant bound for the quadratic factor would fail. The minimum keeps $x$ in the interval where the local bound is valid.

exercises.outcome: Choose $\delta$ after $\varepsilon$ and verify it uniformly for every punctured input.
exercises.prompt: Prove $\lim_{x\to a}2x=2a$ directly from the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition. Give a $\delta$ for each $\varepsilon>0$.
exercises.hint: Express the output error as a constant times $|x-a|$.
exercises.solution: Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\varepsilon/2$. If $0<|x-a|<\delta$, then $|(2x)-(2a)|=2|x-a|<2\delta=\varepsilon$.
rubric: Choose positive $\delta$ after arbitrary $\varepsilon$.
Make the choice independent of $x$.
Use the punctured input condition and strict output inequality.

exercises.outcome: Solve an affine output-error inequality to choose a valid $\delta$.
exercises.prompt: Prove $\lim_{x\to2}(3x+1)=7$. State a valid $\delta$ and show the implication for every allowed $x$.
exercises.hint: Factor $(3x+1)-7$ before choosing $\delta$.
exercises.solution: Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\varepsilon/3$. Then $0<|x-2|<\delta$ gives $|(3x+1)-7|=3|x-2|<3\delta=\varepsilon$.
rubric: Factor the output error exactly.
Choose a positive $\delta$ depending on $\varepsilon$, not $x$.
Verify the strict implication.

exercises.outcome: Use a fixed $\varepsilon$ and a violating input in every $\delta$-neighborhood to disprove all candidate limits.
exercises.prompt: Let $h(x)=-1$ for $x<2$ and $h(x)=3$ for $x>2$, with any value assigned at $2$. Prove that $h$ has no finite limit as $x\to2$.
exercises.hint: For any candidate $L$, at least one of $-1$ and $3$ is at least $2$ units from $L$.
exercises.solution: For any proposed $L$, at least one of $|-1-L|$ and $|3-L|$ is at least 2. Fix $\varepsilon_0=1$. For every $\delta>0$, choose $x=2-\delta/2$ or $x=2+\delta/2$ from a side with that value. Then $0<|x-2|<\delta$ and $|h(x)-L|\geq2>\varepsilon_0$. Thus no $L$ is the limit; $h(2)$ is irrelevant.
rubric: Quantify over every candidate $L$.
Fix $\varepsilon$ before taking an arbitrary $\delta$.
Choose an allowed violating input inside that $\delta$.
Exclude the point value from the argument.

exercises.outcome: Translate an $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ implication into a punctured input interval mapped into an output tolerance interval.
exercises.prompt: For $f(x)=5x-3$ as $x\to2$, write the input and output intervals that verify $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)=7$. Give a valid $\delta$ in terms of $\varepsilon$.
exercises.hint: Use $|f(x)-7|=5|x-2|$ and keep $x=2$ out of the input interval.
exercises.solution: Choose $\delta=\varepsilon/5$. Every $x\in(2-\delta,2+\delta)\setminus\{2\}$ satisfies $|f(x)-7|=5|x-2|<\varepsilon$, so its image lies in $(7-\varepsilon,7+\varepsilon)$.
rubric: Use the punctured input interval.
Derive the correct $\delta$ from the output error.
State the output tolerance interval with strict bounds.

exercises.outcome: Use a uniform bound on an oscillating factor to construct a finite-limit $\delta$.
exercises.prompt: Prove $\lim_{x\to0}x^5(2+\cos(1/x))=0$ by an $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ estimate.
exercises.hint: $|2+\cos(1/x)|\leq3$ for every nonzero $x$.
exercises.solution: For $x\ne0$, $|2+\cos(1/x)|\leq3$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=(\varepsilon/3)^{1/5}$. Then $0<|x|<\delta$ gives $|x^5(2+\cos(1/x))|\leq3|x|^5<3\delta^5=\varepsilon$.
rubric: Use a bound valid throughout the punctured neighborhood.
Choose $\delta$ only after an arbitrary positive $\varepsilon$.
Do not assume the oscillating factor has a limit.

exercises.outcome: Restrict the input to bound a factored term locally before choosing the minimum $\delta$.
exercises.prompt: Use an estimate to prove $\lim_{x\to2}x^3=8$. Choose a local bound and a valid $\delta$.
exercises.solution: Factor $|x^3-8|=|x-2|(x^2+2x+4)$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, set $\delta=\min\{1,\varepsilon/19\}$. If $0<|x-2|<\delta$, then $1<x<3$, so $x^2+2x+4<19$ and $|x^3-8|<19|x-2|<19\delta\leq\varepsilon$.
rubric: Factor the difference correctly.
Justify the local bound using $|x-2|<1$.
Use the minimum to enforce both conditions.
Keep the final inequalities strict.

sections.title: Continuity depends on the domain
sections.text: At an endpoint of an interval, continuity is tested through the domain, so only the available side matters. At an interior point, existence of the finite limit and equality to the point value are both required.

sections.title: Existence is not uniqueness
sections.text: For $f(x)=x^{3}-x-1$, $f(1)=-1$ and $f(2)=5$. Polynomial continuity and the intermediate value theorem give a zero in $(1,2)$. This theorem alone does not count zeros. Bisection repeatedly retains an interval whose endpoint values bracket zero; discontinuity would invalidate its existence guarantee.

exercise.prompt: Why does a sign change in $f(x)=1/x$ between $-1$ and 1 not guarantee a zero?
exercise.hint: Which hypothesis fails on the closed interval?
exercise.solution: The function is not defined or continuous at zero, so IVT cannot be applied on $[-1,1]$. Indeed $1/x$ is never zero on its domain.
rubric: Check the entire interval, not just its endpoints.
Separate a failed theorem application from the truth of its conclusion.

contentBlocks.title: Check all three conditions at a point
contentBlocks.statement: $f$ is continuous at $a$ when $f(a)$ is defined, the finite limit $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ exists, and that limit equals $f(a)$.
hypotheses: The target belongs to the domain.
The relevant finite two-sided limit exists and equals the point value.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Verify the lecture root-sum example
contentBlocks.strategy: Check domain and theorem hypotheses before concluding.

steps.label: Domain
steps.text: $4$ lies in $x\le5$, and the square root is defined on both sides near 4.

steps.label: Limit
steps.text: By the sum, power, and root laws, $\lim_{x\to4}f(x)=4^2+\sqrt{5-4}=17=f(4)$.

contentBlocks.result: $f$ is continuous at 4.
contentBlocks.verification: The point value and limit are checked separately; a formula alone is not the three-condition test.

contentBlocks.title: Identify which continuity condition fails
contentBlocks.statement: For a function defined near $a$, discontinuity occurs when the point is missing, its finite two-sided limit fails, or its limit differs from its assigned value. A finite limit with a missing or wrong point value is removable; an unbounded approach is infinite; unequal one-sided limits give a jump.
hypotheses: Check nearby domain values on both sides.
Classify from limit behavior before using the point marker.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Separate hole, wrong value, pole, and jump
contentBlocks.strategy: Check domain and theorem hypotheses before concluding.
contentBlocks.setup: Lecture page 9 presents $(x^2-x-2)/(x-2)$, a $1/x^2$ branch with value 1 at zero, the same quotient assigned value 1 at 2, and $\lfloor x\rfloor$.

steps.label: Hole and wrong value
steps.text: For $x\ne2$, $(x^2-x-2)/(x-2)=x+1\to3$. The unassigned version has a hole; the version with $f(2)=1$ has a wrong point value. Both are removable.

steps.label: Pole and jump
steps.text: $1/x^2$ grows without a finite limit at zero even if its point value is 1. At an integer $n$, $\lfloor x\rfloor$ approaches $n-1$ from the left and $n$ from the right.

contentBlocks.result: The four examples fail different continuity conditions.
contentBlocks.verification: Changing a single point can repair only a finite removable discontinuity, not the pole or jump.

contentBlocks.title: Test the available side at an endpoint
contentBlocks.statement: $f$ is right-continuous at $a$ when $\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=f(a)$, and left-continuous when $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=f(a)$.
hypotheses: The point value is defined.
Approach only through domain values on the specified side.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Read the floor function at an integer
contentBlocks.strategy: Check domain and theorem hypotheses before concluding.

steps.label: Right
steps.text: For $n\le x<n+1$, $f(x)=n$, so the right limit equals $n=f(n)$.

steps.label: Left
steps.text: For $n-1\le x<n$, $f(x)=n-1$, so the left limit differs from $f(n)$.

contentBlocks.result: $f$ is right-continuous but not left-continuous at each integer.
contentBlocks.verification: The value at the integer is not interchangeable with the left approach.

contentBlocks.title: Check interior and included endpoints
contentBlocks.statement: $f$ is continuous on an interval when it is continuous at every interior point and, at each included endpoint, continuous from the side inside the interval.
hypotheses: Check all interior domain points.
Use right continuity at an included left endpoint and left continuity at an included right endpoint.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Verify the lecture closed-interval exercise
contentBlocks.strategy: Check domain and theorem hypotheses before concluding.

steps.label: Interior
steps.text: $1-x^2>0$ for $-1<x<1$, so polynomial, root, and difference continuity apply.

steps.label: Endpoints
steps.text: As $x\to-1^+$ or $x\to1^-$, $1-x^2\to0^+$ and the root tends to 0, matching $f(-1)=f(1)=2$.

contentBlocks.result: $f$ is continuous on $[-1,1]$.
contentBlocks.verification: No value is required outside the natural domain; only inward endpoint approaches count.

contentBlocks.title: Build continuous functions with eligible operations
contentBlocks.statement: If $f,g$ are continuous at $a$, then $f+g$, $f-g$, $cf$, and $fg$ are continuous there. The quotient $f/g$ is continuous at $a$ when $g(a)\ne0$.
hypotheses: Both functions are continuous at the point.
For a quotient, the denominator value is nonzero; on an interval it stays nonzero at every point used.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Use the source rational exercise only on its domain
contentBlocks.strategy: Check domain and theorem hypotheses before concluding.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.text: The numerator equals $-8+12-1=3$, so rational continuity gives the limit $3/11$.

contentBlocks.result: The limit is $3/11$.
contentBlocks.verification: At $x=5/3$ the denominator vanishes and this quotient theorem cannot be used.

contentBlocks.title: Use finite law proof for standard classes
contentBlocks.statement: Every polynomial is continuous on $\mathbb R$ by finite sums of constant multiples of powers. A rational function $P/Q$ is continuous wherever $Q\ne0$.
hypotheses: The polynomial has finitely many terms.
A rational function is evaluated only at a point where its denominator is nonzero.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Justify polynomial continuity before citing it
contentBlocks.strategy: Check domain and theorem hypotheses before concluding.
contentBlocks.setup: For $P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^n c_i x^i$ and any real $a$:

steps.label: Term limits
steps.text: $x^i\to a^i$ and $c_i x^i\to c_i a^i$ by finite limit laws.

steps.label: Finite sum
steps.text: $\lim_{x\to a}P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^n c_i a^i=P(a)$.

contentBlocks.result: Every polynomial is continuous at every real $a$.
contentBlocks.verification: This proves continuity, rather than assuming it from the graph. A rational quotient still needs $Q(a)\ne0$.

contentBlocks.title: Move continuity at zero to any angle
contentBlocks.statement: The radian limits $\sin h\to0$ and $\cos h\to1$ as $h\to0$, together with addition formulas, show that sine and cosine are continuous at every real $a$.
hypotheses: Use radian-angle limits at zero.
Write $x=a+h$ and let $h\to0$ in the addition formulas.
prerequisites: Trigonometric addition formulas and Lecture03 chord bounds

contentBlocks.title: Use the addition formulas at an arbitrary angle
contentBlocks.strategy: Translate the target angle to a small increment.
contentBlocks.setup: Check continuity of sine and cosine at a fixed real $a$.

steps.label: Sine
steps.text: $\sin(a+h)=\sin a\cos h+\cos a\sin h\to\sin a$ as $h\to0$.

steps.label: Cosine
steps.text: $\cos(a+h)=\cos a\cos h-\sin a\sin h\to\cos a$. The source zero-angle limits come from the earlier unit-circle bounds.

contentBlocks.result: Both functions are continuous at every real $a$.
contentBlocks.verification: The quotient $\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ still excludes angles where $\cos x=0$.

contentBlocks.title: Keep elementary-family domain restrictions
contentBlocks.statement: Polynomial, rational, power, algebraic, trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions are continuous where their real formulas are defined. In particular, $\tan x$ requires $\cos x\ne0$, $\sqrt{u}$ requires $u\ge0$, and $\log_b x$ requires $x>0$, $b>0$, and $b\ne1$.
hypotheses: Check the actual real domain of each family.
Apply quotient restrictions at every excluded trigonometric pole.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Locate tangent discontinuities
contentBlocks.strategy: Check domain and theorem hypotheses before concluding.
contentBlocks.setup: $\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ on its domain.

steps.label: Eligible points
steps.text: Sine and cosine are continuous; the quotient is continuous wherever $\cos x\ne0$.

steps.label: Excluded points
steps.text: $\cos x=0$ at odd multiples of $\pi/2$, so tangent is undefined there and has unbounded one-sided behavior.

contentBlocks.result: Tangent is continuous on each interval between consecutive odd half-turns.
contentBlocks.verification: The source list says $b>0$ for logarithms but omits $b\ne1$; the guide includes the required real logarithm-base restriction.

contentBlocks.title: Move a limit through a continuous outer function
contentBlocks.statement: If $g(x)\to b$ as $x\to a$ and $f$ is continuous at $b$, with nearby $g(x)$ in the domain of $f$, then $f(g(x))\to f(b)$.
hypotheses: The inner finite limit $b$ exists.
The outer function is continuous at $b$ and the composition is defined near $a$.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Prove the lecture root-law exercise
contentBlocks.strategy: Check domain and theorem hypotheses before concluding.

steps.label: Odd root
steps.text: For odd positive $n$, the real root is continuous at every real $b$; hence $\sqrt[n]{g(x)}\to\sqrt[n]b$.

steps.label: Even root
steps.text: For even $n$, the lecture assumes $b>0$, so $g(x)>0$ eventually and the root is continuous at $b$.

contentBlocks.result: The source root law follows under its stated even-root positivity condition.
contentBlocks.verification: At $b=0$ an even root may have a one-sided domain issue; the lecture theorem deliberately assumes $b>0$.

contentBlocks.title: Transfer pointwise continuity through a composition
contentBlocks.statement: If $g$ is continuous at $a$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(a)$, then $f\circ g$ is continuous at $a$ wherever the composition is defined.
hypotheses: The inner point value $g(a)$ exists.
The outer function is continuous at that value; each nearby inner output is in its domain.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Resolve every restriction in the lecture nested example
contentBlocks.strategy: Check domain and theorem hypotheses before concluding.

steps.label: Inner domain
steps.text: $x^2+7>0$ for all real $x$, so the square root is defined and continuous.

steps.label: Outer denominator
steps.text: $\sqrt{x^2+7}=4$ exactly when $x^2=9$, so exclude $x=\pm3$.

contentBlocks.result: $F$ is continuous on $(-\infty,-3)\cup(-3,3)\cup(3,\infty)$.
contentBlocks.verification: The source uses four composition stages; continuity does not fill the excluded denominator zeros.

contentBlocks.title: Fill a finite removable limit with its limit value
contentBlocks.statement: If $f$ is defined near but not at $a$ and $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ is finite, defining $F(a)=L$ and $F(x)=f(x)$ elsewhere makes $F$ continuous at $a$.
hypotheses: The deleted-domain limit exists and is finite.
The new point value is exactly that limit.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Solve the lecture extension exercise
contentBlocks.strategy: Check domain and theorem hypotheses before concluding.

steps.label: Cancel on the deleted domain
steps.text: Factor to get $f(x)=(x-3)(x+2)/[(x-3)(x+3)]=(x+2)/(x+3)$ on the original domain $x\ne\pm3$.

steps.label: Fill the point
steps.text: The replacement limit at 3 is $5/6$. Define $F(3)=5/6$ so the point value matches the limit.

contentBlocks.result: $F(3)=5/6$ gives a continuous extension at 3.
contentBlocks.verification: The full original domain also excludes $x=-3$; the extension only fills the removable point at 3. Any other value at 3 leaves discontinuity.

contentBlocks.title: Check the entire closed interval for IVT
contentBlocks.statement: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, and $N$ lies strictly between unequal $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, there is some $c\in(a,b)$ with $f(c)=N$. The theorem guarantees existence, not uniqueness.
hypotheses: Continuity holds at every interior point and inward at both endpoints.
The target is strictly between the unequal endpoint values.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Verify the lecture high-degree root bracket
contentBlocks.strategy: Check domain and theorem hypotheses before concluding.

steps.label: Continuity
steps.text: $p$ is a polynomial, so it is continuous on the entire closed interval; IVT with target 0 gives a root in $(5,6)$.

contentBlocks.result: At least one root lies in $(5,6)$.
contentBlocks.verification: The source page 34 prints $6^{200}-44$, but direct arithmetic gives $6^{200}+44$; either sign is positive. This guide records the corrected calculation.

contentBlocks.title: Bracket a target using robust bounds
contentBlocks.statement: To prove $f(c)=N$ for some interior $c$, find a closed interval of continuity whose endpoint values lie on opposite sides of $N$. Bounds on a varying term may establish those inequalities without exact evaluation.
hypotheses: The full bracket interval lies in the continuity domain.
One endpoint value is below and the other above the target.

contentBlocks.title: Solve the lecture sine-plus-square target exercise
contentBlocks.strategy: Check domain and theorem hypotheses before concluding.

steps.label: Upper bound
steps.text: At $x=32$, $f(32)=1024+10\sin32\ge1014>1000$ because $\sin32\ge-1$. The function is continuous on $[0,32]$.

contentBlocks.result: IVT gives at least one $c\in(0,32)$ with $f(c)=1000$.
contentBlocks.verification: No decimal approximation to $\sin32$ or uniqueness claim is needed.

contentBlocks.title: Use disjoint sign-change brackets to count distinct roots
contentBlocks.statement: For a continuous function, each pair of endpoints with opposite signs brackets at least one zero. Disjoint open brackets produce distinct zeros; a degree bound can separately limit how many there are.
hypotheses: Each closed bracket lies in a continuity interval.
Endpoint signs are strictly opposite and the open brackets are disjoint.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Solve the lecture three-solution exercise
contentBlocks.strategy: Check domain and theorem hypotheses before concluding.

steps.label: Apply IVT three times
steps.text: The disjoint intervals $(-4,-3)$, $(-3,1)$, and $(1,4)$ each contain a root. A nonzero cubic has at most three real roots.

contentBlocks.result: There are exactly three distinct roots in $[-4,4]$.
contentBlocks.verification: IVT alone gives at least three; the cubic degree supplies the upper bound.

exercises.outcome: Check value, limit, and equality.
exercises.prompt: Let $f(x)=x^2+\sqrt{9-x}$ for $x\le9$. Is $f$ continuous at 5?
exercises.hint: Check the domain, then take each component limit.
exercises.solution: The point 5 is in the domain. The sum, power, and root laws give $\lim_{x\to5}f(x)=25+\sqrt4=27=f(5)$, so all three conditions hold.
rubric: Verify the point lies in the domain.
Compute the finite limit with eligible laws.
Compare with the actual point value.

exercises.outcome: Classify a removable mismatch and a jump.
exercises.prompt: For $x\ne1$, let $u(x)=(x^2-1)/(x-1)$ and set $u(1)=9$. Also let $v(x)=0$ for $x<1$ and $v(x)=2$ for $x\ge1$. Classify discontinuity at 1 and say what a point-value change can repair.
exercises.hint: Find nearby left and right limits first.
exercises.solution: On $x\ne1$, $u=x+1\to2$ but $u(1)=9$, so the mismatch is removable by setting $u(1)=2$. For $v$, the left and right limits are 0 and 2, so it has a jump; changing only $v(1)$ cannot make the two-sided limit exist.
rubric: Compute limits on deleted domains.
Distinguish removable mismatch from jump.
State exactly which point-value repair works.

exercises.outcome: Decide continuity from each side.
exercises.prompt: Let $f(x)=2$ for $x<0$ and $f(x)=5$ for $x\ge0$. At 0, which one-sided continuity statements hold?
exercises.hint: Compare each one-sided limit with $f(0)$.
exercises.solution: Here $f(0)=5$. The right limit is 5, so $f$ is continuous from the right. The left limit is 2, so it is not continuous from the left or two-sided continuous.
rubric: Find the actual point value.
Check each one-sided limit against that value.
Do not claim two-sided continuity.

exercises.outcome: Use inward endpoint limits.
exercises.prompt: Is $g(x)=\sqrt{4-x^2}$ continuous on $[-2,2]$? Explain the endpoints.
exercises.hint: The square-root argument is nonnegative on this interval.
exercises.solution: The composition is continuous for every interior point. At $-2$, the right limit is 0 and equals $g(-2)$; at 2, the left limit is 0 and equals $g(2)$. Hence $g$ is continuous on the closed interval.
rubric: Check the natural domain.
Use the inward side at each endpoint.
Conclude continuity at every point of the interval.

exercises.outcome: Check quotient eligibility before substitution.
exercises.prompt: Where is $h(x)=(x^2+1)/(x-4)$ continuous, and what is $\lim_{x\to2}h(x)$?
exercises.hint: Use polynomial continuity and exclude the denominator zero.
exercises.solution: The numerator and denominator are polynomials, and $x-4\ne0$ exactly when $x\ne4$, so $h$ is continuous on $\mathbb R\setminus\{4\}$. At 2, the denominator is -2 and the limit is $(4+1)/(-2)=-5/2$.
rubric: State each component is continuous.
Exclude the denominator zero from the domain.
Evaluate at an eligible point.

exercises.outcome: Prove polynomial continuity and restrict a quotient.
exercises.prompt: Explain why $P(x)=2x^3-x+7$ is continuous everywhere and where $P(x)/(x^2-9)$ is continuous.
exercises.hint: Use finite sums and products, then solve the denominator restriction.
exercises.solution: Each monomial and constant is continuous, so their finite sum $P$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$. The quotient is continuous wherever $x^2-9\ne0$, namely $\mathbb R\setminus\{-3,3\}$.
rubric: Use finite limit-law closure for the polynomial.
Factor the denominator.
State the quotient domain precisely.

exercises.outcome: Check a trigonometric quotient and a logarithm domain.
exercises.prompt: Where are $q(x)=1/\cos x$ and $r(x)=\log_2(x-3)$ continuous?
exercises.hint: Find denominator zeros and logarithm input positivity.
exercises.solution: The secant quotient is continuous exactly where $\cos x\ne0$, excluding odd multiples of $\pi/2$. The logarithm is continuous where $x-3>0$, namely $(3,\infty)$; base 2 is positive and not 1.
rubric: Use the quotient nonzero condition.
Use the positive logarithm input and valid base.
State continuity only on each actual domain.

exercises.outcome: Check inner limit and outer continuity.
exercises.prompt: If $g(x)\to9$ and $g(x)$ is defined near $a$, justify $\sqrt{g(x)}\to3$. What changes if the claimed inner limit is $-1$?
exercises.hint: The square root is continuous at positive inputs.
exercises.solution: Because $g(x)\to9>0$, it is eventually positive; square root is continuous at 9, so the composite limit is $\sqrt9=3$. For inner limit -1, a real square root is not defined at the limiting input, so the real theorem cannot apply.
rubric: Check the finite inner limit.
Check outer continuity and nearby real domain.
Explain the negative-limit failure.

exercises.outcome: Find the domain of a nested continuous expression.
exercises.prompt: Where is $H(x)=1/(\sqrt{x^2+5}-3)$ continuous?
exercises.hint: Solve where the outer denominator vanishes.
exercises.solution: The square root is defined for every real x. Its value is 3 when $x^2+5=9$, so $x=\pm2$ are excluded. Every remaining stage is continuous, giving continuity on $\mathbb R\setminus\{-2,2\}$.
rubric: Check the inner root domain.
Solve the outer denominator restriction.
State the resulting continuity domain.

exercises.outcome: Choose the unique continuous point value.
exercises.prompt: Near $x=2$, let $f(x)=(x^2-4)/(x^2+x-6)$ on its domain $x\ne2,-3$. What value at 2 gives a continuous extension?
exercises.hint: Factor both polynomials before using the quotient law.
exercises.solution: For $x\ne2,-3$, $f(x)=(x+2)/(x+3)$ after canceling $x-2$. The replacement limit at 2 is $4/5$; assigning $F(2)=4/5$ makes the extension continuous there. The separate pole at $-3$ remains excluded, and no other point value at 2 matches the limit.
rubric: Cancel only where the original is defined.
Evaluate the finite replacement limit.
Assign exactly that value.

exercises.outcome: Reject a false IVT application across a pole.
exercises.prompt: For $f(x)=1/x$ on endpoints -1 and 1, does the endpoint sign change guarantee a zero? State the failed hypothesis.
exercises.hint: Inspect the entire closed interval, not just endpoints.
exercises.solution: Although $f(-1)=-1<0<f(1)=1$, $f$ is undefined at 0 and is not continuous on $[-1,1]$. IVT gives no guarantee; in fact $1/x$ never vanishes.
rubric: Check all points of the closed interval.
Identify the missing continuity hypothesis.
Distinguish theorem inapplicability from the actual absence of a zero.

exercises.outcome: Use a uniform oscillatory bound to bracket a target.
exercises.prompt: Show that $x^2+7\sin x=500$ for some $x\in(0,23)$.
exercises.hint: Bound sine below by -1 at the right endpoint.
exercises.solution: The function is continuous on $[0,23]$ and equals 0 at 0. At 23 it is $529+7\sin23\ge522>500$, so IVT gives some $c\in(0,23)$ with the target value.
rubric: Establish continuity on the full interval.
Use a bound valid for every sine value.
Conclude only existence in the interior.

exercises.outcome: Certify three distinct roots in disjoint brackets.
