exercises.prompt: Show that $q(x)=x^3-4x$ has three distinct zeros in $[-3,3]$ using three disjoint sign-change brackets, then identify why there cannot be more.
exercises.hint: Try endpoints -3, -1, 1, and 3, with 0 available to split the center bracket.
exercises.solution: The signs are $q(-3)=-15<0$, $q(-1)=3>0$, $q(1)=-3<0$, and $q(3)=15>0$, so IVT gives roots in $(-3,-1)$, $(-1,1)$, and $(1,3)$. The intervals are disjoint. Since a nonzero cubic has at most three real roots, these are exactly three.
rubric: Prove continuity on each bracket.
Compute alternating endpoint signs.
Use disjointness for distinctness and degree for the upper bound.

exercises.outcome: Compute a polynomial endpoint bracket and prove a root exists.
exercises.prompt: Show that $q(x)=x^9-3x^8+x-5$ has a zero strictly between 3 and 4. Do not assume it is unique.
exercises.hint: Factor the two leading terms as $x^8(x-3)$ when evaluating endpoints.
exercises.solution: The polynomial is continuous on $[3,4]$. At 3, $q(3)=3^8(3-3)+3-5=-2<0$. At 4, $q(4)=4^8(4-3)+4-5=4^8-1>0$. Thus IVT gives at least one $c\in(3,4)$ with $q(c)=0$; uniqueness does not follow.
rubric: State polynomial continuity on the closed bracket.
Compute both endpoint signs without unstable large-number subtraction.
Conclude interior existence without claiming uniqueness.

exercises.outcome: Use an addition formula and zero-angle limits to check translated trigonometric continuity.
exercises.prompt: Prove $\lim_{x\to a}\sin(x+a)=\sin(2a)$ for a fixed real $a$. Explain why the same argument does not make $\tan x$ continuous at $a=\pi/2$.
exercises.hint: Write $x=a+h$ and use $\sin(2a+h)=\sin(2a)\cos h+\cos(2a)\sin h$.
exercises.solution: As $h\to0$, $\cos h\to1$ and $\sin h\to0$, so the addition formula gives $\sin(2a+h)\to\sin(2a)$. For tangent at $\pi/2$, the denominator $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ and the function is undefined, so quotient continuity does not apply.
rubric: Translate to an increment tending to zero.
Apply both zero-angle limits to the addition formula.
Identify tangent’s excluded denominator zero.

sections.title: Derive before substituting
sections.text: For $f(x)=x^{2}$, the secant quotient at a is $((a+h)^{2}-a^{2})/h=2a+h$ for $h\ne 0$. The derivative is the limit 2a. On the graph, the secant line uses two distinct points; the tangent is the limiting line, not a zero-length secant.

sections.title: Two derivative functions
sections.text: A derivative at a is a number. The derivative function $f'$ assigns that number to every point where the limit exists. If $f$ measures metres and $x$ seconds, $f'$ measures metres per second; a second derivative measures metres per second squared.

exercise.prompt: Use the definition to differentiate $f(x)=1/x$ at $a\ne 0$.
exercise.hint: Combine the fractions before cancelling $h$; keep $a+h$ nonzero.
exercise.solution: The quotient is $(1/(a+h)-1/a)/h=-1/(a(a+h))$. As $h\to 0$ this tends to $-1/a^{2}$. Choose a neighborhood with $|h|<|a|/2$ to keep denominators nonzero.
rubric: Show the algebraic cancellation only for $h\ne 0$.
State $a\ne 0$ and control nearby denominators.

contentBlocks.title: Take the limit of nonzero secants
contentBlocks.statement: If $a$ is an interior domain point and the finite two-sided limit exists, $f\prime(a)=\lim_{h\to0}[f(a+h)-f(a)]/h$. Setting $x=a+h$ gives the equivalent $(f(x)-f(a))/(x-a)$ form.
hypotheses: The point value $f(a)$ and nearby values are defined.
Use nonzero increments on both sides; the quotient must converge to a finite real number.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Solve the lecture cubic derivative exercise
contentBlocks.strategy: Form the relevant limit and check domain before interpreting it.
contentBlocks.setup: Find the derivative of $f(x)=x^3-3x+2$ at a general real $a$.

steps.label: Divide and limit
steps.text: For $h\ne0$, the quotient is $3a^2+3ah+h^2-3$, whose limit is $3a^2-3$.

contentBlocks.result: $f\prime(a)=3a^2-3$.
contentBlocks.verification: The cancellation is valid only for $h\ne0$; plugging in $h=0$ before division is invalid.

contentBlocks.title: Interpret a finite derivative with the right units
contentBlocks.statement: A finite derivative $f\prime(a)$ is the slope of the tangent $y=f(a)+f\prime(a)(x-a)$ and the instantaneous rate of output change per input unit. For position $s(t)$ in metres, $s\prime(t)$ is velocity in metres per second.
hypotheses: The base point is in the domain and has a finite derivative.
A secant uses two distinct inputs; its limiting slope, not a single sampled secant, defines the rate.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Connect tangent slope and instantaneous velocity
contentBlocks.strategy: Form the relevant limit and check domain before interpreting it.
contentBlocks.setup: Use the guide-created position $s(t)=t^2$ metres with $t$ in seconds at $t=3$.

steps.label: Interpret
steps.text: The limit is $6$ m/s, and the tangent to the position graph at $(3,9)$ is $y=9+6(t-3)$.

contentBlocks.result: The instantaneous velocity is 6 m/s and the tangent slope is 6.
contentBlocks.verification: Pages 3–7 state the interpretations; this numeric example is guide-created, not a source example.

contentBlocks.title: Form a derivative function only where limits exist
contentBlocks.statement: The derivative function assigns $f\prime(x)=\lim_{h\to0}[f(x+h)-f(x)]/h$ at each point with a finite two-sided limit. Its domain may be smaller than the domain of $f$.
hypotheses: The original function is defined at and on both sides of each interior point.
Exclude points where the finite two-sided derivative limit fails.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Rationalize the source square-root quotient
contentBlocks.strategy: Form the relevant limit and check domain before interpreting it.
contentBlocks.setup: For $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ with domain $[0,\infty)$, find $f\prime$ and its domain.

steps.label: Interior
steps.text: For $x>0$ and $h\ne0$, rationalization gives $[\sqrt{x+h}-\sqrt{x}]/h=1/(\sqrt{x+h}+\sqrt{x})\to1/(2\sqrt{x})$.

steps.label: Boundary
steps.text: At 0 only $h>0$ is allowed and $\sqrt h/h=1/\sqrt h\to+\infty$; there is no finite two-sided derivative.

contentBlocks.result: $f\prime(x)=1/(2\sqrt{x})$ on $(0,\infty)$.
contentBlocks.verification: The original domain includes 0; the derivative domain does not. An unbounded one-sided slope is not a finite derivative.

contentBlocks.title: Read slope sign from a function graph
contentBlocks.statement: Where a derivative exists, $f\prime$ is positive at an increasing tangent, negative at a decreasing tangent, and zero at a horizontal tangent. The graph of $f\prime$ records these slopes point by point.
hypotheses: Use points where the finite derivative exists.
Read a tangent slope, not the height $f(x)$, when locating $f\prime(x)$.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Read the lecture paired graphs
contentBlocks.strategy: Form the relevant limit and check domain before interpreting it.
contentBlocks.setup: Physical page 10 marks horizontal tangents at $A,B,C$ and estimates the rising tangent at $P$ with slope $m\approx3/2$.

steps.label: Zeros
steps.text: The paired derivative graph crosses its horizontal axis at $A\prime,B\prime,C\prime$, matching the three zero tangent slopes.

steps.label: Positive slope
steps.text: At the marked input $x=5$, the source graph estimates the tangent slope as $m\approx3/2$, so the derivative graph places $P\prime$ near $(5,1.5)$.

contentBlocks.result: The derivative graph encodes slopes, not the original graph heights.
contentBlocks.verification: A positive function value does not imply a positive derivative; the source graph has positive heights while decreasing on some intervals.

contentBlocks.title: Translate derivative notations without treating them as a fraction
contentBlocks.statement: For $y=f(x)$, $f\prime(x)$, $y\prime$, $dy/dx$, and $Df(x)$ denote the same first derivative. The evaluation notation $[dy/dx]_{x=a}$ means $f\prime(a)$.
hypotheses: Specify the dependent and independent variables.
At this stage $dy/dx$ is derivative notation, not an ordinary ratio of two independent numbers.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Evaluate a derivative in Leibniz notation
contentBlocks.strategy: Form the relevant limit and check domain before interpreting it.
contentBlocks.setup: Guide-created example for page 13 notation: let $y=x^2$ and evaluate at $x=3$.

steps.label: Differentiate
steps.text: The definition gives $f\prime(x)=2x$.

steps.label: Translate
steps.text: $dy/dx=2x$ and $[dy/dx]_{x=3}=f\prime(3)=6$.

contentBlocks.result: Both notations report the same slope 6 at the same point.
contentBlocks.verification: $d^2y/dx^2$ later denotes a new derivative, not the square of $dy/dx$.

exercises.outcome: Derive a point derivative by cancellation before the limit.
exercises.prompt: Use the definition to find $g\prime(a)$ for $g(x)=x^3+2x$. Show the nonzero-increment quotient.
exercises.hint: Expand $(a+h)^3$ and cancel $g(a)$.
exercises.solution: For $h\ne0$, $[g(a+h)-g(a)]/h=3a^2+3ah+h^2+2$. Letting $h\to0$ gives $g\prime(a)=3a^2+2$.
rubric: Show the expansion and cancellation for nonzero $h$.
Take the two-sided finite limit.
State the derivative as a function of $a$.

exercises.outcome: Compute a finite rate and tangent equation.
exercises.prompt: For $s(t)=t^2+2t$ metres, find instantaneous velocity at $t=1$ and the tangent line to the position graph there from the definition.
exercises.hint: Simplify $[s(1+h)-s(1)]/h$ for nonzero $h$.
exercises.solution: The quotient is $(4h+h^2)/h=4+h$, so velocity is $4$ m/s. Since $s(1)=3$, the tangent is $y=3+4(t-1)$.
rubric: Use a nonzero displacement quotient.
Give velocity with units.
Use the point value and limiting slope in the tangent equation.

exercises.outcome: Distinguish a function domain from its derivative domain.
exercises.prompt: For $g(x)=\sqrt{x+2}$, find the domain of $g$ and derive $g\prime(x)$ where it exists. What happens at $x=-2$?
exercises.hint: Rationalize the quotient for $x>-2$; inspect the allowed side at the endpoint.
exercises.solution: The original domain is $[-2,\infty)$. For $x>-2$, $g\prime(x)=1/(2\sqrt{x+2})$. At $-2$, only right increments are allowed and the quotient is $1/\sqrt h\to+\infty$, so no finite derivative exists there; the derivative domain is $(-2,\infty)$.
rubric: State the original real domain.
Derive the interior quotient.
Exclude the endpoint for the correct reason.

exercises.outcome: Infer derivative signs and zeros from slope information.
exercises.prompt: A differentiable graph has horizontal tangents at $x=-1$ and $x=2$, decreases for $x<-1$, increases for $-1<x<2$, and decreases for $x>2$. State $f\prime$ at those inputs and its signs on the three intervals.
exercises.hint: Translate decreasing/increasing to slope signs.
exercises.solution: The derivative vanishes at $-1$ and $2$. Differentiability and decreasing/increasing behavior give nonpositive slopes on $(-\infty,-1)$, nonnegative slopes on $(-1,2)$, and nonpositive slopes on $(2,\infty)$. Strict signs are not guaranteed: a differentiable function can flatten at an isolated point while remaining monotone.
rubric: Use horizontal tangents for zero derivatives.
Give nonpositive, nonnegative, and nonpositive slopes on the three intervals; do not assume strict signs.
Do not infer derivative values from graph heights.

exercises.outcome: Translate first-derivative symbols at a fixed input.
exercises.prompt: If $y=3x^2$ and $x=2$, write $f\prime(x)$, $dy/dx$, and $[dy/dx]_{x=2}$.
exercises.hint: Differentiate from the definition or the known quadratic result, then evaluate.
exercises.solution: The derivative function is $f\prime(x)=6x$, so $dy/dx=6x$ and $[dy/dx]_{x=2}=f\prime(2)=12$. The symbols describe one operation and its value at 2.
rubric: State the derivative function.
Use equivalent notation consistently.
Evaluate only after forming the function.

contentBlocks.title: Use a finite derivative to prove continuity
contentBlocks.statement: If $f\prime(a)$ exists as a finite real limit, then $f(a+h)-f(a)=h\,[f(a+h)-f(a)]/h\to0$, so $f(x)\to f(a)$ as $x\to a$. The converse need not hold.
hypotheses: The point value and nearby difference quotient are defined.
The derivative limit is finite; multiplication by the increment then tends to zero.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Prove the one-way implication and test its converse
contentBlocks.strategy: Form the relevant limit and check domain before interpreting it.
contentBlocks.setup: Use the lecture theorem on pages 14–15 and its $|x|$ counterexample on page 19.

steps.label: Forward
steps.text: If the quotient tends to finite $f\prime(a)$, multiply by $h\to0$ to obtain $f(a+h)-f(a)\to0$.

steps.label: Converse failure
steps.text: $|x|\to0=|0|$ at zero, but $|h|/h$ tends to $-1$ from the left and 1 from the right.

contentBlocks.result: Differentiability implies continuity; continuity alone does not imply differentiability.
contentBlocks.verification: The reverse implication is refuted by a continuous function with unequal one-sided secant slopes.

contentBlocks.title: Use noncontinuity as a derivative obstruction
contentBlocks.statement: The contrapositive of differentiability implying continuity is: if $f$ is not continuous at $a$, then $f\prime(a)$ does not exist as a finite derivative.
hypotheses: Establish a genuine continuity failure at the target.
Do not infer differentiability merely from continuity elsewhere.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Diagnose a discontinuous piecewise function
contentBlocks.strategy: Form the relevant limit and check domain before interpreting it.
contentBlocks.setup: Use the guide-created jump $j(x)=0$ for $x<0$ and $j(x)=1$ for $x\ge0$ at zero.

steps.label: Continuity
steps.text: Left limit 0 differs from $j(0)=1$, so the two-sided limit and continuity fail.

steps.label: Derivative
steps.text: The theorem rules out a derivative at 0. Directly, $[j(h)-j(0)]/h=-1/h$ for $h<0$, so no finite two-sided quotient limit exists.

contentBlocks.result: $j$ is not differentiable at 0.
contentBlocks.verification: This is a guide-created contrast for the lecture page 20 obstruction, not a claimed source formula.

contentBlocks.title: Compare finite one-sided slopes at a corner
contentBlocks.statement: If the left and right difference quotients at $a$ have distinct finite limits, the two-sided derivative does not exist. A continuous point can still have this corner failure.
hypotheses: The function is defined at and near the point.
Calculate the one-sided quotient limits separately.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Recover the derivative domain of absolute value
contentBlocks.strategy: Form the relevant limit and check domain before interpreting it.
contentBlocks.setup: For $f(x)=|x|$, calculate all derivative cases as on lecture pages 16–19.

steps.label: Away from zero
steps.text: For $x>0$, nearby $|x|=x$ gives $f\prime(x)=1$; for $x<0$, nearby $|x|=-x$ gives $f\prime(x)=-1$.

steps.label: At zero
steps.text: $[f(h)-f(0)]/h=|h|/h$ has limits -1 and 1 from opposite sides.

contentBlocks.result: $f\prime(x)=-1$ for $x<0$, $1$ for $x>0$, and is undefined at 0.
contentBlocks.verification: $|x|$ remains continuous at zero, so the failure is a corner rather than a discontinuity.

contentBlocks.title: Separate infinite slope from a finite derivative
contentBlocks.statement: A vertical tangent may be described geometrically when secant slopes grow without bound to the same infinite direction. The usual derivative does not exist there because its defining limit must be finite.
hypotheses: Check the function is continuous at the point when claiming a geometric tangent.
Show both allowed side quotients have the asserted unbounded sign.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Solve the lecture signed-root vertical-tangent exercise
contentBlocks.strategy: Form the relevant limit and check domain before interpreting it.

steps.label: Continuity
steps.text: Both branches tend to 0 and $f(0)=0$.

steps.label: Slope
steps.text: For $h>0$, $f(h)/h=1/\sqrt h\to+\infty$; for $h<0$, $f(h)/h=(-\sqrt{-h})/h=1/\sqrt{-h}\to+\infty$.

contentBlocks.result: The graph has a vertical tangent at zero but no finite derivative there.
contentBlocks.verification: The point is continuous; unlike a corner, the one-sided slopes share the same unbounded direction.

contentBlocks.title: Interpret a second derivative as a rate of a rate
contentBlocks.statement: For position $s(t)$, velocity is $v(t)=s\prime(t)$ and acceleration is $a(t)=v\prime(t)=s\prime\prime(t)$ wherever those finite derivatives exist. Signed velocity uses displacement per unit time; acceleration uses change in velocity per unit time.
hypotheses: Differentiate position once for velocity and the velocity function once more for acceleration.
Keep time and position units distinct.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Compute velocity and acceleration separately
contentBlocks.strategy: Form the relevant limit and check domain before interpreting it.
contentBlocks.setup: Use the guide-created position $s(t)=t^3-3t^2+2$ metres, with time in seconds.

steps.label: Second rate
steps.text: $a(t)=v\prime(t)=6t-6$, so $a(1)=0$ metres per second squared.

contentBlocks.result: At one second the object moves in the negative direction despite zero instantaneous acceleration.
contentBlocks.verification: Page 26 states the physical interpretation; the polynomial motion example is guide-created.

contentBlocks.title: Iterate derivatives and read order notation
contentBlocks.statement: When successive finite derivatives exist, $f^{(3)}=(f\prime\prime)\prime$, $f^{(4)}=(f^{(3)})\prime$, and $f^{(n)}$ is the result of $n$ differentiations; $d^ny/dx^n$ denotes that operation.
hypotheses: Each lower-order derivative exists on a neighborhood sufficient to differentiate again.
The superscript $(n)$ is an order label, not an ordinary power of $f$.
contentBlocks.status: Source theorem or consequence used without proof

contentBlocks.title: Iterate the lecture higher-derivative notation
contentBlocks.strategy: Form the relevant limit and check domain before interpreting it.
contentBlocks.setup: For the lecture polynomial $f(x)=x^3-x$, continue after $f\prime\prime(x)=6x$.

steps.label: Fourth and later
steps.text: $f^{(4)}(x)=0$, and every further derivative is zero. Thus $f^{(4)}$ is not $[f(x)]^4$.

contentBlocks.result: The derivative orders are $3x^2-1$, $6x$, $6$, $0$, then zero.
contentBlocks.verification: The source page 27 states order notation; this worked continuation is guide-created from its page 25 polynomial.

contentBlocks.title: Differentiate the derivative by its own limit
contentBlocks.strategy: Find the first derivative, then form a fresh difference quotient for that derivative.
contentBlocks.setup: For $f(x)=x^3-x$, find $f''(x)$ from the definition, as in Lecture 06 Example 6.

steps.label: First derivative
steps.text: Expand $f(x+h)-f(x)$ and divide only for $h\ne0$.

steps.label: New quotient
steps.text: Apply the derivative definition to $f'$, rather than taking the old quotient's limit twice.

steps.label: Second limit
steps.text: Now let the nonzero increment tend to zero.

contentBlocks.result: $f''(x)=6x$ is the rate of change of $f'(x)$.
contentBlocks.verification: Both quotients are defined only for $h\ne0$; a second derivative exists here because $f'$ is differentiable everywhere.

supplementalBlocks.title: Higher derivatives track different rates
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Differentiate the position function successively; interpret each derivative with its own units.

steps.label: Velocity
steps.text: Differentiate position once.

steps.label: Acceleration
steps.text: Differentiate velocity, not position again by a new rule.

steps.label: At one second
steps.text: $v(1)=-3 m/s$ and $a(1)=0 m/s^{2}$. Zero acceleration at an instant does not mean zero velocity.

supplementalBlocks.result: At $t=1$, motion is in the negative direction at 3 $m/s$ while acceleration vanishes.
supplementalBlocks.verification: $a(t)$ changes sign at 1; it is not identically zero near that time.

exercises.outcome: Use the finite derivative implication and a converse counterexample.
exercises.prompt: Show that $g(x)=|x-2|$ is continuous at 2 but not differentiable there. Why can no function with a jump at a be differentiable at a?
exercises.hint: Compare $|h|/h$ from each side; use the contrapositive of the theorem.
exercises.solution: As $x\to2$, $g(x)\to0=g(2)$, so it is continuous. Its quotient at 2 is $|h|/h$, with left limit -1 and right limit 1, so no derivative exists. A jump breaks continuity, and differentiability would imply continuity, so a jump cannot be differentiable.
rubric: Prove continuity by a matching point limit.
Compare both secant-slope limits.
Apply the theorem only in its valid direction.

exercises.outcome: Rule out a derivative from a point-value mismatch.
exercises.prompt: For $x\ne1$, let $f(x)=x+1$ and assign $f(1)=7$. Is $f\prime(1)$ defined?
exercises.hint: Compare the nearby limit with the assigned value before forming a quotient.
exercises.solution: The nearby limit is 2 but $f(1)=7$, so $f$ is discontinuous at 1. By the contrapositive theorem it cannot be differentiable there. Indeed $[f(1+h)-7]/h=(h-5)/h$ has no finite two-sided limit.
rubric: Identify the continuity failure.
Invoke the correct contrapositive.
Optionally verify with the difference quotient.

exercises.outcome: Compute side slopes for a shifted corner.
exercises.prompt: Find the derivative domain of $f(x)=|x-3|$ and its derivative on each side.
exercises.hint: Set $u=x-3$ and inspect the quotient at $x=3$.
exercises.solution: For $x<3$ the local formula is $3-x$, giving derivative -1; for $x>3$ it is $x-3$, giving 1. At 3, the quotient is $|h|/h$, whose side limits disagree. Thus the derivative domain is $\mathbb R\setminus\{3\}$.
rubric: Derive each side slope on an open region.
Compare the two quotient limits at 3.
Give the derivative domain.

exercises.outcome: Certify a vertical tangent without assigning a finite derivative.
exercises.prompt: For $g(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$, decide continuity and differentiability at 0 and whether its graph has a vertical tangent.
exercises.hint: Compute $g(h)/h$ for positive and negative $h$.
exercises.solution: The cube root is continuous at 0. For either sign of nonzero $h$, $g(h)/h=1/|h|^{2/3}\to+\infty$. Thus the graph has a vertical tangent, but $g\prime(0)$ does not exist as a finite real number.
rubric: Check continuity at zero.
Analyze the quotient from both sides.
Distinguish geometric vertical tangent from finite derivative.

exercises.outcome: Interpret velocity and acceleration with distinct units.
exercises.prompt: A particle has $s(t)=t^3-6t^2+5$ metres for $t\ge0$. Find $v(2)$ and $a(2)$ and state whether it is at rest.
exercises.hint: Rest is decided by velocity, not acceleration.
exercises.solution: The velocity is $v(t)=3t^2-12t$, so $v(2)=-12$ m/s. Acceleration is $a(t)=6t-12$, so $a(2)=0$ metres per second squared. The particle is moving, not at rest.
rubric: Differentiate in the right order.
Keep the two units distinct.
Use velocity for rest.

exercises.outcome: Compute third and fourth derivatives as iterations.
exercises.prompt: For $p(x)=x^4-2x^2$, find $p\prime\prime$, $p^{(3)}$, and $p^{(4)}$ and distinguish $p^{(4)}$ from $[p(x)]^4$.
exercises.hint: Differentiate each previous derivative, not the original expression repeatedly by name alone.
exercises.solution: The derivatives are $p\prime=4x^3-4x$, $p\prime\prime=12x^2-4$, $p^{(3)}=24x$, and $p^{(4)}=24$. The fourth derivative is the constant 24, not the fourth power of $p$.
rubric: Show successive derivatives in order.
Use the order notation correctly.
Contrast derivative order with an ordinary power.

exercises.outcome: Compute a second derivative by taking the difference-quotient limit of the first derivative.
exercises.prompt: For $g(x)=x^3+2x^2$, first find $g'(x)$. Then use $\lim_{h\to0}(g'(x+h)-g'(x))/h$ to find $g''(x)$; show the quotient before taking its limit.
exercises.hint: After $g'(x)=3x^2+4x$, expand $g'(x+h)$ and cancel the matching terms before dividing by nonzero $h$.
rubric: Find the first derivative before forming the new quotient.
Show cancellation for $h\ne0$ before taking the limit.
Conclude $g''(x)=6x+4$, not $g'(x)$ again.

exercises.outcome: Compute and interpret first and second derivatives separately.
exercises.prompt: A particle has position $s(t)=t^4-4t^3$ metres for $t\ge0$. Find velocity and acceleration at $t=2$, and decide whether it is instantaneously at rest.
exercises.hint: Differentiate once for velocity and twice for acceleration; rest means velocity zero.
exercises.solution: $v(t)=4t^3-12t^2$, so $v(2)=32-48=-16 m/s$. $a(t)=12t^2-24t$, so $a(2)=0 m/s^{2}$. The particle is moving, not at rest.
rubric: Differentiate in the right order.
Keep units for each derivative.
Use velocity, not acceleration, to decide rest.

sections.title: A second derivative requires a new limit
sections.text: If $f'$ is differentiable at $x$, its derivative is $f''(x)=\lim_{h\to0}(f'(x+h)-f'(x))/h$. Existence of $f'(x)$ alone does not guarantee this second limit. The notation $d^2y/dx^2$ means differentiating $dy/dx$ once more, not squaring it.

sections.title: Three obstructions
sections.text: For $|x|$ at zero, the difference quotient is $-1$ from the left and 1 from the right: a corner. For $x^{1/3}$, its quotient at zero is $|h|^{-2/3}$, which has no finite limit: a vertical tangent does not supply a finite derivative. A discontinuity also prevents differentiability.

sections.title: Why differentiability implies continuity
sections.text: Write $f(a+h)-f(a)=h\cdot ((f(a+h)-f(a))/h)$. If the quotient has a finite limit, multiplying by $h\to 0$ gives an increment tending to zero. The converse fails, as $|x|$ demonstrates.

exercise.prompt: Is $f(x)=|x-2|$ differentiable at 2? State the one-sided quotients.
exercise.hint: Set $x=2+h$.
exercise.solution: The quotient $|h|/h$ equals $-1$ for $h<0$ and 1 for $h>0$. It has no two-sided limit, although $f$ is continuous at 2.
rubric: Compute the two signs.
Distinguish continuity from differentiability.

supplementalBlocks.title: Build the algebraic families
supplementalBlocks.note: Each displayed derivative requires the indicated derivatives to exist at the input. The quotient requires $g(x)\ne0$. Positive and negative integer powers have their own domains; for arbitrary real $s$, use $x^s$ only on $x>0$. Trigonometric formulas assume radian measure; reciprocal rules also require their denominators nonzero.

supplementalBlocks.title: Why both factors contribute
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Add and subtract one mixed product before dividing by the input increment.

steps.label: Split
steps.text: Insert $f(x+h)g(x)$ into the numerator.

steps.label: Limit
steps.text: Differentiability gives $f(x+h)\to f(x)$ and both quotient limits.
steps.usesHypothesis: Differentiability of both factors at $x$ implies continuity there.

supplementalBlocks.verification: For $f=g=x$, the result gives $(x^2)'=x+x=2x$, unlike $f'g'=1$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Trigonometric derivatives in radians
supplementalBlocks.tex: \begin{aligned}(\sin x)'&=\cos x &(\cos x)'&=-\sin x\\(\tan x)'&=\sec^2x &(\cot x)'&=-\csc^2x\\(\sec x)'&=\sec x\tan x &(\csc x)'&=-\csc x\cot x\end{aligned}
supplementalBlocks.note: All angles are measured in radians. $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are differentiable for every real $x$. $\tan x$ and $\sec x$ require $\cos x\ne0$; $\cot x$ and $\csc x$ require $\sin x\ne0$. The four quotient formulas follow from the quotient rule.

supplementalBlocks.title: Start with the difference quotient
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Substitute the function into the definition, simplify for nonzero h, then take the limit.

steps.label: Constant function
steps.text: For $f(x)=c$, the numerator is zero for every nonzero $h$.

steps.label: Identity function
steps.text: For $f(x)=x$, the increment in the output equals the increment $h$.

steps.label: Graph meaning
steps.text: The graph $y=c$ is horizontal, so its slope agrees with the derivative $0$.

supplementalBlocks.result: A constant has derivative 0; the identity function has derivative 1 at every real input.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The cancellations are performed only for $h\ne0$, then the limit $h\to0$ is taken.

supplementalBlocks.title: Expand a positive integer power
supplementalBlocks.statement: For real $a,b$ and positive integer $n$, $(a+b)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n}{k}a^k b^{n-k}$, where $\binom{n}{k}=n!/[k!(n-k)!]$ for $0\le k\le n$, and $0!=1$.
hypotheses: $a,b\in\mathbb R$.
$n$ is a positive integer.
$k$ is an integer with $0\le k\le n$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Find the terms linear in h
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Expand $(x+h)^n$ and separate the term proportional to $h$ from terms with higher powers of $h$.

steps.label: Expand
steps.text: Apply the binomial theorem to x+h.

steps.label: Subtract and divide
steps.text: The constant term cancels, and division by h lowers each remaining h power by one.

supplementalBlocks.result: The coefficient of h in the expansion is the term that survives the difference quotient limit.
supplementalBlocks.verification: As $h\to0$, the terms $3xh$ and $h^2$ vanish, leaving $3x^2$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Derive the positive integer power rule
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Expand by the binomial theorem, cancel $x^n$, divide by $h$, and let every remaining positive power of $h$ vanish.

steps.label: Form the difference quotient
steps.text: Subtract $x^n$ and divide by $h\ne0$.

steps.label: Take the limit
steps.text: For every $k\le n-2$, the remaining exponent $n-k-1$ is at least $1$, so each remainder term tends to zero.

steps.label: Handle n=1
steps.text: The case omitted from the expansion proof is direct.

supplementalBlocks.result: For every positive integer $n$ and every real $x$, $\frac{d}{dx}(x^n)=nx^{n-1}$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The $n=1$ case is checked separately; the proof for $n\ge2$ uses only terms whose powers of $h$ are positive.

supplementalBlocks.title: Differentiate a linear combination
supplementalBlocks.statement: If $f,g$ are differentiable at $a$ and $c$ is constant, then $(cf)'(a)=cf'(a)$, $(f+g)'(a)=f'(a)+g'(a)$, and $(f-g)'(a)=f'(a)-g'(a)$. Repeated use gives the rule for any finite sum.
hypotheses: $f$ and $g$ have finite two-sided derivatives at $a$.
$c$ is constant with respect to the input.
prerequisites: Limits of sums and constant multiples

supplementalBlocks.title: Split the difference quotient
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Factor constants and separate each summand before taking limits.
supplementalBlocks.setup: At a, let f and g be differentiable and let c be constant.

steps.label: Constant multiple
steps.text: Factor c out of the difference quotient.

steps.label: Sum
steps.text: Split the numerator into the two increments and use the sum limit law.

steps.label: Difference and finite sums
steps.text: Write $f-g=f+(-1)g$; induction extends the sum rule to any finite list.

supplementalBlocks.result: Constant multiples, sums, and differences differentiate term by term under the stated pointwise hypotheses.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The constant c is fixed; it is not a function of the input.

supplementalBlocks.title: Combine the linearity rules
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Differentiate each term, retaining its coefficient and sign.

steps.label: Differentiate term by term
steps.text: Use the constant multiple, power, identity, and constant rules.

steps.label: Check at a point
steps.text: Substitute $x=1$ only after obtaining the derivative function.

supplementalBlocks.result: $F\prime(x)=6x-2$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The constant term contributes zero; the negative coefficient remains negative.

supplementalBlocks.title: The product rule at one input
supplementalBlocks.statement: If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $a$, then $fg$ is differentiable at $a$ and $(fg)\prime(a)=f(a)g\prime(a)+g(a)f\prime(a)$.
hypotheses: $f$ and $g$ have finite two-sided derivatives at $a$, so both are continuous there.
supplementalBlocks.status: Complete proof follows in the product-rule-increments derivation

supplementalBlocks.title: The quotient rule needs a nonzero denominator
supplementalBlocks.statement: If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $a$ and $g(a)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is defined near $a$ and $(f/g)\prime(a)=[f\prime(a)g(a)-f(a)g\prime(a)]/[g(a)]^2$.
hypotheses: $f$ and $g$ have finite two-sided derivatives at $a$.
$g(a)\ne0$; continuity of $g$ then keeps $g$ nonzero on some neighborhood of $a$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Separate numerator and denominator changes
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Put the difference of quotients over a common denominator, then add and subtract $f(a)g(a)$.
supplementalBlocks.setup: Assume $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $a$ and $g(a)\ne0$. For sufficiently small $h$, $g(a+h)\ne0$ by continuity.

steps.label: Combine the quotients
steps.text: Use a common denominator before dividing by h.

steps.label: Insert the mixed product
steps.text: Add and subtract $f(a)g(a)$ in the numerator.

steps.label: Take the limit
steps.text: The denominator tends to $g(a)^2\ne0$, while the difference quotients tend to $f\prime(a)$ and $g\prime(a)$.

supplementalBlocks.result: The numerator order is $f\prime g-fg\prime$; the denominator is $g^2$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The condition $g(a)\ne0$ justifies the quotient near $a$ and the nonzero limiting denominator.

supplementalBlocks.title: Simplify before differentiating
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Compare the quotient-rule expansion with a factorization that cancels a common factor on the original domain.
supplementalBlocks.setup: For $y=(x^2-2x+4)/(x^3+8)$, the denominator is nonzero exactly when $x\ne-2$.

steps.label: Apply the quotient rule
steps.text: Differentiate the numerator and denominator in the correct order.

steps.label: Expand
steps.text: Collecting like terms gives the source's unsimplified result.

steps.label: Factor the sum of cubes
steps.text: Since $x^2-2x+4=(x-1)^2+3>0$, the only excluded input is $x=-2$; cancel on that original domain.

steps.label: Differentiate the simpler form
steps.text: Differentiate 1/(x+2) on its domain.

supplementalBlocks.result: The expanded quotient derivative equals $-1/(x+2)^2$ for $x\ne-2$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The expanded numerator is $-(x^2-2x+4)^2$, so cancellation agrees with the derivative of the simplified form.

supplementalBlocks.title: Negative integer powers exclude zero
hypotheses: $n$ is a positive integer.
$x\ne0$, the domain of $x^{-n}$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Rewrite a negative power as a quotient
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Apply the quotient rule to $1/x^n$.
supplementalBlocks.setup: For $x\ne0$, write $x^{-n}=1/x^n$, where $n$ is a positive integer.

steps.label: Apply the quotient rule
steps.text: The numerator derivative is zero and the denominator derivative is $nx^{n-1}$.

steps.label: Simplify the power
steps.text: Combine exponents only after using $x\ne0$.

supplementalBlocks.result: $\frac{d}{dx}(x^{-n})=-n x^{-n-1}$ for $x\ne0$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The point $x=0$ is excluded because the original negative power is undefined there.

supplementalBlocks.title: Use the general power rule on positive inputs
supplementalBlocks.statement: For every real $s$, $x^s$ is differentiable for $x>0$ and $\frac{d}{dx}(x^s)=sx^{s-1}$.
hypotheses: $s\in\mathbb R$.
$x>0$. This common domain makes $x^s$ real and differentiable for every real $s$.
supplementalBlocks.status: The source states the general rule without a domain; this guide supplies a safe domain for arbitrary real exponents.

supplementalBlocks.title: Read the square-root derivative as a power
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Write the root as a fractional power, then apply the real-power rule on $x>0$.
supplementalBlocks.result: The derivative is $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$ for $x>0$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: At $x=0$ the displayed derivative is not finite; the theorem\'s open positive domain avoids claiming it there.

supplementalBlocks.title: Turn a derivative into tangent and normal lines
supplementalBlocks.statement: At $P=(a,f(a))$, if $f\prime(a)=m$, the tangent line has slope $m$. If $m\ne0$, the normal line through $P$ has slope $-1/m$; if $m=0$, the normal is vertical.
hypotheses: $f$ is defined and differentiable at $a$.
The normal is the line through $P$ perpendicular to the tangent; the reciprocal-slope formula assumes $m\ne0$.
supplementalBlocks.status: The source works the nonzero-slope case; the horizontal-tangent exception is stated for completeness.

supplementalBlocks.title: Find both lines at the source point
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Differentiate the quotient, evaluate the slope, then use point-slope form and the perpendicular-slope relation.
supplementalBlocks.setup: Let $y=\sqrt{x}/(1+x^2)$, $x>0$. Find tangent and normal lines at $(1,1/2)$.

steps.label: Differentiate
steps.text: Use the quotient rule and $\frac{d}{dx}(\sqrt{x})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$.

steps.label: Evaluate the tangent slope
steps.text: Substitute $x=1$.

steps.label: Write the tangent
steps.text: Use the point (1,1/2) and slope -1/4.

steps.label: Write the normal
steps.text: The perpendicular slope is 4, the negative reciprocal of -1/4.

supplementalBlocks.result: The tangent is $y=-x/4+3/4$ and the normal is $y=4x-7/2$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Both pass through $(1,1/2)$; their slopes multiply to $(-1/4)(4)=-1$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Catch two tempting shortcuts
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Evaluate the correct rule and the tempting incorrect formula at the same input.
supplementalBlocks.setup: Let $p(x)=(x+1)(x+2)$ with factors $p_1=x+1,p_2=x+2$, and $q(x)=(x^2+1)/(x+2)$. Compare their derivatives at $x=1$.

steps.label: Product
steps.text: Differentiate both factors and keep each companion factor.

steps.label: Quotient
steps.text: Use numerator order f'g-fg' and square the denominator.

steps.label: Reject the reversed numerator
steps.text: Reversing the terms changes the sign; dividing the derivatives also gives a different value.

supplementalBlocks.result: The product and quotient shortcuts fail even at $x=1$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The correct quotient derivative is 4/9, not -4/9 or 2.

supplementalBlocks.title: Trigonometric derivative formulas use radians
supplementalBlocks.statement: The input $x$ to $\sin x$ and the other trigonometric functions is its radian measure. As $h\to0$, $\cos h\to1$, $\sin h\to0$, and the fundamental radian limit $\sin(h)/h\to1$.
hypotheses: $h$ is measured in radians.
The limit $\sin(h)/h\to1$ is the standard fundamental sine limit used by the source\'s derivative proof.
supplementalBlocks.status: The source states the angle convention and basic limits, then uses the sine limit in the next proof.

supplementalBlocks.title: A degree input contributes a scale factor
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Convert the numeric degree input to radians before applying the sine limit.
supplementalBlocks.setup: Let $S(d)=\sin(\pi d/180)$, where $d$ is a number of degrees.

steps.label: Use the derivative definition at zero
steps.text: Set $u=\pi h/180$ in the difference quotient.

steps.label: Apply the radian limit
steps.text: The standard limit is 1 only when its input is in radians.

supplementalBlocks.result: The derivative of the sine of a degree-valued input is not $1$ at zero; it is $\pi/180$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: This factor is exactly the degrees-to-radians conversion scale.

supplementalBlocks.title: Derive the sine rule from its difference quotient
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Use the sine addition formula, split the quotient into two limits, and apply the radian limits.
supplementalBlocks.setup: Fix $x\in\mathbb R$ and let $h\to0$ in radians.

steps.label: Expand the increment
steps.text: Apply the sine addition formula to expand the increment.

steps.label: Justify the cosine-difference limit
steps.text: For $h$ near zero, use $1-\cos(h)=\sin^2(h)/(1+\cos(h))$.

steps.label: Take the remaining limits
steps.text: Use $\sin(h)/h\to1$ and the previous limit.

supplementalBlocks.result: For every real $x$, $\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x)=\cos x$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The sine quotient limit requires radian input; the cosine-difference limit is shown rather than inferred from cos(h)→1 alone.

supplementalBlocks.title: Derive the cosine rule from its difference quotient
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Use the cosine addition formula and the same two radian limits.
supplementalBlocks.setup: Fix $x\in\mathbb R$ and let $h\to0$ in radians.

steps.label: Expand the increment
steps.text: Apply the cosine addition formula to expand the increment.

steps.label: Take the limits
steps.text: The cosine-difference quotient tends to zero and $\sin(h)/h$ tends to one.

supplementalBlocks.result: For every real $x$, $\frac{d}{dx}(\cos x)=-\sin x$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The negative sign comes from the minus sign in the cosine addition formula.

supplementalBlocks.title: Apply sine and cosine derivatives
supplementalBlocks.statement: For every $x\in\mathbb R$, $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are differentiable and $(\sin x)\prime=\cos x$, $(\cos x)\prime=-\sin x$, with $x$ measured in radians.
hypotheses: $x$ is real and interpreted as an angle in radians.
supplementalBlocks.status: Theorem used without proof; derivations are given in the preceding blocks

supplementalBlocks.title: Differentiate a linear combination of sine and cosine
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Apply the two derivative formulas and evaluate only after differentiating.

steps.label: Differentiate
steps.text: Use linearity and the sine/cosine rules.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.text: Substitute $x=\pi/3$.

supplementalBlocks.result: $F\prime(x)=3\cos(x)+2\sin(x)$, and $F\prime(\pi/3)=3/2+\sqrt{3}$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The minus sign in $-2\cos(x)$ combines with $(\cos x)\prime=-\sin x$ to make a positive sine term.

supplementalBlocks.title: Derive the tangent derivative
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Write tangent as sine over cosine, apply the quotient rule, then use the Pythagorean identity.
supplementalBlocks.setup: Where $\cos(x)\ne0$, $\tan(x)=\sin(x)/\cos(x)$. All angles are in radians.

steps.label: Apply the quotient rule
steps.text: Use the sine and cosine derivatives.
steps.equation: (\tan x)'=\frac{\cos x\cos x-\sin x(-\sin x)}{\cos^2 x}

steps.label: Simplify
steps.text: Apply $\sin^2(x)+\cos^2(x)=1$.

supplementalBlocks.result: $(\tan x)\prime=\sec^2(x)$ for $\cos(x)\ne0$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The excluded inputs are $x=\pi/2+k\pi$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Reciprocal trigonometric derivative formulas
supplementalBlocks.statement: Where defined, $(\sec x)\prime=\sec x\tan x$, $(\csc x)\prime=-\csc x\cot x$, and $(\cot x)\prime=-\csc^2x$.
hypotheses: Angles are measured in radians.
$\sec x$ requires $\cos x\ne0$.
$\csc x$ and $\cot x$ require $\sin x\ne0$.
supplementalBlocks.status: Derivations follow by the quotient rule

supplementalBlocks.title: Derive the remaining three trigonometric rules
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Rewrite sec and csc as reciprocals, and cot as a quotient; retain each function's domain.

steps.label: Secant
steps.text: Differentiate $1/\cos(x)$ where $\cos(x)\ne0$.
steps.equation: (\sec x)'=-\frac{(\cos x)'}{\cos^2 x}=\frac{\sin x}{\cos^2 x}=\sec x\tan x

steps.label: Cosecant
steps.text: Differentiate $1/\sin(x)$ where $\sin(x)\ne0$.
steps.equation: (\csc x)'=-\frac{(\sin x)'}{\sin^2 x}=-\frac{\cos x}{\sin^2 x}=-\csc x\cot x

steps.label: Cotangent
steps.text: Apply the quotient rule to $\cos(x)/\sin(x)$ where $\sin(x)\ne0$.

supplementalBlocks.result: The quotient rule gives all three reciprocal-trigonometric derivative formulas.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The denominators show why sec excludes zeros of cosine and csc/cot exclude zeros of sine.

supplementalBlocks.title: Differentiate constants and the identity
supplementalBlocks.statement: For every real $c$ and every real input $a$, the constant function $f(x)=c$ has $f'(a)=0$; the identity function $\operatorname{id}(x)=x$ has $\operatorname{id}'(a)=1$.
hypotheses: The constant function $f(x)=c$ and the identity function $\operatorname{id}(x)=x$ are defined on all of $\mathbb R$.
supplementalBlocks.status: Complete calculations follow in the worked example.

supplementalBlocks.title: Differentiate positive integer powers
supplementalBlocks.statement: For every positive integer $n$ and every real $x$, $\frac{d}{dx}(x^n)=nx^{n-1}$.
hypotheses: $n$ is a positive integer.
$x\in\mathbb R$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Keep the original quotient domain
supplementalBlocks.text: Factor numerator and denominator, record where the original denominator $g(x)\ne0$, then cancel common factors only on that original domain.

supplementalBlocks.title: Test tempting derivative shortcuts
supplementalBlocks.text: For products, retain each changing-factor contribution. For quotients, keep numerator order $f'g-fg'$ and denominator $g^2$; compare a proposed shortcut on concrete functions.

supplementalBlocks.title: Differentiate tangent on its domain
supplementalBlocks.statement: For radian inputs with $\cos x\ne0$, $\frac{d}{dx}(\tan x)=\sec^2x$. The excluded inputs are $x=\pi/2+k\pi$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$.
hypotheses: Angles are measured in radians.
$\cos x\ne0$, so $\tan x$ is defined.

exercises.outcome: Differentiate a product while retaining both changing contributions.
exercises.prompt: Differentiate $x^2\sin x$ and check the derivative at $x=\pi$ without graphing.
exercises.hint: Treat $x^2$ and $\sin x$ as separate factors.
exercises.solution: The derivative is $2x\sin x+x^2\cos x$. At $x=\pi$ it is $-\pi^2$ because $\sin\pi=0$ and $\cos\pi=-1$.
rubric: Differentiate both factors.
Keep the original companion factor in each term.
Evaluate the trig values in radians.

exercises.outcome: Derive a trigonometric derivative with its domain rather than memorizing it.
exercises.prompt: Derive $(\tan x)'=\sec^2x$ from $\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$. State its domain.
exercises.hint: Use the quotient rule and $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$.
exercises.solution: When $\cos x\ne0$, the quotient rule gives $(\cos^2x+\sin^2x)/\cos^2x=1/\cos^2x=\sec^2x$. The derivative is only defined where $x\ne\pi/2+k\pi$ for integer $k$.
rubric: Apply quotient numerator order correctly.
Use the Pythagorean identity.
Exclude zeros of cosine.

exercises.outcome: Find the derivative of a constant function from its definition.
exercises.prompt: Use the difference quotient to find the derivative of $f(x)=-7$ at an arbitrary input $a$.
exercises.hint: Write $f(a+h)-f(a)$ and simplify for $h\ne0$.
rubric: Substitute the same constant at $a+h$ and $a$.
Simplify before taking the limit; division by $h$ is for $h\ne0$.
State that the derivative is zero for every $a$.

exercises.outcome: Find the derivative of the identity function from its definition.
exercises.prompt: For $g(t)=t$, use the difference quotient at an arbitrary input $b$ to find $g\prime(b)$.
exercises.hint: The output increment is $(b+h)-b$.
exercises.solution: For $h\ne0$, $[g(b+h)-g(b)]/h=[(b+h)-b]/h=1$, hence $g\prime(b)=1$.
rubric: Substitute $b+h$ and $b$ into $g$.
Cancel $h$ only after noting $h\ne0$.
Take the limit and state the result.

exercises.outcome: Expand a positive integer power using binomial coefficients.
exercises.prompt: Expand $(t+h)^4$ and identify the term that is linear in $h$.
exercises.solution: $(t+h)^4=t^4+4t^3h+6t^2h^2+4th^3+h^4$. The term linear in $h$ is $4t^3h$.
rubric: Use the five coefficients $1,4,6,4,1$.
Pair each coefficient with the matching powers of $t$ and $h$.
Identify only $4t^3h$ as linear in $h.

exercises.outcome: Differentiate positive integer powers.
exercises.prompt: Differentiate $x^6$ and $r^4$ with respect to their displayed variables.
exercises.hint: Bring the positive integer exponent down and reduce it by one.
exercises.solution: $\frac{d}{dx}(x^6)=6x^5$ and $\frac{d}{dr}(r^4)=4r^3$.
rubric: Use the exponent as the coefficient.
Reduce each exponent by one.
Differentiate with respect to the displayed variable.

exercises.outcome: Differentiate a finite linear combination term by term.
exercises.prompt: Differentiate $Q(t)=-2t^3+5t^2-6t+9$.
exercises.hint: Keep every coefficient and sign, and differentiate the constant term to zero.
rubric: Apply the power rule to each nonconstant term.
Preserve the negative signs and coefficients.
Give zero contribution from the constant.

exercises.outcome: Apply the quotient rule and state where the quotient is defined.
exercises.prompt: Differentiate $R(t)=(t^2-3)/(t+1)$ and state its domain.
exercises.hint: Use numerator order $f\prime g-fg\prime$ and square the denominator.
rubric: Keep the numerator order $f\prime g-fg\prime$.
Square the denominator.
Exclude $t=-1$ from the original function\'s domain.

exercises.outcome: Factor a quotient before differentiating and preserve the original domain.
exercises.prompt: For $y=(x^2+2x+4)/(x^3-8)$, compare the quotient-rule derivative with simplifying first. State the domain.
exercises.solution: The original domain is $x\ne2$. Factoring gives $y=1/(x-2)$, so $y\prime=-1/(x-2)^2$. The quotient-rule numerator is $-(x^2+2x+4)^2$, yielding the same derivative after cancellation.
rubric: Factor the difference of cubes correctly.
State the original denominator restriction before cancelling.
Differentiate the simpler form and check agreement with the quotient rule.

exercises.outcome: Differentiate a negative integer power on its domain.
exercises.prompt: Differentiate $t^{-4}$ and state its domain.
exercises.hint: Use $n=4$ in the negative integer power rule.
rubric: Bring down $-4$.
Reduce the exponent by one.
Exclude $t=0$.

exercises.outcome: Apply the real power rule on positive inputs.
exercises.prompt: For $x>0$, differentiate $x^{-3/2}$ and state the domain used.
exercises.hint: Use $s=-3/2$ and retain the restriction $x>0$.
rubric: Use the exponent as the coefficient.
Subtract one from the exponent.
Keep $x>0$ as the stated domain for arbitrary real exponents.

exercises.outcome: Use a derivative to find tangent and normal lines at a point.
exercises.prompt: Find tangent and normal lines to $y=x^2/(x+1)$ at $x=1$.
exercises.hint: Find $y(1)$ and $y\prime(1)$; the normal slope is the negative reciprocal of the nonzero tangent slope.
exercises.solution: At $x=1$, $y=1/2$ and $y\prime=[2x(x+1)-x^2]/(x+1)^2=3/4$. Thus the tangent is $y-1/2=(3/4)(x-1)$, and the normal is $y-1/2=-(4/3)(x-1)$.
rubric: Evaluate the function and derivative at $x=1$.
Use the derivative as the tangent slope.
Use the negative reciprocal for the normal slope and retain the same point.

exercises.outcome: Reject common product- and quotient-rule shortcuts by checking values.
exercises.prompt: At $x=0$ compare $r(x)=(x+2)(x+4)$ with the shortcut $r_1\prime(0)r_2\prime(0)$. At $x=1$ compare $q(x)=(x^2+2)/(x+3)$ with $f\prime(1)/g\prime(1)$ and the reversed quotient numerator. Identify the invalid shortcuts.
exercises.hint: For $r$, let $r_1=x+2$ and $r_2=x+4$. For $q$, use $f=x^2+2$ and $g=x+3$.
exercises.solution: For $r$, $r\prime(0)=1\cdot4+2\cdot1=6$, while $r_1\prime(0)r_2\prime(0)=1$. For $q$ at $x=1$, $f=3$, $g=4$, $f\prime=2$ and $g\prime=1$, so $q\prime(1)=(2\cdot4-3\cdot1)/16=5/16$. Reversing the numerator gives $-5/16$, and $f\prime(1)/g\prime(1)=2$. The shortcuts are invalid.
rubric: Compute the product derivative with both changing contributions.
Use $f\prime g-fg\prime$ for the quotient.
Show the wrong formulas give different values.

exercises.outcome: Account for the radian conversion when an input is measured in degrees.
exercises.prompt: Let $S(d)=\sin(\pi d/180)$, where $d$ is measured in degrees. Use the definition and the radian sine limit to find $S\prime(30)$.
exercises.hint: Write $\alpha=\pi h/180$ in the difference quotient and expand $\sin(\pi/6+\alpha)-\sin(\pi/6)$.
exercises.solution: With $\alpha=\pi h/180$, the difference quotient is $[\sin(\pi/6)(\cos\alpha-1)+\cos(\pi/6)\sin\alpha]/h$. The first term tends to zero; the second tends to $(\pi/180)\cos(\pi/6)=\pi\sqrt3/360$.
rubric: Convert the degree increment $h$ to the radian increment $\alpha=\pi h/180$.
Use the sine addition identity in the difference quotient.
Retain the factor $\pi/180$.

exercises.outcome: Derive the sine derivative from its definition.
exercises.prompt: Use the derivative definition at $x=\pi/6$ to show the slope of $\sin x$ is $\cos(\pi/6)$.
exercises.hint: Use $\sin(x+h)=\sin x\cos h+\cos x\sin h$, plus $\sin h/h\to1$ and $(\cos h-1)/h\to0$.
exercises.solution: The quotient is $\sin(\pi/6)(\cos h-1)/h+\cos(\pi/6)\sin h/h$. Its limit is $0+\cos(\pi/6)=\sqrt3/2$.
rubric: Start from the difference quotient.
Apply the sine addition identity.
Use both radian limits and state the slope.

exercises.outcome: Derive the cosine derivative from its definition.
exercises.prompt: Use the derivative definition at $x=\pi/6$ to show the slope of $\cos x$ is $-\sin(\pi/6)$.
exercises.hint: Use $\cos(x+h)=\cos x\cos h-\sin x\sin h$.
exercises.solution: The quotient is $\cos(\pi/6)(\cos h-1)/h-\sin(\pi/6)\sin h/h$. Its limit is $0-\sin(\pi/6)=-1/2$.
rubric: Start from the difference quotient.
Use the cosine addition identity with its minus sign.
Apply the radian limits and state the slope.

exercises.outcome: Apply both sine and cosine derivative rules.
exercises.prompt: Differentiate $H(x)=2\cos x+\sin x$ and evaluate $H\prime(\pi/6)$.
exercises.hint: Use $(\cos x)\prime=-\sin x$ and $(\sin x)\prime=\cos x$.
exercises.solution: $H\prime(x)=-2\sin x+\cos x$, so $H\prime(\pi/6)=-1+\sqrt3/2$.
rubric: Apply the cosine derivative with the negative sign.
Apply the sine derivative.
Evaluate both trigonometric values at $\pi/6$.

exercises.outcome: Apply the tangent derivative where cosine is nonzero.
exercises.prompt: Differentiate $p(x)=2\tan x$ and state the full domain of $p$ and $p\prime$.
exercises.hint: Use $(\tan x)\prime=\sec^2x$ and exclude zeros of $\cos x$.
exercises.solution: $p\prime(x)=2\sec^2x$ on $x\ne\pi/2+k\pi$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$, the domain of $\tan x$.
rubric: Keep the constant factor $2$.
Use the tangent derivative formula.
Exclude every zero of cosine.

exercises.outcome: Apply the secant, cosecant, and cotangent derivative formulas with their domains.
exercises.prompt: Differentiate $J(x)=2\sec x-3\csc x+\cot x$ and state where the original function is defined.
exercises.hint: Use the three quotient-derived formulas; all three terms must be defined.
exercises.solution: $J\prime(x)=2\sec x\tan x+3\csc x\cot x-\csc^2x$. The domain excludes $\sin x=0$ and $\cos x=0$, so $x\ne k\pi/2$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$.
exercises.solutionTex: J'(x)=2\sec x\tan x+3\csc x\cot x-\csc^2x,\quad x\ne k\frac{\pi}{2},\ k\in\mathbb{Z}
rubric: Differentiate secant, cosecant, and cotangent with the correct signs.
Preserve the coefficient $-3$ when differentiating $-3\csc x$.
Exclude zeros of both sine and cosine.

sections.title: Choose the outer operation
sections.text: A product differentiates as $f'g+fg'$; a quotient as $(f'g-fg')/g^2$ where $g\ne0$. In radians, $(\sin x)'=\cos x$ and $(\cos x)'=-\sin x$. The expression $x\sin x$ is a product, so its derivative is $\sin x+x\cos x$.

sections.title: A quotient worked through
sections.text: For $q(x)=\sin x/x$ on $x\ne0$, numerator derivative is $\cos x$ and denominator derivative is $1$. Thus $q'(x)=(x\cos x-\sin x)/x^2$. The derivative formula has the same excluded zero; any extension at zero must be defined and differentiated separately.

sections.title: Keep power-rule domains distinct
sections.text: The positive integer rule applies to every real $x$. For positive integer $n$, $x^{-n}$ is defined only for $x\ne0$. For arbitrary real exponent $s$, this guide states $\frac{d}{dx}(x^s)=sx^{s-1}$ on $x>0$, where $x^s$ is real and differentiable for every real $s$.

sections.title: Simplify only on the original quotient domain
sections.text: Before applying the quotient rule, factor numerator and denominator when possible. Cancelling a common factor preserves the function only where the original denominator $g(x)\ne0$; state that domain before using the simpler form.

sections.title: Use radians for the trigonometric rules
sections.text: The standard sine limit and the derivative formulas use radian measure. A degree-valued input $d$ must be converted to radians, so $\sin(\pi d/180)$ has derivative $\pi/180$ at $d=0$, not $1$.

sections.title: A normal line is perpendicular to the tangent
sections.text: At a point where the tangent slope $m$ is nonzero, the normal slope is $-1/m$. If $m=0$, the normal is vertical; do not apply a reciprocal-slope formula that divides by zero.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $(x^2+1)/(x-1)$ and state its domain.
exercise.hint: Use the quotient rule with the numerator derivative 2x.
rubric: Preserve the minus sign before the entire numerator.
Square the denominator.
State $x\ne 1$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Keep the zero inner increment case
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Express both differentiability errors with coefficients that tend to zero; avoid dividing by the inner increment.

steps.label: Inner estimate
steps.text: $k=g'(a)h+o(h)$, so $k/h$ stays bounded as $h\to0$.

steps.label: Outer estimate
steps.text: $f(u+k)-f(u)=f'(u)k+k\eta(k)$, including $k=0$.

steps.label: Combine
steps.text: The error divided by $h$ is $f'(u)(k/h-g'(a))+\eta(k)(k/h)$; both terms tend to zero.

supplementalBlocks.result: $(f\circ g)'(a)=f'(g(a))g'(a)$, even when $g'(a)=0$ or some nonzero $h$ gives $k=0$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: No step divides by $k$, so a locally flat inner function causes no gap.

exercises.outcome: Apply the chain rule when the inner derivative vanishes without invalid division.
exercises.prompt: For $g(x)=x^2$ and differentiable $f$ at 0, find $(f\circ g)'(0)$. Explain why dividing a difference quotient by $g(h)-g(0)$ is unsafe as a general proof step.
exercises.hint: Use $f(k)=f(0)+f'(0)k+o(k)$ with $k=h^2$.
exercises.solution: The increment is $f(h^{2})-f(0)=f'(0)h^{2}+o(h^{2})$. Dividing by $h$ gives $f'(0)h+o(h)\to 0$. A general $g$ can have $g(a+h)=g(a)$ for some nonzero $h$, so dividing by its increment may be undefined; the remainder proof avoids it.
rubric: Use the outer differentiability at zero.
Obtain derivative zero.
Explain the zero-increment division issue.

sections.title: Make little-o explicit
sections.text: The notation $r(h)=o(h)$ means $r(h)/h\to 0$. Differentiability of $g$ at a says $g(a+h)=g(a)+g'(a)h+o(h)$. Differentiability of $f$ at $g(a)$ lets its output increment be $f'(g(a))$ times the inner increment plus a smaller error. Combining gives derivative $f'(g(a))g'(a)$; the argument also covers $g'(a)=0$.

sections.title: Layers and domains
sections.text: For $y=\sin(x^{2})$, the outer function is $\sin$ and the inner is $x^{2}$, giving $y'=\cos(x^{2})\cdot 2x$. For $\ln(1+x^{2})$, divide the inner derivative 2x by the positive inner value $1+x^{2}$. Naming layers prevents replacing $\cos(x^{2})$ by $\cos x$.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $(1+\sin x)^3$.
exercise.hint: Differentiate the cube with respect to its input, then multiply by the derivative of that input.
exercise.solution: The derivative is $3(1+\sin x)^2\cos x$, for every real $x$.
rubric: Keep the full inner expression in the squared factor.
Include the inner derivative.

sections.title: Differentiate an identity on a branch
sections.text: From $x^{2}+y^{2}=25$, assuming a differentiable local branch $y(x)$, differentiate to get $2x+2yy'=0$. Where $y\ne 0$, $y'=-x/y$. At $(3,4)$ the tangent slope is $-3/4$. At $y=0$ this formula cannot solve for $y'$; a different local graph may be needed.

sections.title: Rates carry units
sections.text: For a spherical balloon $V=(4\pi /3)r^{3}$, differentiation in time gives $dV/dt=4\pi r^{2} dr/dt$. If $dV/dt=12\pi cm^{3}/s$ at $r=3$ cm, then $dr/dt=1/3 cm/s$. Substitute the instantaneous radius after differentiating, since it varies in time.

exercise.prompt: A 5 $m$ ladder has foot distance $x$ and height $y$ with $x^2+y^2=25$. At $x=3$ $m$ its foot moves outward at 2 $m/s$. Find $dy/dt$.
exercise.hint: Use $y=4$ and differentiate with respect to time.
exercise.solution: 2x $dx/dt+2y dy/dt=0$, so $dy/dt=-(3/4)\cdot 2=-3/2 m/s$. The negative sign means the top descends.
rubric: Differentiate both changing quantities.
Use the positive height.
Interpret sign and units.

supplementalBlocks.title: Read the remainder notation precisely
items: $R(h)=O(h^2)$ means there are $C,\delta>0$ with $|R(h)|\le C|h|^2$ whenever $0<|h|<\delta$.
An $O(h^2)$ bound implies $o(|h|)$, but a bare $o(|h|)$ statement supplies no fixed quadratic constant.

supplementalBlocks.title: One exact error, two kinds of control
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Subtract the affine model and compare the residual with powers of the step.

steps.label: Model
steps.text: $f(1)=1$ and $f'(1)=2$, so the affine approximation is $1+2h$.

steps.label: Residual
steps.text: The exact remainder is $h^2$.

supplementalBlocks.verification: For a specified tolerance $\varepsilon$, $|h|<\sqrt\varepsilon$ ensures the exact error $h^2<\varepsilon$.

exercises.outcome: Distinguish a uniform quadratic bound from first-order asymptotic smallness.
exercises.prompt: For $R(h)=|h|^{3/2}$, decide whether $R(h)=o(|h|)$ and whether $R(h)=O(h^2)$ as $h\to0$. Justify each answer from a ratio or bound.
exercises.hint: Compare $R(h)/|h|$ and $R(h)/h^2$ separately.
exercises.solution: $R(h)/|h|=|h|^{1/2}\to 0$, so $R=o(|h|)$. But $R(h)/h^{2}=1/\sqrt{|h|}$ is unbounded near zero, so no fixed $C$ gives $R\leq C h^{2}$ on a deleted neighborhood; $R$ is not $O(h^{2})$.
rubric: Check each notation by its own definition.
Use a deleted neighborhood.
Do not infer a quadratic bound from little-o of first order.

sections.title: Linear versus affine
sections.text: The derivative is the linear map $h\mapsto f'(a)h$. The approximating graph $x\mapsto f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)$ is affine because it includes an offset. Differentiability guarantees error $o(|x-a|)$, not a chosen finite error bound for arbitrary steps.

sections.title: Approximate with an error bound
sections.text: For $\sqrt{x}$ near $a=4$, $L(x)=2+(x-4)/4$, so $L(4.1)=2.025$. Taylor’s theorem gives error at most $M(0.1)^{2}/2$ if $|f''|\leq M$ between 4 and 4.1. Here $|f''|=1/(4x^{3/2}) \leq 1/32$, so the error is at most 0.00015625. This finite bound is stronger than a bare little-o statement.

exercise.prompt: Use linearization at 0 to approximate $\sin(0.02)$. What extra information would certify an error bound?
exercise.hint: Use $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$; a remainder estimate needs derivative control.
exercise.solution: The linear estimate is 0.02. Taylor’s theorem and $|\sin''x|\leq 1$ give error at most $(0.02)^{2}/2=0.0002$. A sharper cubic bound is possible using additional vanishing terms.
rubric: Identify the base point.
Separate approximation from equality.
State the theorem and derivative bound for the error.

sections.title: A convention for candidates
sections.text: Here a critical point is an interior domain point where $f'=0$ or $f'$ does not exist; a stationary point has $f'=0$. Endpoints are checked separately. Fermat’s theorem says that a differentiable interior local extremum is stationary, not that every stationary point is an extremum.

sections.title: List, then compare
sections.text: For $f(x)=x^{3}-3x$ on $[-2,2]$, $f'=3x^{2}-3$ vanishes at $\pm 1$. Evaluate endpoints and stationary points: $f(-2)=-2$, $f(-1)=2$, $f(1)=-2$, $f(2)=2$. The global minimum is $-2$ at $-2$ and 1; the maximum is 2 at $-1$ and 2. Compactness and continuity ensure attainment.

exercise.prompt: Why does $f(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$ have a maximum even though $f'$ never vanishes?
exercise.hint: Is the maximum an interior point?
exercise.solution: The maximum is $f(1)=1$ at an endpoint. Fermat’s necessary condition applies only to differentiable interior extrema, so there is no contradiction.
rubric: State endpoint eligibility.
Do not infer no extrema from no stationary points.

contentBlocks.title: Rolle’s theorem
contentBlocks.statement: If $f(a)=f(b)$, some $c$ strictly between $a$ and $b$ has $f'(c)=0$.
hypotheses: $a<b$ and $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$.
$f$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$.

contentBlocks.title: Why Rolle’s point exists
contentBlocks.strategy: Use an attained extremum; equal endpoint values force a nonconstant function’s relevant extremum inside.

steps.label: Attainment
steps.text: Continuity on the closed interval gives both a maximum and a minimum.

steps.label: Interior point
steps.text: If $f$ is constant, choose any $c\in(a,b)$. Otherwise a value differs from $k$, so the maximum or minimum in that direction cannot occur at either endpoint.

steps.label: Stationarity
steps.text: At that interior extremum, Fermat’s theorem gives $f'(c)=0$.

contentBlocks.result: There is $c\in(a,b)$ with $f'(c)=0$.
contentBlocks.verification: The constant case also has derivative zero at every interior point.

contentBlocks.title: Mean value theorem
contentBlocks.statement: Some $c\in(a,b)$ satisfies $f'(c)=(f(b)-f(a))/(b-a)$.
hypotheses: $a<b$ and $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$.
$f$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$.

contentBlocks.title: Subtract the secant
contentBlocks.strategy: Make an equal-endpoint function and apply Rolle’s theorem.

steps.label: Endpoint check
steps.text: $g(a)=g(b)=0$ by the definition of $m$.

steps.label: Apply Rolle
steps.text: $g$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, so $g'(c)=0$ for some interior $c$.
steps.usesHypothesis: Both regularity hypotheses on $f$; subtracting a linear function preserves them.

steps.label: Recover the slope
steps.text: Since $g'(c)=f'(c)-m$, its vanishing gives the required secant slope.

contentBlocks.result: $f'(c)=(f(b)-f(a))/(b-a)$ for some $a<c<b$.
contentBlocks.verification: When $f(a)=f(b)$, the formula reduces to Rolle’s zero-slope conclusion.

contentBlocks.title: Locate the matching tangent
contentBlocks.strategy: Compute the secant slope, then solve the derivative equation within the interval.

steps.label: Eligibility
steps.text: A polynomial is continuous and differentiable on the required intervals; $b>0$ makes this a nondegenerate interval.

steps.label: Secant
steps.text: The average slope is $b$.

steps.label: Tangent
steps.text: Solve $2c=b$, giving $c=b/2$.

exercises.outcome: Use the mean value theorem to prove a global consequence from local slopes.
exercises.prompt: Let $f$ be continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'(x)=0$ throughout $(a,b)$. Prove $f$ is constant on $[a,b]$.
exercises.hint: Choose arbitrary $u<v$ in the interval. Apply the theorem on $[u,v]$.
exercises.solution: For any $u<v$ in $[a,b]$, MVT gives $c\in(u,v)$ with $(f(v)-f(u))/(v-u)=f'(c)=0$. Thus $f(v)=f(u)$. Since the pair was arbitrary, $f$ is constant.
rubric: Apply MVT to arbitrary points, not only the original endpoints.
State continuity and differentiability on the chosen subinterval.
Conclude equality of all values.

sections.title: Rolle’s theorem supplies the bridge
sections.text: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f(a)=f(b)$, extrema are attained. If $f$ is constant, any interior point has derivative zero. Otherwise a value differs from the common endpoint value, so a maximum or minimum occurs inside; Fermat gives derivative zero there.

sections.title: Subtract the secant
sections.text: Set $g(x)=f(x)-f(a)-m(x-a)$, where $m=(f(b)-f(a))/(b-a)$. Then $g(a)=g(b)=0$. Rolle provides $c$ with $g'(c)=0$, hence $f'(c)=m$. For $f(x)=x^{2}$ on $[1,3]$, $m=4$ and $c=2$.

exercise.prompt: Why can the mean value theorem not be used for $|x|$ on $[-1,1]$?
exercise.hint: Check differentiability at the interior junction.
exercise.solution: The endpoint slope is zero, but $|x|$ is not differentiable at zero and its derivative elsewhere is $\pm 1$. The missing differentiability hypothesis prevents the claimed conclusion.
rubric: Name the failed hypothesis and its location.
Compute the secant and available derivatives.

sections.title: Continuity is indispensable
sections.text: The derivative signs constrain nearby motion but do not fix a separately assigned point height. The example $f(x)=-|x|$ for $x\ne 0$ with $f(0)=-1$ has the positive-to-negative derivative pattern and nevertheless a strict local minimum at zero.

sections.title: Zero second derivative gives no verdict
sections.text: At zero, $x^{4}$ has a strict minimum, $-x^{4}$ a strict maximum, and $x^{3}$ neither, although all three have first and second derivatives zero there. Check derivative signs or the original value comparison. An inflection point requires a change of concavity, not merely $f''=0$.

exercise.prompt: Classify $x^4$ at zero without using an inconclusive second-derivative test.
exercise.hint: Compare $f(x)$ with $f(0)$ for nonzero $x$.
exercise.solution: For $x\ne 0$, $x^{4}>0=f(0)$, so zero is a strict global and local minimum. Equivalently $f'=4x^{3}$ changes from negative to positive.
rubric: Identify why the second-derivative test is inconclusive.
Supply a direct inequality or valid sign test.

sections.title: Separate the two tails
sections.text: For rational functions, divide by the highest denominator power separately as $x\to +\infty$ and $x\to -\infty$. For $\sqrt{x^{2}+1}/x$, factoring produces $|x|/x$ times $\sqrt{1+1/x^{2}}$, giving limits 1 and $-1$. Replacing $\sqrt{x^{2}}$ by $x$ would lose the negative tail.

sections.title: A sketch is an assembled argument
sections.text: For $f(x)=x+1/x$, domain excludes zero. Its slant asymptote is $y=x$ because $f(x)-x\to 0$ at both infinities. Derivative $1-1/x^{2}$ is positive for $|x|>1$ and negative for $0<|x|<1$; stationary points are $-1$ and 1. Add the separate vertical behavior at zero before drawing connected pieces.

exercise.prompt: Find the slant asymptote of $(x^2+1)/(x-1)$.
exercise.hint: Perform polynomial division.
exercise.solution: $(x^{2}+1)/(x-1)=x+1+2/(x-1)$. The remainder tends to zero at either infinity, so $y=x+1$ is the slant asymptote; $x=1$ remains excluded.
rubric: Show the vanishing difference.
Keep the finite-domain restriction separate.

sections.title: Model the feasible set
sections.text: A rectangle with perimeter 20 has $y=10-x$ and area $A=x(10-x)$. Positive side lengths require $0<x<10$; including degenerate rectangles closes the set to $[0,10]$. Differentiate A to get $10-2x$, whose zero is $x=5$. Then $y=5$ and $A=25$.

sections.title: Justify a global answer
sections.text: The identity $A=25-(x-5)^{2}$ proves $A\leq 25$ throughout the feasible set. This proves global optimality directly, whereas a positive-to-negative sign change by itself describes local behavior. Check units: perimeter in metres gives area in square metres.

exercise.prompt: Find the largest area rectangle with perimeter $P>0$.
exercise.hint: Eliminate one side and complete the square.
exercise.solution: With $y=P/2-x$, $A=x(P/2-x)=P^{2}/16-(x-P/4)^{2}$. Its maximum $P^{2}/16$ occurs at $x=y=P/4$, within the positive feasible interval.
rubric: State positivity and the feasible interval.
Prove global optimality.
Retain units and parameter dependence.

sections.title: Derive the update
sections.text: The tangent at $x_n$ has equation $y=f(x_{n})+f'(x_{n})(x-x_{n})$. Setting $y=0$ gives $x_{n+1}=x_{n}-f(x_{n})/f'(x_{n})$, provided the derivative is nonzero. It finds a tangent intercept, not an exact root of the original curve.

sections.title: Failure deserves an example
sections.text: For $f(x)=x^{3}-2x+2$, starting at 0 gives 1 and starting at 1 gives 0, so Newton cycles. For $x^{2}-2$, starting at zero is undefined because $f'(0)=0$. A small step alone is not proof of a root; check the residual and the domain, and use a bracket when available.

exercise.prompt: Perform two Newton steps for $x^2-2$ from $x_0=1$.
exercise.solution: $x_{1}=3/2$ and $x_{2}=17/12$. The residual at the second iterate is $(17/12)^{2}-2=1/144$; it is an approximation, not an exact root.
rubric: Calculate both steps.
Check the residual.
Avoid claiming universal convergence.

sections.title: Why the constant is the only freedom
sections.text: If $F'=G'$ on an interval, then $(F-G)'=0$. Applying MVT between any two points gives equal values of $F-G$. Thus $F-G$ is constant on that interval. On a disconnected domain the constants may differ between components.

sections.title: Use initial data
sections.text: If velocity is $v(t)=3t^{2}-2$ and $s(0)=5$, integrating gives $s(t)=t^{3}-2t+C$. The initial value sets $C=5$. Differentiation recovers the velocity and checks the answer; the constant carries position units.

exercise.prompt: Find every antiderivative of $1/x$ on $\mathbb R$ excluding zero.
exercise.hint: Treat the negative and positive intervals separately.
exercise.solution: The answer is ${\ln|x|+C_-}$ for $x<0$ and ${\ln|x|+C_+}$ for $x>0$, with independent constants. No interval in this domain connects the two sides.
rubric: Use $\ln|x|$, not $\ln x$ on negative inputs.
Allow separate constants on disconnected components.

contentBlocks.title: Existence of an inverse
contentBlocks.statement: A continuous strictly monotone function on an interval has an inverse on its range.
hypotheses: The domain is an interval.
$f$ is continuous and strictly monotone on it.
prerequisites: Continuity and the intermediate value theorem

contentBlocks.title: Local inverse derivative theorem
contentBlocks.statement: Near $a$, the inverse exists and is differentiable near $f(a)$; at a corresponding input, $(f^{-1})'(f(a))=1/f'(a)$.
hypotheses: $f$ is continuously differentiable near $a$.
Use a one-to-one local branch.

contentBlocks.title: Differentiate after existence is known
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the inverse identity only after the theorem supplies a differentiable inverse.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $y=f(x)$ on the local branch, so $x=f^{-1}(y)$.

steps.label: Identity
steps.text: On that branch $f(f^{-1}(y))=y$.

steps.label: Chain rule
steps.text: Differentiate the identity where the inverse is differentiable.
steps.usesHypothesis: The imported local inverse derivative theorem; this calculation does not prove existence.

steps.label: Divide
steps.text: The derivative at the corresponding input is nonzero, so division is valid.

contentBlocks.verification: For $f(x)=x^3$, $f'(0)=0$ and its inverse cube root has no finite derivative at zero; the hypothesis matters.

contentBlocks.title: Differentiate an inverse at an output
contentBlocks.strategy: Find the input first, check the theorem’s conditions, then take the reciprocal slope.

steps.label: Eligibility
steps.text: $f'(x)=3x^2+1>0$ everywhere, so $f$ is strictly increasing and the derivative is nonzero.

steps.label: Reciprocal
steps.text: $f'(1)=4$; the inverse slope at output 2 is its reciprocal.

contentBlocks.verification: The reciprocal is evaluated at input 1, not at output 2.

exercises.outcome: Choose an inverse branch before using the derivative formula.
exercises.prompt: For $f(x)=x^2$ on all real numbers, a student writes $(f^{-1})'(4)=1/4$. Explain the problem. Give the inverse derivative at 4 on each monotone branch.
exercises.hint: One output has two inputs. Restrict the domain to $[0,\infty)$ or $(-\infty,0]$ first.
exercises.solution: There is no inverse function on all real inputs: 4 comes from both 2 and $-2$. On the nonnegative branch the inverse is $\sqrt{y}$, with derivative $1/(2\sqrt4)=1/4$. On the nonpositive branch the inverse is $-\sqrt{y}$, with derivative $-1/4$ at 4.
rubric: Identify the lack of injectivity on the original domain.
Name each branch and its range.
Keep the negative branch’s derivative sign.

sections.title: Existence precedes the derivative
sections.text: A continuous strictly monotone function on an interval has an inverse on its range. A sufficient local differentiability theorem assumes $f$ is continuously differentiable near a and $f'(a)\ne 0$; then its local inverse is differentiable near $f(a)$. Only after this theorem may differentiating $f(f^{-1}(y))=y$ establish $(f^{-1})'(y)=1/f'(f^{-1}(y))$.

sections.title: Zero derivative is a warning
sections.text: The inverse of $x^{3}$ is the cube root. Although $x^{3}$ is one-to-one, its derivative at zero vanishes and the inverse has no finite derivative there. For $x^{2}$, choose a branch such as $[0,\infty )$ before naming $\sqrt{x}$ as its inverse.

exercise.prompt: For $f(x)=x^3+x$, find the derivative of its inverse at $y=2$.
exercise.hint: Find the input mapped to 2, then evaluate $f'$ there.
exercise.solution: $f(1)=2$ and $f'(1)=3+1=4$, so $(f^{-1})'(2)=1/4$. Since $f'=3x^{2}+1>0$, the inverse is well-defined and differentiable.
rubric: Evaluate at the inverse input, not at $y$ directly.
Check the derivative is nonzero.

sections.title: A definition must have a foundation
sections.text: One rigorous route defines $\ln x$ as the integral from $1$ to $x$ of $1/t$ for $x>0$, then uses the fundamental theorem to obtain derivative $1/x$. Its inverse is $\exp$; the inverse derivative theorem yields $\exp'=\exp$. If integration has not been developed yet, these facts are imported theorems.

sections.title: Logarithmic differentiation
sections.text: For $y=x^{x}$ on $x>0$, take $\ln y=x\ln x$. Differentiate to obtain $y'/y=\ln x+1$, hence $y'=x^{x}(\ln x+1)$. The positive domain permits logarithms; this argument does not define a real differentiable $x^x$ on all negative inputs.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $\ln(x^2-1)$ over its real domain.
exercise.hint: First require $x^{2}-1>0$.
exercise.solution: The domain is $(-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty )$. The derivative is $2x/(x^{2}-1)$ on that domain.
rubric: Solve the strict domain inequality.
Include the inner derivative.

contentBlocks.title: Cauchy’s mean value theorem (imported)
contentBlocks.statement: There is $c\in(a,b)$ such that $(f(b)-f(a))g'(c)=(g(b)-g(a))f'(c)$.
hypotheses: $f$ and $g$ are continuous on $[a,b]$.
$f$ and $g$ are differentiable on $(a,b)$.

supplementalBlocks.title: A one-sided $0/0$ rule
supplementalBlocks.statement: If $f/g$ has $0/0$ form at $a$ and $f'(x)/g'(x)\to L$, then $f(x)/g(x)\to L$ from the same side under the listed conditions.
hypotheses: $f$ and $g$ are continuous to $a$ from that side, with $f(a)=g(a)=0$.
$f$ and $g$ are differentiable on a deleted one-sided interval.
$g'(x)\ne0$ there and the derivative ratio has a finite or signed infinite limit $L$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Where Cauchy’s theorem enters
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Compare each nearby point with the endpoint at which both functions vanish.
supplementalBlocks.setup: For $x$ on the chosen side of $a$, apply Cauchy’s mean value theorem to $f,g$ on the interval between $a$ and $x$.

steps.label: Intermediate point
steps.text: There is $c_x$ between $a$ and $x$ with $f(x)g'(c_x)=g(x)f'(c_x)$.
steps.usesHypothesis: Continuity up to the endpoint and differentiability inside; both endpoint values are zero.

steps.label: Divide
steps.text:
$g'(c_x)
e0$; Cauchy’s relation and the mean value theorem for $g$ make $g(x)
e0$ for $x
e a$.

steps.label: Limit
