steps.text: As $x\to a$, $c_x\to a$, so the derivative-ratio limit passes to the original quotient.

supplementalBlocks.result: $f(x)/g(x)\to L$ from the chosen side.
supplementalBlocks.verification: This proves the endpoint $0/0$ case; an $\infty/\infty$ case needs a separate argument rather than setting infinite endpoint values.

supplementalBlocks.title: A one-sided $\infty/\infty$ version (imported)
supplementalBlocks.statement: If $|f(x)|,|g(x)|\to\infty$ and $f'(x)/g'(x)\to L$ for finite $L$, then $f(x)/g(x)\to L$ under the listed conditions.
hypotheses: $f,g$ are differentiable on a one-sided interval approaching the endpoint.
$g'(x)\ne0$ there, and $|g(x)|\to\infty$.
The derivative ratio tends to a finite $L$.
prerequisites: Cauchy’s mean value theorem plus a fixed interior comparison point

supplementalBlocks.title: Convert a product before using the rule
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Identify the indeterminate form, rewrite as a quotient, then check the new quotient.

steps.label: Form
steps.text: $x\to0^+$ and $\ln x\to-\infty$, so the original expression is a product, not an eligible quotient.

steps.label: Convert
steps.text: $x\ln x=\ln x/(1/x)$ has magnitude $\infty /\infty$; both functions are differentiable for $x>0$, and the denominator derivative is nonzero.

steps.label: Derivative ratio
steps.text: The ratio of derivatives tends to zero.

supplementalBlocks.result: $x\ln x\to0$ as $x\to0^+$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The quotient rule here concerns limits of ratios, not equality between the original quotient and its derivative quotient at each $x$.

exercises.outcome: Classify eligible, convertible, and ineligible expressions before applying L’Hôpital’s rule.
exercises.prompt: As $x\to0^+$, classify $(e^x-1)/x$, $x^x$, and $(x+1)/x$ as directly eligible, convertible, or ineligible for $L$’$H$ôpital. Evaluate $x^x$ using a justified conversion.
exercises.hint: Take a logarithm of the positive power, then rewrite $x\ln x$ as a quotient.
exercises.solution: $(e^x-1)/x$ is direct $0/0$. The positive power $x^x$ is $0^0$ and first requires $\ln(x^x)=x\ln x=\ln x/(1/x)$, an $\infty/\infty$ quotient. Its derivative ratio is $-x\to0$, so $\ln(x^x)\to0$ and $x^x\to1$. $(x+1)/x$ has numerator approaching 1 and denominator approaching 0, so neither rule applies; it diverges to $+\infty$ from the right.
rubric: Check the form of each original expression.
Use logarithms only for the positive power.
Check differentiability and nonzero denominator derivative after conversion.
Reject the ineligible nonindeterminate quotient.

sections.title: State a usable version
sections.text: For a $0/0$ quotient near a, assume $f$,$g$ are differentiable on a punctured one-sided interval, $g$ and $g'$ are nonzero there, both $f$ and $g$ tend to zero, and $f'$/$g'$ tends to $L$ (finite or infinite). Then $f/g$ tends to $L$. An $\infty/\infty$ version has its own hypotheses. The justification imports Cauchy’s mean value theorem, a two-function extension of MVT.

sections.title: Normalize before applying
sections.text: A product $x\ln x$ as $x\to0^+$ is not itself a quotient. Rewrite it as $\ln x/(1/x)$, an $\infty/\infty$ form. Differentiating numerator and denominator gives $(1/x)/(-1/x^2)=-x\to0$. By contrast, differentiating numerator and denominator of $(x+1)/x$ near zero without checking form would incorrectly discard its infinite behavior.

exercise.prompt: Find $\lim_{x\to0}(e^x-1-x)/x^2$, checking the form at each step.
exercise.hint: The first derivative quotient is $(e^x-1)/(2x)$.
exercise.solution: Initially both numerator and denominator tend to zero. After one application they still do. The second derivative quotient is $e^{x}/2\to 1/2$. Derivatives of the denominators are nonzero on each punctured side, so the limit is $1/2$.
rubric: Verify $0/0$ at both applications.
Use the rule on each side and match the results.

sections.title: An indefinite integral is a family
sections.text: The notation $\int f(x)dx$ denotes antiderivatives $F(x)+C$ on an interval. It is not a signed area with unspecified endpoints. Differentiate a candidate to verify it, and handle disconnected domains separately.

sections.title: Reverse a chain rule carefully
sections.text: For $\int 2x \cos(x^{2})dx$, notice that 2x is the derivative of the inner $x^{2}$. The answer is $\sin(x^{2})+C$. Omitting 2x would produce a different problem; there is no general rule integrating a composition by simply integrating the outer function.

exercise.prompt: Find $\int(3x^2-4x+2)\,dx$ and verify it.
exercise.hint: Integrate each power, then differentiate.
exercise.solution: $x^{3}-2x^{2}+2x+C$ differentiates to $3x^{2}-4x+2$. Every antiderivative on $\mathbb{R}$ differs by one constant.
rubric: Include the constant.
Use differentiation as an independent check.

supplementalBlocks.title: Constants belong to interval components
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable definition, then compute without skipping its conditions.

steps.text: On each interval, $\frac{d}{dx}\ln|x|=1/x$.
The domain is disconnected, so differentiation cannot compare the constants across zero.
Write $F(x)=\ln|x|+C_-$ for $x<0$ and $F(x)=\ln x+C_+$ for $x>0$.

supplementalBlocks.result: Two independent constants $C_-$ and $C_+$ are allowed.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Differentiating either branch gives $1/x$; changing only one constant still gives an antiderivative.

supplementalBlocks.title: Use the table and linearity
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable definition, then compute without skipping its conditions.
supplementalBlocks.setup: Integrate $3x^2-2\cos x$ on the real line.

steps.text: Integrate each term: $\int3x^2\,dx=x^3$ and $\int(-2\cos x)\,dx=-2\sin x$.
Combine the terms and add one constant on this connected interval.

supplementalBlocks.result: $x^3-2\sin x+C$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Differentiation returns $3x^2-2\cos x$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Why an interval has one constant
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Compare two antiderivatives by subtracting them and apply the mean value theorem on the interval.
supplementalBlocks.setup: Suppose $F$ and $G$ are antiderivatives of the same $f$ on an interval $I$. Explain every possible difference.

steps.label: Differentiate the difference
steps.text: Put $H=G-F$. Since $F' =G'=f$ on $I$, $H'=0$ throughout $I$.

steps.label: Use the interval
steps.text: For any $u<v$ in $I$, the mean value theorem on $[u,v]$ gives $H(v)-H(u)=H'(c)(v-u)=0$ for some $c\in(u,v)$.

steps.label: Conclude
steps.text: Every pair of points in $I$ has the same $H$ value, so $G=F+C$ on that entire interval.

supplementalBlocks.result: All antiderivatives on one interval form the family $F+C$. Separate interval components may have separate constants.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The converse is immediate: $(F+C)'=F'=f$. The mean value theorem does not compare points across a gap in the domain.

exercises.outcome: Find antiderivatives on a disconnected domain.
exercises.prompt: Find every antiderivative of $1/x^2$ on $(-\infty,0)\cup(0,\infty)$. Explain the constants.
exercises.hint: Integrate $x^{-2}$ on each connected interval.
exercises.solution: $-1/x+C_-$ for negative $x$ and $-1/x+C_+$ for positive $x$. The constants can differ because the domain has two components.
rubric: Differentiate both branches.
Allow independent constants on separate intervals.

exercises.outcome: Prove uniqueness up to a constant on an interval and respect disconnected components.
exercises.prompt: Let $F$ and $G$ both differentiate to $3x^2$ on $(-2,4)$. Prove that $G-F$ is one constant there. Would the same conclusion force one shared constant on $(-2,0)\cup(0,4)$?
exercises.hint: Apply the mean value theorem to $H=G-F$ between any two points in the same interval.
exercises.solution: On $(-2,4)$, $H'=G'-F'=0$. For any $u<v$ in that interval, the mean value theorem gives $H(v)-H(u)=H'(c)(v-u)=0$, so $H=C$. On the disconnected domain, the argument works separately on each component but cannot compare their constants; two independent constants are possible.
rubric: Use the derivative of the difference.
Apply the mean value theorem to arbitrary points in one interval.
Distinguish a connected interval from two disconnected components.

sections.title: A partition is more than equal bars
sections.text: Partition $[a,b]$ into subintervals, choose a tag in each, and sum $f(tag)$ times width. Riemann integrability means all such sums approach one number as the largest width tends to zero, independently of tags. Continuous functions on a closed interval are integrable; this result uses uniform continuity.

sections.title: Signed accumulation
sections.text: For $f(x)=x$ on $[-1,1]$, negative left-hand contributions cancel positive right-hand contributions, giving integral zero. The geometric area is instead $\int |x|dx=1$. Increasing equal bars supplies evidence but is not the definition’s all-partition proof.

exercise.prompt: Compute right-endpoint sums for $x$ on $[0,1]$ and their limit.
exercise.hint: Use width $1/n$ and $\sum k=n(n+1)/2$.
exercise.solution: The sum is $\sum (k/n)(1/n)=(n+1)/(2n)$, tending to $1/2$. Continuity independently ensures this limit equals the Riemann integral.
rubric: Include the subinterval width.
Distinguish one sequence of sums from the full integrability theorem.

supplementalBlocks.title: Compare left and right parabola sums
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Use the same partition width with left and right sample points, then compare both limits.
supplementalBlocks.setup: On $[0,1]$, construct left and right endpoint sums for $f(x)=x^2$.

steps.label: Partition
steps.text: For $n$ equal pieces, $\Delta x=1/n$; the left tags are $(i-1)/n$ and the right tags are $i/n$.

steps.label: Compare limits
steps.text: Because $x^2$ increases on $[0,1]$, $L_n\le S_n\le R_n$ for every tagged sum on this equal partition. Both endpoint sums tend to $1/3$.

supplementalBlocks.result: $L_n\to1/3$ and $R_n\to1/3$; every tagged sum on these equal partitions has the same limit.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The gap is $R_n-L_n=1/n$. Arbitrary partitions still require the all-partitions definition or a separate argument.

supplementalBlocks.title: Read width, tags, and interval from a limit
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable definition, then compute without skipping its conditions.

steps.text: The width is $3/n$, so the interval has length 3.
The tags $2+3i/n$ start at 2 and end at 5; the integrand is $x^4$.

supplementalBlocks.result: The limit is $\int_2^5 x^4\,dx$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The right-endpoint form matches $a+i(b-a)/n$ with $a=2$, $b=5$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Use signed area and order
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable definition, then compute without skipping its conditions.
supplementalBlocks.setup: Compare $\int_{-1}^1x\,dx$ with geometric area and compare $x^2$ to $x$ on $[0,1]$.

steps.text: Odd cancellation gives $\int_{-1}^1x\,dx=0$, while $\int_{-1}^1|x|\,dx=1$.
Since $0\le x^2\le x$ on $[0,1]$, comparison gives $0\le\int_0^1x^2\,dx\le\int_0^1x\,dx$.

supplementalBlocks.verification: The inequalities agree with the values from integration, and the signed result is not geometric area.

supplementalBlocks.title: Subtract adjacent intervals and reverse orientation
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Apply each integral rule with its stated bounds and hypotheses.

steps.text: Additivity gives $\int_3^7f=\int_0^7f-\int_0^3f=4$.
Reversing the endpoints changes the sign: $\int_7^3f=-\int_3^7f$.

supplementalBlocks.verification: Reversing again recovers $\int_3^7f=4$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Separate a linear combination
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Apply each integral rule with its stated bounds and hypotheses.

steps.text: The two integrals are $1/2$ and $1$.

supplementalBlocks.verification: Direct antiderivative evaluation gives $[x^2+3x]_0^1=4$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Every tag and every fine partition agree
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Compare each tagged rectangle with a telescoping endpoint difference and bound the total error by the mesh.
supplementalBlocks.setup: For $f(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$, let $0=x_0<\cdots<x_n=1$ be any partition, $t_i\in[x_{i-1},x_i]$, and $h=\max_i(x_i-x_{i-1})$.

steps.label: Compare one interval
steps.text: Write $\Delta_i=x_i-x_{i-1}$. Since $t_i$ lies between the endpoints, $|t_i\Delta_i-(x_i^2-x_{i-1}^2)/2|\le\Delta_i^2/2$.

steps.label: Sum and telescope
steps.text: The endpoint differences sum to $1/2$, while $\sum_i\Delta_i^2\le h\sum_i\Delta_i=h$.

steps.label: Take the mesh limit
steps.text: Every choice of tags and every partition with mesh $h$ satisfies $|\sum_i t_i\Delta_i-1/2|\le h/2$, which tends to zero.

supplementalBlocks.result: $\int_0^1x\,dx=1/2$ by the all-tags, all-partitions condition.
supplementalBlocks.verification: This bound is uniform in the number, widths, and tags of the subintervals; a single right-endpoint sequence would not give that conclusion.

exercises.outcome: Identify an integral from a new Riemann sum.
exercises.prompt: Express $\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^n(1+2i/n)^2(2/n)$ as an integral and evaluate it.
exercises.hint: Read the left endpoint 1 and width $2/n$.
rubric: Identify both interval endpoints and width.
Evaluate the resulting integral.

exercises.outcome: Combine orientation, additivity, and linearity.
exercises.prompt: If $\int_0^2f=5$ and $\int_0^5f=9$, find $\int_5^2(3f(x)-2)\,dx$.
exercises.hint: First find $\int_2^5f$, then reverse bounds. The interval length is 3.
rubric: Apply additivity and orientation before linearity.
Keep the constant term’s reversed interval sign.

exercises.outcome: Prove sample-point independence for a new linear integrand.
exercises.prompt: For $f(x)=2x$ on $[0,1]$, prove that every tagged Riemann sum over every partition of mesh $h$ differs from $1$ by at most $h$. Explain why a right-endpoint sequence alone would not prove this.
exercises.hint: Compare $2t_i\Delta_i$ with $x_i^2-x_{i-1}^2$ on each subinterval.
exercises.solution: Because $t_i\in[x_{i-1},x_i]$, $|2t_i\Delta_i-(x_i^2-x_{i-1}^2)|\le\Delta_i^2$. Summing and telescoping gives $|\sum_i2t_i\Delta_i-1|\le\sum_i\Delta_i^2\le h\sum_i\Delta_i=h$. The bound applies to every partition and every tag choice, so all sums converge to $1$ as $h\to0$. One selected right-endpoint sequence cannot establish that quantifier.
rubric: Keep partitions and tags arbitrary.
Bound each interval error and telescope.
Conclude uniform convergence over all tagged partitions.

sections.title: Average height
sections.text: On $[a,b]$ with $a<b$, the integral average is $(b-a)^{-1}\int f$. It is the constant height producing the same signed accumulation. For a continuous function, an integral mean-value theorem ensures some $c$ has $f(c)$ equal to that average.

sections.title: Attainment needs care
sections.text: For $f=x^{2}$ on $[0,2]$, the integral is $8/3$ and average $4/3$, attained at $c=2/\sqrt{3}$. A discontinuous function taking only values 0 and 1 can have average $1/2$ without ever taking that value.

exercise.prompt: Find the average of $2x+1$ on $[1,3]$ and where it is attained.
exercise.hint: Divide the integral by interval length 2.
exercise.solution: The integral $[x^{2}+x]_{1}^{3}$ is 10, so the average is 5. Solve $2c+1=5$ to get $c=2$.
rubric: Divide by length, not the upper endpoint.
Separate the average from the point attaining it.

supplementalBlocks.title: Find the height and its witness
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable definition, then compute without skipping its conditions.
supplementalBlocks.setup: For $f(x)=x^2$ on $[0,2]$, find the average and a point attaining it.

steps.text: $\int_0^2x^2\,dx=8/3$ and the interval length is 2.
The average is $4/3$; solve $c^2=4/3$ with $c\in[0,2]$.

supplementalBlocks.result: $f_{\rm avg}=4/3$ at $c=2/\sqrt3$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Continuity on the closed interval ensures some attaining point; the computed point lies inside it.

exercises.outcome: Compute average and attaining point.
exercises.prompt: Find the average of $x^2$ on $[1,3]$ and every $c$ in that interval with $c^2$ equal to the average.
exercises.hint: Divide the integral by the length 2, then solve within the interval.
rubric: Divide by interval length.
Restrict the solution to the given interval.

sections.title: Two directions, two jobs
sections.text: If $f$ is continuous and $A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$, then $A'(x)=f(x)$. If $F'=f$ and $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b f=F(b)-F(a)$. The first constructs an antiderivative; the second evaluates accumulation using one.

sections.title: Moving bounds
sections.text: For $H(x)=\int_x^{x^2}\sin t\,dt$, write $A(x^{2})-A(x)$. Chain rule gives $H'(x)=2x\sin(x^2)-\sin x$. The symbol $t$ is a dummy variable; the moving endpoint $x^{2}$ creates its own derivative factor.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $\int_0^{x^3}e^{t^2}\,dt$.
exercise.hint: Use FTC at the endpoint, then multiply by its derivative.
exercise.solution: The derivative is $3x^{2} e^{x^6}$. No elementary antiderivative of $e^{t^2}$ is needed.
rubric: Substitute the endpoint into the integrand.
Multiply by $3x^{2}$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Why accumulation differentiates
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable definition, then compute without skipping its conditions.

steps.text: The difference quotient is $[A(x+h)-A(x)]/h=(1/h)\int_x^{x+h}f(t)\,dt$.
The integral mean-value theorem gives this average as $f(c_h)$ for a point between $x$ and $x+h$.
Continuity and $c_h\to x$ imply $f(c_h)\to f(x)$.

supplementalBlocks.result: $A\prime(x)=f(x)$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: This uses continuity near $x$; the dummy variable $t$ does not change the endpoint derivative.

supplementalBlocks.title: Evaluate with oriented endpoints
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable definition, then compute without skipping its conditions.

steps.text: An antiderivative is $F(x)=x^4/4$.
Use the stated order of endpoints: $F(-2)-F(1)=4-1/4$.

supplementalBlocks.verification: The result also equals $-\int_{-2}^1x^3\,dx$; reversing endpoints changes the sign.

supplementalBlocks.title: Differentiate each endpoint
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Apply each integral rule with its stated bounds and hypotheses.

steps.text: Write $H(x)=A(x^2)-A(x)$ where $A(y)=\int_0^y\sin t\,dt$.
FTC Part 1 and the chain rule give $A\prime(x^2)2x-A\prime(x)=2x\sin(x^2)-\sin x$.

supplementalBlocks.result: $H\prime(x)=2x\sin(x^2)-\sin x$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: At $x=1$ both endpoints meet, but the derivative formula still follows from the endpoint rates.

exercises.outcome: Differentiate both moving endpoints.
exercises.prompt: Differentiate $H(x)=\int_{x^2}^{2x}\cos(t^2)\,dt$.
exercises.hint: Upper endpoint contribution minus lower endpoint contribution.
exercises.solution: $H\prime(x)=2\cos(4x^2)-2x\cos(x^4)$.
rubric: Apply the chain rule at both bounds.
Subtract the lower-bound contribution.

sections.title: Transform the whole integral
sections.text: For $\int_0^1 2xe^{x^2}\,dx$, choose $u=x^{2}$ and $du=2x$ dx. Bounds become 0 and 1, yielding $\int_0^1e^u\,du=e-1$. In an indefinite integral substitute back; in a definite integral either transform bounds or return to the original variable before evaluating.

sections.title: Why the rule holds
sections.text: If $F'=f$, then $(F(g(x)))'=f(g(x))g'(x)$. FTC therefore gives the substitution formula when the differentiability and continuity assumptions hold. Monotonicity simplifies interpretation of transformed regions, but the signed one-variable identity with $g'$ can also cover paths that reverse direction.

exercise.prompt: Evaluate $\int_0^2x\sqrt{1+x^2}\,dx$.
exercise.hint: Use $u=1+x^{2}$; the extra factor is $du/2$.
exercise.solution: The bounds become 1 and 5. The integral is $(1/2)\int_1^5u^{1/2}\,du =(5\sqrt{5}-1)/3$.
rubric: Transform both endpoints.
Keep the factor $1/2$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Transform factor and endpoints together
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable definition, then compute without skipping its conditions.

steps.text: Set $u=3-5x$, so $du=-5\,dx$ and $dx=-du/5$.
The bounds $x=1,2$ become $u=-2,-7$ respectively.

supplementalBlocks.verification: The integrand is positive; the answer must be positive. Direct differentiation of $1/[5(3-5x)]$ verifies the antiderivative.

supplementalBlocks.title: Use the inner derivative of a radical
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable definition, then compute without skipping its conditions.

steps.text: Set $u=\sqrt{2x+1}$; then $u^2=2x+1$ and $dx=u\,du$.
The bounds become $u=1$ and $u=3$, so the integral is $\int_1^3u^2\,du$.

supplementalBlocks.verification: Equivalently, $u=2x+1$ gives the same value with its factor $1/2$.

exercises.outcome: Substitute into a distinct definite integral.
exercises.prompt: Evaluate $\int_0^1 3x^2(1+x^3)^2\,dx$.
exercises.hint: Let $u=1+x^3$ and transform both endpoints.
exercises.solution: $u$ runs from 1 to 2, so $\int_1^2u^2\,du=7/3$.
rubric: Use the full derivative $du=3x^2dx$.
Transform both bounds.

sections.title: Every bad endpoint gets a limit
sections.text: For $\int_1^\infty x^{-2}\,dx$, define lim $R\to \infty \int_1^R x^{-2}\,dx =\lim(1-1/R)=1$. For an interior singularity $c$, split the interval at $c$ and require both one-sided integrals to converge separately.

sections.title: Cancellation cannot rescue divergence
sections.text: The symmetric integrals of $1/x$ on $[-1,-\varepsilon ]$ and $[\varepsilon ,1]$ cancel, but the negative and positive parts diverge separately. Their symmetric principal value zero is a different notion, not convergence of the improper integral.

exercise.prompt: Does $\int_0^1x^{-3/2}\,dx$ converge?
exercise.hint: Replace the lower endpoint by $\varepsilon >0$.
exercise.solution: The integral from $\varepsilon$ to 1 is $2/\sqrt{\varepsilon }-2$, tending to $+\infty$. It diverges.
rubric: Write the limiting definition.
Check the sign of the antiderivative.
Distinguish divergence from a finite numerical cutoff.

supplementalBlocks.title: Test two infinite tails separately
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable definition, then compute without skipping its conditions.

steps.text: The integrand has an interior singularity at zero, so split there before testing either infinite tail.
On $(0,1]$, $\int_\varepsilon^1x^{-2}\,dx=1/\varepsilon-1\to\infty$.

supplementalBlocks.result: The integral diverges, regardless of the behavior at infinite endpoints.
supplementalBlocks.verification: No cancellation or symmetric cutoff can replace separate one-sided limits.

supplementalBlocks.title: Split at an interior discontinuity
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable definition, then compute without skipping its conditions.

steps.text: Split at $x=1$ into $\int_0^1$ and $\int_1^3$.
The left part is $\lim_{t\to1^-}[\ln|x-1|]_0^t=-\infty$; the right part diverges to $+\infty$.

supplementalBlocks.result: The improper integral diverges.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Using $[\ln|x-1|]_0^3=\ln2$ across the pole is invalid.

supplementalBlocks.title: Combine convergent one-sided limits
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Identify the applicable definition, then compute without skipping its conditions.

steps.text: Split at zero and take independent limits: $\lim_{A\to-\infty}\int_A^0=\pi/2$ and $\lim_{B\to\infty}\int_0^B=\pi/2$.
Both limits are finite, so their sum defines the improper integral.

supplementalBlocks.verification: One symmetric cutoff is insufficient as a definition; both tails were checked separately.

supplementalBlocks.title: Test an infinite endpoint
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Apply each integral rule with its stated bounds and hypotheses.

steps.text: Use the finite cutoff $R>1$: $\int_1^R1/x\,dx=\ln R$.
As $R\to\infty$, $\ln R\to\infty$.

supplementalBlocks.result: The integral diverges.
supplementalBlocks.verification: A finite area would require a finite one-sided limit.

supplementalBlocks.title: Use a one-sided finite endpoint limit
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Apply each integral rule with its stated bounds and hypotheses.

steps.text: The left endpoint is singular, so integrate from $2+\varepsilon$ to $5$.
The cutoff value is $[2\sqrt{x-2}]_{2+\varepsilon}^5=2\sqrt3-2\sqrt\varepsilon$.
Let $\varepsilon\to0^+$.

supplementalBlocks.result: $2\sqrt3$, so the improper integral converges.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The antiderivative is used only on the proper interval $[2+\varepsilon,5]$.

exercises.outcome: Test a new interior singularity.
exercises.prompt: Does $\int_0^2 (x-1)^{-2}\,dx$ converge? Show the required limits.
exercises.hint: Split at 1; one divergent side is enough.
rubric: Split at the interior singularity.
Evaluate a one-sided limit before combining.

sections.title: Decide the order on each piece
sections.text: Area between $f$ and $g$ over $[a,b]$ is $\int |f-g|$. Solve their intersections and split wherever their order changes. For $x$ and $x^{2}$ on $[0,1]$, $x\geq x^{2}$ and the area is $\int_0^1(x-x^2)\,dx=1/6$.

sections.title: Horizontal slices are an alternative
sections.text: A horizontal slice contributes right boundary minus left boundary times dy. For $x=y^{2}$ and $x=2-y^{2}$, intersections occur at $y=\pm 1$; the area is $\int_{-1}^1(2-2y^2)\,dy=8/3$. Choose an order that avoids unnecessary inverses and splitting.

exercise.prompt: Find the area between $y=x$ and $y=-x$ on $[-1,1]$.
exercise.hint: Their order switches at zero.
exercise.solution: Area is $\int_{-1}^0(-2x)\,dx+\int_0^1 2x\,dx=2$. The unsplit signed integral of 2x is zero and is not the area.
rubric: Locate the order change.
Use nonnegative slice heights.

contentBlocks.title: Height is upper minus lower
contentBlocks.text: When continuous $f(x)\ge g(x)$ on $[a,b]$, a narrow vertical strip has height $f(x)-g(x)\ge0$ and width $\Delta x$. The limit of its Riemann sums is the area $A=\int_a^b(f-g)\,dx$.

contentBlocks.title: Area when the upper curve stays above
contentBlocks.strategy: Check the order on the full interval, then integrate a nonnegative difference.
contentBlocks.verification: The integrand is nonnegative everywhere on the interval, so this is geometric area rather than cancellation of signed values.

contentBlocks.title: Split where the curves trade places
contentBlocks.strategy: Solve the intersection, determine which curve is upper on each side, then add nonnegative integrals.
contentBlocks.setup: MH1101 Chapter 02 Example 2.2: find the area between $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos x$ for $0\le x\le\pi/2$.

steps.label: Find the crossing
steps.text: $\sin x=\cos x$ at $x=\pi/4$ in this interval. Before it $\cos x\ge\sin x$; after it the order reverses.

steps.label: Integrate each positive height
steps.text: $A=\int_0^{\pi/4}(\cos x-\sin x)\,dx+\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}(\sin x-\cos x)\,dx$.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.text: Each piece contributes $\sqrt2-1$, giving $2\sqrt2-2$.

contentBlocks.verification: The unsplit signed integral of $\sin x-\cos x$ on $[0,\pi/2]$ is zero; it loses the positive geometric area.

exercises.outcome: Use continuous upper-minus-lower strip heights on a fresh interval.
exercises.prompt: Find the area between $y=3-x^2$ and $y=x^2$ for $-1\le x\le1$. Verify which is upper throughout.
exercises.hint: Check $3-2x^2\ge1$ on this interval.
rubric: Check the curve order on the whole interval.
Integrate a nonnegative height with correct bounds.

exercises.outcome: Split a fresh area problem at every change of upper curve.
exercises.prompt: Find the area between $y=x^2$ and $y=x$ over $[-1,2]$. State each subinterval’s upper curve.
exercises.hint: The curves meet at $x=0$ and $x=1$; test all three intervals.
exercises.solution: $x^2$ is upper on $[-1,0]$ and $[1,2]$, while $x$ is upper on $[0,1]$. The three areas are $5/6$, $1/6$, and $5/6$, so the total is $11/6$.
rubric: Locate both intersections and three sign intervals.
Use a nonnegative height on each piece.
Add all three areas without cancellation.

sections.title: A washer removes an inner disk
sections.text: Rotating $y=x$ and $y=x^{2}$ for $0\leq x\leq 1$ about the $x$-axis gives $R=x$ and $r=x^{2}$, so $V=\pi\int_0^1(x^2-x^4)\,dx =2\pi /15$. The slice area is $\pi (R^{2}-r^{2})$, not $\pi (R-r)^{2}$.

sections.title: Measure from the actual axis
sections.text: About $y=-1$ the same region has radii $1+x$ and $1+x^{2}$. The volume becomes $\pi\int_0^1[(1+x)^2-(1+x^2)^2]\,dx=7\pi /15$. Both radii are distances from the axis, not graph heights above zero.

sections.title: The slice shape determines its area
sections.text: A volume built on the base $0\leq x\leq 1$, $x^{2}\leq y\leq x$ need not come from rotation. If every perpendicular section at $x$ is a square, its side is $x-x^{2}$ and area is $(x-x^{2})^{2}$. Thus $V=\int _{0}^{1}(x-x^{2})^{2}dx=1/30$. For an equilateral triangle with that side, multiply the squared side by $\sqrt{3}/4$. A disk or washer factor $\pi$ belongs only to circular slices.

exercise.prompt: Over the base $0\le x\le1$, $x^2\le y\le x$, a solid has perpendicular cross-sections that are equilateral triangles. Find its volume and explain why no washer radius is needed.
exercise.hint: The triangle side is the vertical width $x-x^{2}$; its area is $\sqrt{3}$ times side squared divided by 4.
exercise.solution: $A(x)=\sqrt{3}(x-x^{2})^{2}/4$. Since $\int _{0}^{1}(x-x^{2})^{2}dx=1/30$, $V=\sqrt{3}/120$. The solid is specified by triangular sections, not by rotating the base region.
rubric: Use the actual section shape and vertical base width.
Square the width before integrating over $x$.
Do not insert a circular $\pi$ factor.

sections.title: Unroll a thin shell
sections.text: A shell at radius $r$, height $h$ and thickness dr has volume approximately circumference times height times thickness, $2\pi rh$ dr. Integrating gives the limit. For the region under $y=x$ on $[0,1]$ about the $y$-axis, $V=2\pi\int_0^1x^2\,dx =2\pi /3$.

sections.title: Choose slices relative to the axis
sections.text: Shell slices are parallel to the rotation axis; washer slices are perpendicular. Radii are nonnegative distances. If the region crosses the axis, naive shells from both sides may sweep the same volume twice; first describe the actual solid or split without overlap.

sections.title: Hold the region and axis fixed when comparing methods
sections.text: For the SAME region $0\leq x\leq 1$, $x^{2}\leq y\leq x$ rotated about the $x$-axis, vertical washers use outer radius $x$ and inner radius $x^{2}$: $\pi \int _{0}^{1}(x^{2}-x^{4})dx=2\pi /15$. Horizontal shells use radius $y$ and height $\sqrt{y}-y$: $2\pi \int _{0}^{1}y(\sqrt{y}-y)dy=2\pi /15$. The inversion $x=y$ or $x=\sqrt{y}$ comes from that same region; changing the axis would compare different solids.

exercise.prompt: For the fixed region $0\le x\le1$, $0\le y\le1-x$ rotated about the $y$-axis, set up both shells and perpendicular disks, and verify the same volume.
exercise.hint: Vertical shells have radius $x$ and height $1-x$. Horizontal disks have radius $1-y$.
exercise.solution: Shells give $2\pi \int _{0}^{1}x(1-x)dx=\pi /3$. Disks give $\pi \int _{0}^{1}(1-y)^{2}dy=\pi /3$. Both descriptions use the same triangle and $y$-axis, and neither double-counts the solid.
rubric: Keep the same region and $y$-axis in both setups.
Identify shell radius and height and disk radius with the correct variables.
Evaluate and reconcile both integrals.

sections.title: Repeated and cyclic parts
sections.text: From $(uv)'=u'v+uv'$, $\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$. Repeated parts gives $\int x^{2}e^{x}dx=e^{x}(x^{2}-2x+2)+C$. For $I=\int e^x\cos x\,dx$, two rounds give $I=e^{x}\cos x+e^{x}\sin x-I$; solving yields $I=e^{x}(\sin x+\cos x)/2+C$.

sections.title: Definite terms and choice
sections.text: For $\int_0^1xe^x\,dx$, choose $u=x$, $dv=e^{x}dx$. The boundary term $[xe^{x}]_{0}^{1}=e$ and the remaining integral is $e-1$, so the answer is 1. Choosing $u=e^{x}$ and $dv=x$ dx creates an $x^{2}e^{x}$ integral, increasing the polynomial degree instead of reducing it.

sections.title: Stage the next method after parts
sections.text: For $\int x \arctan$ $x$ dx, choose $u=\arctan$ $x$ and $dv=x$ dx because differentiating the inverse tangent gives a rational function. Parts yields $x^{2}$ arctan $x/2-(1/2)\int x^{2}/(1+x^{2})dx$. Divide $x^{2}/(1+x^{2})=1-1/(1+x^{2})$, then finish with $x^{2}$ arctan $x/2-x/2+\arctan x/2+C$. The second method is chosen after seeing the simpler remainder.

exercise.prompt: Choose and justify the first method for $\int_0^1 x\arctan x\,dx$, then identify the second method needed for the remainder and evaluate.
exercise.hint: Let $u=\arctan$ $x$ and $dv=x$ dx. After parts, divide $x^{2}$ by $1+x^{2}$ before integrating.
exercise.solution: Parts is useful because $d(\arctan x)=dx/(1+x^2)$. It gives $[x^2\arctan x/2]_0^1-(1/2)\int_0^1x^2/(1+x^2)\,dx$. Divide $x^2/(1+x^2)=1-1/(1+x^2)$; the result is $\pi/4-1/2$. Choosing $u=x$ makes the antiderivative of $\arctan x$ the harder first step.
rubric: Justify the $u$,dv choice before calculating.
Use rational division for the remainder.
Apply both endpoint terms and simplify.

sections.title: Use parity to choose a substitution
sections.text: For $\sin^m x\cos^n x$ with a positive odd sine power, reserve $\sin x\,dx$ and replace $\sin^2x$ by $1-\cos^2x$; then use $u=\cos x$. With an odd cosine power, reverse the roles. If both powers are even, use half-angle identities.

sections.title: Work both branches
sections.text: $\int\sin^3x\cos^2x\,dx$ becomes $-\int(1-u^2)u^2\,du=-u^3/3+u^5/5+C$. For $\int\cos^2x\,dx$, use $\cos^2x=(1+\cos2x)/2$, giving $x/2+\sin2x/4+C$.

exercise.prompt: Find $\int\sin x\cos^3x\,dx$.
exercise.hint: Reserve $\sin x\,dx$ and use $u=\cos x$.
exercise.solution: The integral is $-\int u^3\,du=-\cos^4x/4+C$. Differentiating restores $\sin x\cos^3x$.
rubric: Carry the minus sign in du.
Verify by differentiating.

sections.title: Fix a branch before simplifying
sections.text: For $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$ with $a>0$, choose $x=a\sin\theta$ and $\theta\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$, so $\cos\theta\ge0$ and $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}=a\cos\theta$. Without the range restriction the root is $a|\cos\theta|$. For $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$, $x=a\tan\theta$ on the same open angle interval gives $a\sec\theta$.

sections.title: Include the differential
sections.text: For $\int\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx$, $x=\sin\theta$ and $dx=\cos\theta\,d\theta$ give $\int\cos^2\theta\,d\theta$. Substituting back gives $(\arcsin x+x\sqrt{1-x^2})/2+C$ on the interior of $[-1,1]$. A diagram helps recover the factors but does not replace the branch choice.

sections.title: The secant branch depends on the x-domain
sections.text: For $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$, $a>0$ and $x\ge a$, take $x=a\sec\theta$ with $0\le\theta<\pi/2$. Then $\tan\theta\ge0$ and $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}=a\tan\theta$, not $a|\tan\theta|$. On $x\le-a$ use $x=-a\sec\theta$ on the same angle range and transform $dx$ with its negative sign. One substitution formula cannot silently cross the gap $(-a,a)$.

sections.title: The tangent branch keeps secant positive
sections.text: For $\sqrt{x^2+4}$, $x=2\tan\theta$ with $-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2$ gives $\sec\theta>0$, so $\sqrt{x^2+4}=2\sec\theta$. In $\int dx/(x^2+4)^{3/2}$, $dx=2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ reduces the integrand to $\cos\theta/4$. The result is $x/[4\sqrt{x^2+4}]+C$. Without the angle range, replacing $\sqrt{\sec^2\theta}$ by $\sec\theta$ could have the wrong sign.

exercise.prompt: Evaluate $A=\int_2^4 dx/\sqrt{x^2-4}$ and $B=\int_0^3 dx/(x^2+9)^{3/2}$ by trigonometric substitutions. Choose secant or tangent for each, state the branches, and transform the bounds.
exercise.hint: For A use $x=2sec \theta$, $0\leq \theta \leq \pi /3$. For $B$ use $x=3tan \theta$, $0\leq \theta \leq \pi /4$. Check the sign of each square root on its chosen branch.
exercise.solution: A: $x=2\sec\theta$ gives $\sqrt{x^2-4}=2\tan\theta$ and $dx=2\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta$ on $0\le\theta\le\pi/3$, so $A=\int_0^{\pi/3}\sec\theta\,d\theta=\ln(2+\sqrt3)$. $B$: $x=3\tan\theta$ gives $\sqrt{x^2+9}=3\sec\theta>0$ and $dx=3\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ on $0\le\theta\le\pi/4$, so $B=(1/9)\int_0^{\pi/4}\cos\theta\,d\theta=\sqrt2/18$. Both signs follow from the declared branches.
rubric: Choose secant for the difference and tangent for the sum, with explicit branches.
Transform bounds, differentials, and square-root signs for both.
Evaluate both transformed integrals.

supplementalBlocks.title: Divide before decomposing an improper fraction
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Compare degrees before choosing partial-fraction terms; decompose only the proper remainder.
supplementalBlocks.setup: For the notes' example, integrate $R(x)=(x^4-2x^2+4x+1)/(x^3-x^2-x+1)$ on an interval avoiding $x=-1,1$.

steps.label: Divide
steps.text: Since the numerator has degree four and the denominator degree three, long division gives $R(x)=x+1+4x/(x^3-x^2-x+1)$.

steps.label: Factor and choose terms
steps.text: $x^3-x^2-x+1=(x-1)^2(x+1)$, so the proper remainder needs $A/(x-1)+B/(x-1)^2+C/(x+1)$. Solving $4x=A(x-1)(x+1)+B(x+1)+C(x-1)^2$ gives $(A,B,C)=(1,2,-1)$.

steps.label: Integrate on a domain component
steps.text: $\int R(x)\,dx=x^2/2+x+\ln|x-1|-2/(x-1)-\ln|x+1|+C$. The constant may differ on $(-\infty,-1)$, $(-1,1)$, and $(1,\infty)$.

supplementalBlocks.result: Division precedes the repeated-factor template whenever the original rational function is improper.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Differentiate the result on any component and recover $x+1+1/(x-1)+2/(x-1)^2-1/(x+1)=R(x)$.

exercises.outcome: Choose polynomial division before repeated-factor decomposition for an improper rational integrand.
exercises.prompt: Integrate $\int (x^4-3x^2-3x-7)/[(x+1)^2(x-2)]\,dx$ on an interval where it is defined. State why division comes first, include every repeated-factor term, and verify by differentiation.
exercises.hint: The numerator degree exceeds the denominator degree. Division gives quotient $x$ and remainder $-x-7$; write $A/(x+1)+B/(x+1)^2+C/(x-2)$ for the proper part.
exercises.solution: The denominator is $x^3-3x-2$, so division gives $x+(-x-7)/[(x+1)^2(x-2)]$. Multiplying the template through and solving gives $(A,B,C)=(1,2,-1)$. Hence the integrand is $x+1/(x+1)+2/(x+1)^2-1/(x-2)$ and the antiderivative is $x^2/2+\ln|x+1|-2/(x+1)-\ln|x-2|+C$ on each component of $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1,2\}$. Differentiation recovers the decomposition and original quotient.
rubric: Compare polynomial degrees and divide before decomposing.
Include both powers of the repeated factor and solve the coefficient identity.
Integrate on a domain component and check the derivative.

sections.title: The denominator determines the template
sections.text: First divide if numerator degree is at least denominator degree. For each repeated linear factor $(x-a)^k$ include $A_{1}/(x-a)+…+A_{k}/(x-a)^k$. For an irreducible quadratic $q$, use a linear numerator $(Bx+C)/q$; repeat terms for powers of $q$.

sections.title: Solve coefficients explicitly
sections.text: For $(x^{2}+1)/(x(x-1)^{2})$, write $A/x+B/(x-1)+C/(x-1)^{2}$. Multiplying through gives $x^{2}+1=A(x-1)^{2}+Bx(x-1)+Cx$. Setting $x=0$ gives $A=1$, $x=1$ gives $C=2$, and the $x^{2}$ coefficient gives $B=0$. Integrating yields $\ln|x|-2/(x-1)+C_{0}$ on each component. For $(x+1)/(x^{2}+1)$, split into a logarithmic derivative and an arctangent: $(1/2)\ln(x^{2}+1)+\arctan$ $x$.

sections.title: Decide the algebra before integrating
sections.text: For a rational integrand, first compare polynomial degrees and divide if improper. Factor the remaining denominator over the reals, then include every power of a repeated linear factor and a linear numerator over each irreducible quadratic. Solve the coefficient identity and only then integrate. This algebraic route differs from parts, which is chosen for a product whose differentiated factor simplifies. Verify a proposed antiderivative by differentiation on each domain component.

exercise.prompt: Choose the first algebraic step, then integrate $\int(2x+3)/[x(x+1)^2]\,dx$ on one interval avoiding its poles. Explain why a repeated-factor term is required.
exercise.hint: The rational function is proper. Write $A/x+B/(x+1)+C/(x+1)^{2}$ before solving coefficients.
exercise.solution: No division is needed. The repeated factor requires both $1/(x+1)$ and $1/(x+1)^{2}$ terms. Solving $2x+3=A(x+1)^{2}+Bx(x+1)+Cx$ gives $A=3$, $B=-3$, $C=-1$. Integrating gives $3\ln|x|-3\ln|x+1|+1/(x+1)+C$ on each interval separated by $-1$ and 0.
rubric: Check properness and factor structure before choosing the template.
Include both powers of the repeated factor and solve the identity.
Integrate with logarithm signs and domain components intact.

sections.title: Signed errors reveal geometry
sections.text: For a convex function, chords lie above the graph, so the trapezoidal rule overestimates; midpoint underestimates when convexity holds on each panel. Error signs require hypotheses, not just a visual impression.

sections.title: Choose n from a bound
sections.text: For a twice continuously differentiable function with $|f''|\leq M$, composite midpoint error is at most $M(b-a)^{3}/(24n^{2})$, and trapezoidal error at most $M(b-a)^{3}/(12n^{2})$. Solve the inequality for $n$ and round up; these are certified bounds, unlike agreement between two numerical estimates.

exercise.prompt: How many trapezoids guarantee error at most 0.001 for $\int_0^1x^2\,dx$?
exercise.hint: Here $M=2$; require $2/(12n^{2})\leq 0.001$.
exercise.solution: $n^{2}\geq 500/3$, so $n\geq 13$ is sufficient. The bound is $1/(6\cdot 169)$, below 0.001.
rubric: Use an upper derivative bound on the whole interval.
Round $n$ upward.

sections.title: Pairs of panels
sections.text: Composite Simpson requires an even number $n$ of equal subintervals with width $h$. Its weights are 1,4,2,4,…,2,4,1 and overall factor $h/3$. It integrates every polynomial of degree at most three exactly, although each local interpolant is quadratic.

sections.title: A fourth-derivative guarantee
sections.text: If $f$ has a continuous fourth derivative bounded in magnitude by $M$, the error is at most $M(b-a)^{5}/(180n^{4})$. More panels do not make this bound applicable at a singularity; check smoothness first.

exercise.prompt: Apply Simpson with $n=2$ to $x^3$ on $[0,1]$.
exercise.hint: Use values at 0, $1/2$ and 1.
exercise.solution: With $h=1/2$, the result is $(1/6)[0+4(1/8)+1]=1/4$, exactly the integral.
rubric: Use the $h/3$ factor.
Explain exactness for a cubic.

sections.title: The input is an index
sections.text: A sequence converges to $L$ if for every $\varepsilon >0$ some integer $N$ makes $|a_{n}-L|<\varepsilon$ for every $n\geq N$. The tail matters: changing finitely many terms cannot change the limit. An infinite sequence does not automatically converge.

sections.title: A quantitative tail
sections.text: For $a_{n}=1+1/n$, $|a_{n}-1|=1/n$. Choose an integer $N>1/\varepsilon$; then all $n\geq N$ satisfy the required inequality. A plot of the first hundred values cannot alone establish an assertion about every later term.

exercise.prompt: Give an $N$ ensuring $|(2+3/n)-2|<0.01$ for every $n\ge N$.
exercise.hint: Solve $3/n<0.01$ with a strict inequality.
exercise.solution: Any integer $N\geq 301$ works. $N=300$ fails at its first term because the error equals 0.01.
rubric: Respect strict inequality.
Make a statement about all later indices.

sections.title: Subsequences inherit a genuine limit
sections.text: A subsequence selects indices $n_{1}<n_{2}<…$ tending to infinity. If $a_{n}\to L$, every subsequence tends to $L$. Hence two subsequences with distinct limits refute convergence. For $(-1)^n$, the even and odd subsequences tend to 1 and $-1$.

sections.title: Bounded does not mean convergent
sections.text: Every convergent real sequence is bounded, but $(-1)^n$ is a bounded counterexample to the converse. Bolzano–Weierstrass states that every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence. It does not say the whole sequence converges.

exercise.prompt: Does $a_n=(-1)^n+1/n$ converge?
exercise.hint: Separate even and odd indices.
exercise.solution: The even subsequence tends to 1 and the odd subsequence to $-1$. Therefore the sequence diverges while remaining bounded.
rubric: Use subsequences whose indices tend to infinity.
Distinguish boundedness from convergence.

sections.title: Normalize polynomial growth
sections.text: For $(3n^{2}+n)/(2n^{2}-1)$, divide by $n^{2}$ to obtain $(3+1/n)/(2-1/n^{2})$, whose limit is $3/2$. The denominator limit 2 is nonzero, allowing the quotient law.

sections.title: A zero denominator gives no automatic result
sections.text: The sequences $1/n$ and $1/n^{2}$ both tend to zero, but their quotient is $n$ and diverges. Reversing them gives $1/n\to 0$. Equal component limits therefore do not settle an indeterminate quotient.

exercise.prompt: Find $\lim_{n\to\infty}(\sqrt{n^2+n}-n)$.
exercise.hint: Rationalize before taking limits.
exercise.solution: The expression equals $n/(\sqrt{n^{2}+n}+n)=1/(\sqrt{1+1/n}+1)$, tending to $1/2$.
rubric: Avoid subtracting two divergent limits.
Use a valid algebraic identity for positive $n$.

sections.title: Prove bounds for a recurrence
sections.text: Let $a_{1}=1$ and $a_{n+1}=\sqrt{2+a_{n}}$. If $1\leq a_{n}\leq 2$, then $1\leq a_{n+1}\leq 2$; induction bounds every term. On $[1,2]$, $\sqrt{2+x}\geq x$ because $2+x-x^{2}=(2-x)(x+1)\geq 0$, so the sequence is increasing.

sections.title: Only now solve the fixed point
sections.text: An increasing bounded real sequence converges by completeness. Taking limits gives $L=\sqrt{2+L}$, hence $L=2$ or $-1$ after squaring. The proven bounds force $L=2$. Solving the equation before proving convergence would produce candidates without showing that the sequence approaches any of them.

exercise.prompt: Let $b_1=3$ and $b_{n+1}=(b_n+2)/2$. Prove convergence and find the limit.
exercise.hint: Show $b_{n}\geq 2$ and $b_{n+1}\leq b_{n}$ by induction.
exercise.solution: The recurrence preserves $b_{n}\geq 2$, and $b_{n+1}-b_{n}=(2-b_{n})/2\leq 0$. Thus it converges. Its limit satisfies $L=(L+2)/2$, giving $L=2$; explicitly $b_{n}=2+2^{1-n}$.
rubric: Prove both boundedness and monotonicity.
Invoke convergence before passing the limit through the recurrence.

sections.title: Sum means a limit of partial sums
sections.text: For a series starting at $n=0$, define $S_N$ as its first $N$ terms, from $n=0$ through $n=N-1$. Its value is the limit of these partial sums, when that limit exists. For $r\ne1$, $S_N=1+r+\cdots+r^{N-1}=(1-r^N)/(1-r)$; $S_1=1$. The sum is $1/(1-r)$ only when $|r|<1$. For $r=1$, the partial sum grows as $N$; for $r=-1$, it alternates between 0 and 1. Keep the first term, term count, and last index distinct. Some books instead use $S_N$ for the sum through index $N$; that has $N+1$ terms and numerator $1-r^{N+1}$.

sections.title: Keep the surviving boundary terms
sections.text: For $\sum_{n=1}^\infty1/[n(n+1)]$, split each term into $1/n-1/(n+1)$. The $N$th partial sum is $1-1/(N+1)$, tending to $1$. Writing the finite cancellation first prevents informal infinity-minus-infinity errors.

exercise.prompt: Find $\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(1/3)^n$.
exercise.hint: Identify the first term, not just the ratio.
exercise.solution: The first term is $1/9$ and ratio $1/3$, so the sum is $(1/9)/(1-1/3)=1/6$.
rubric: Use the correct starting index.
Check the ratio magnitude.

contentBlocks.title: Derive the finite geometric sum before taking a limit
contentBlocks.strategy: Match the notes’ $n=1$ indexing and subtract $r s_k$ from $s_k$.

steps.label: Cancel finite sums
steps.text: If $r\ne1$, then $r s_k=ar+\cdots+ar^k$, so $(1-r)s_k=a(1-r^k)$ and $s_k=a(1-r^k)/(1-r)$.

steps.label: Take only justified limits
steps.text: If $|r|<1$, then $r^k\to0$ and $s_k\to a/(1-r)$. If $r=1$, $s_k=ka$; if $r=-1$, $s_k$ alternates between 0 and $a$; if $|r|>1$, $r^k$ prevents a finite limit.

contentBlocks.result: The series converges exactly when $|r|<1$ and then sums to $a/(1-r)$.
contentBlocks.verification: At $k=1$, the finite formula gives $s_1=a$. This uses Example 4.20 and Theorem 6 on pages 24–25; the source’s displayed $a^2$ in the finite row is a typographical slip for $ar^2$.

contentBlocks.title: Cancel a finite telescoping sum
contentBlocks.strategy: Decompose first, then show the two surviving boundary terms before taking a limit.

steps.label: Take the limit
steps.text: Since $1/(k+1)\to0$, the series converges with sum 1.

contentBlocks.result: Cancellation proves the sum only after the finite partial sum is written.
contentBlocks.verification: For $k=1$, $s_1=1/2$ agrees with the first term; the infinite value is 1.

exercises.outcome: Determine a signed geometric series from its finite partial sums and common ratio.
exercises.prompt: For $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}5(-2/3)^{n-1}$, find $s_k$, decide convergence, and give the sum. Explain why the sign changes do not imply divergence.
exercises.hint: The first term is 5, the ratio is $-2/3$, and there are $k$ terms through index $k$.
exercises.solution: Subtract $r s_k$ from $s_k$ to obtain $s_k=5[1-(-2/3)^k]/[1-(-2/3)]=3[1-(-2/3)^k]$. Since $|-2/3|<1$, the final power tends to zero and the series sums to 3. Alternation alone is not a divergence test.
rubric: Use $k$ terms, ending at exponent $k-1$.
Check the absolute value of the ratio.
Take a limit of partial sums, not just a term limit.

exercises.outcome: Use finite boundary terms to evaluate a telescoping series with a two-step shift.
exercises.prompt: Find the exact sum of $\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}2/[(n+1)(n+3)]$. Write the $N$th partial sum from $n=2$ through $n=N$ first.
exercises.hint: $2/[(n+1)(n+3)]=1/(n+1)-1/(n+3)$. List the first two positive and last two negative terms.
exercises.solution: For $N\ge2$, $s_N=\sum_{n=2}^{N}[1/(n+1)-1/(n+3)]=1/3+1/4-1/(N+2)-1/(N+3)$. The two trailing terms tend to zero, so the series sums to $7/12$.
rubric: Decompose with the two-step shift correctly.
Keep both surviving terms at each boundary.
Take the limit after forming the finite sum.

sections.title: Necessary is not sufficient
sections.text: If partial sums converge, then $a_{n}=S_{n}-S_{n-1}\to 0$. Thus failure of $a_{n}\to 0$ proves divergence. A zero term limit is inconclusive: $\sum 1/n$ diverges, whereas $\sum 1/n^{2}$ converges.

sections.title: A harmonic-series proof
sections.text: Group terms from $2^{k-1}+1$ to $2^k$. There are $2^{k-1}$ terms, each at least $1/2^k$, so each group contributes at least $1/2$. Arbitrarily many groups force partial sums to grow without bound, despite individual terms tending to zero.

exercise.prompt: What does the term test say about $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n/(n+1)$ and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n^2$?
exercise.hint: Compute the term limits and distinguish a verdict from inconclusiveness.
exercise.solution: The first term limit is 1, so its series diverges. The second term limit is zero, so this test alone gives no verdict; a $p$-series or integral argument proves convergence.
rubric: Use the test only to rule out convergence.
Do not call the second result a proof of convergence.

contentBlocks.title: Shrinking terms can still have unbounded partial sums
contentBlocks.strategy: Group consecutive harmonic terms into blocks that each contribute at least one half.

steps.label: Bound a block
steps.text: For each $j\ge1$, the indices $2^{j-1}+1$ through $2^j$ give $2^{j-1}$ terms, each at least $1/2^j$, so their sum is at least $1/2$.

steps.label: Count blocks
steps.text: $H_{2^m}\ge1+m/2\to\infty$. Since all terms are positive, the full partial-sum sequence is unbounded and the series diverges.

steps.label: Compare with term limit
steps.text: Yet $1/n\to0$. The term test gives no convergence verdict when the term limit is zero.

contentBlocks.result: The limit of terms and limit of partial sums answer different questions.
contentBlocks.verification: The notes use a strict lower bound for most blocks; the weak inequality here holds for every $m\ge1$, including $m=1$.

exercises.outcome: Construct an unbounded partial-sum subsequence despite terms tending to zero.
exercises.prompt: Does $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/(2n)$ converge? Use partial sums at $N=2^m$ and explain what the term test can and cannot say.
exercises.hint: The partial sum is one half of $H_N$. Use the dyadic block bound for $H_{2^m}$.
exercises.solution: The terms tend to zero, so the term test alone is inconclusive. But $\sum_{n=1}^{2^m}1/(2n)=H_{2^m}/2\ge1/2+m/4\to\infty$. Thus the full positive partial-sum sequence is unbounded and the series diverges.
rubric: State that a zero term limit is inconclusive.
Give an unbounded sequence of finite partial sums.
Explain why this proves series divergence.

sections.title: A comparison of positive tails
sections.text: If $f$ is positive, continuous and decreasing eventually, with $a_n=f(n)$, then $\sum a_n$ and $\int f$ share convergence behavior. Finite initial exceptions do not affect convergence. This is not an equality between sum and integral.

sections.title: A logarithmic benchmark
sections.text: For $n\geq 2$, compare $\sum 1/[n(\log n)^p]$ with $\int_2^\infty dx/[x(\log x)^p]$. Positivity and eventual decrease hold for every fixed real $p$. Substituting $u=\log x$ gives $\int_{\log 2}^{\infty}u^{-p}\,du$: it converges exactly when $p>1$. The boundary $p=1$ diverges, despite the extra logarithm. This benchmark is useful when a plain $p$-series comparison loses the decisive $\log$ factor.

sections.title: Bound the remainder
sections.text: For a convergent positive decreasing series, $\int_{N+1}^\infty f(x)\,dx\le\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty a_n\le\int_N^\infty f(x)\,dx$. For $a_n=1/n^2$ this gives $1/(N+1)\le R_N\le1/N$, a usable accuracy guarantee.

exercise.prompt: How large must $N$ be to guarantee remainder at most $0.001$ for $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n^2$?
exercise.hint: Use the upper integral bound $1/N$.
exercise.solution: $N\geq 1000$ suffices, since $R_N\leq 1/N\leq 0.001$. The bound is conservative and does not claim equality.
rubric: Use the upper bound for a guarantee.
State the positive decreasing hypothesis.

sections.title: Match the inequality to the conclusion
sections.text: For nonnegative terms, $a_n\le b_n$ and convergence of $\sum b_n$ imply convergence of $\sum a_n$. If $a_n\ge b_n$ and $\sum b_n$ diverges, $\sum a_n$ diverges. Reversing these directions gives no conclusion.

sections.title: Limit comparison
sections.text: For positive $a_n,b_n$, if $a_{n}/b_{n}\to L$ with $0<L<\infty$, the series share behavior. For $a_{n}=1/(n^{2}+n)$, use $b_{n}=1/n^{2}$: their ratio $n/(n+1)\to 1$, so the series converges. Ratio zero or infinity requires a one-sided argument rather than the same equivalence.

exercise.prompt: Decide whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/\sqrt{n^2+1}$ converges.
exercise.hint: Compare to $1/n$ and compute the ratio.
exercise.solution: The ratio $n/\sqrt{n^{2}+1}=1/\sqrt{1+1/n^{2}}$ tends to 1. The harmonic series diverges, so this positive series diverges.
rubric: Choose the dominant-power comparison.
Verify a finite strictly positive ratio.

contentBlocks.title: Alternating Series Test (imported)
contentBlocks.statement: If $b_n>0$ decreases to $0$, then $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n-1}b_n$ converges. This alone does not decide absolute convergence.
hypotheses: The signs alternate and the magnitudes $b_n$ are eventually nonincreasing and tend to $0$.

contentBlocks.title: Convergence and absolute convergence are separate
contentBlocks.strategy: First establish the signed series using the alternating test, then test its magnitudes with a positive-series benchmark.
contentBlocks.setup: Classify $S=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n-1}/\sqrt n$, the example on MH1101 Chapter 05 Notes physical page 17.

steps.label: Check the alternating hypotheses
steps.text: The positive magnitudes $b_n=1/\sqrt n$ decrease and tend to $0$, so the Alternating Series Test proves convergence of $S$.

steps.label: Test absolute convergence separately
steps.text: Taking absolute values removes the signs and produces a $p$-series with $p=1/2\le1$, which diverges.

contentBlocks.result: $S$ is conditionally convergent: the signed sum converges, but its absolute-value series diverges.
contentBlocks.verification: The fact that $b_n\to0$ is necessary but does not by itself prove convergence; the decrease and alternating signs supply the signed-series verdict.

sections.title: Separate two convergence questions
sections.text: Absolute convergence means $\sum|a_n|$ converges and implies convergence of $\sum a_n$. Conditional convergence means $\sum a_n$ converges but $\sum|a_n|$ diverges. The alternating harmonic series is conditional: its magnitudes decrease to zero, but their harmonic sum diverges.

sections.title: Alternating remainder
sections.text: If positive magnitudes decrease to zero, the error after $N$ alternating terms has magnitude at most the next term and its sign matches the next term. For $\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^{n+1}/n$, the error is at most $1/(N+1)$. Without eventual decrease, this bound needs another justification.

exercise.prompt: Classify $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^n/n^2$.
exercise.hint: Test the absolute-value series first.
exercise.solution: Its absolute-value series $\sum 1/n^{2}$ converges, so the original series converges absolutely. Calling it conditional merely because signs alternate is incorrect.
rubric: Test magnitudes independently.
Use the definition of conditional convergence.

exercises.outcome: Classify a signed alternating series by checking its magnitudes and its absolute-value series separately.
exercises.prompt: Classify $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n-1}n/(n^2+1)$ as absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent. Justify both tests you use.
exercises.hint: For $b_n=n/(n^2+1)$, inspect the derivative of $x/(x^2+1)$ on $x\ge1$. Compare the positive series with $\sum 1/n$ by a limit ratio.
exercises.solution: For $x\ge1$, the derivative of $x/(x^2+1)$ is $(1-x^2)/(x^2+1)^2\le0$. Thus $b_n$ decreases to $0$, so the alternating series converges. But $b_n/(1/n)=n^2/(n^2+1)\to1$; limit comparison with the divergent harmonic series shows $\sum b_n$ diverges. The signed series is conditionally convergent.
rubric: Establish positive magnitudes, eventual decrease and zero limit before applying the alternating test.
Test absolute values using a valid positive-series comparison.
State conditional convergence only after both verdicts.

sections.title: Different tests suit different forms
sections.text: For $a_{n}=x^n/n$!, the absolute ratio is $|x|/(n+1)\to 0$, so the series converges for every fixed $x$. For $a_{n}=(n/(2n+1))^n$, the nth-root magnitude tends to $1/2$, giving absolute convergence without expanding a complicated neighboring-term ratio.

sections.title: A limit of one is inconclusive
sections.text: Both $1/n$ and $1/n^{2}$ have ratio and nth-root limits equal to 1, yet one series diverges and the other converges. For ratio or root limit below 1, conclude absolute convergence; above 1, terms fail to tend to zero. More general limsup forms need their own statement.

sections.title: Choose the test from the term's structure
sections.text: Before calculating a limit, ask what conclusion is needed. If terms do not approach zero, stop: the series diverges. For nonnegative terms resembling $1/[n(\log n)^p]$, justify the integral test and check its positivity and decrease hypotheses. A factorial often favors the ratio test; a whole expression raised to $n$ favors the root test. An alternating sign calls for separate absolute and signed convergence checks. If a ratio or root limit is 1, switch to a comparison or integral benchmark. For a power series, the ratio or root calculation only finds the open radius; test both endpoints as separate numerical series.

exercise.prompt: Choose a test before calculating for each: $A=\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}1/[n(\log n)^2]$, $B=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n/3^n$, and $C=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(x-2)^n/n$. Classify $A$ and $B$; find $C$'s interval, checking both endpoints.
exercise.hint: A has a logarithmic benchmark, $B$ has an exponential and factorial factors ratio, and $C$ needs a radius followed by two separate endpoint series.
exercise.solution: For A use the integral test: $f(x)=1/[x(\log x)^{2}]$ is positive, continuous and eventually decreasing; $u=\log x$ makes the tail integral finite, so A converges. For $B$ the ratio of successive positive terms tends to $1/3$, so $B$ converges. For $C$ the ratio gives $|x-2|<1$. At $x=1$ the alternating harmonic series converges conditionally; at $x=3$ the harmonic series diverges. Its interval is $[1,3)$. The ratio limit 1 at the endpoints alone proves neither result.
rubric: Justify each test choice from the term structure before computing.
State the integral-test hypotheses for A and the ratio limit for $B$.
Treat $C$'s two endpoints independently and distinguish conditional convergence.

sections.title: Endpoints are separate series
sections.text: For $\sum_{n=1}^\infty x^n/n$, the ratio test gives convergence for $|x|<1$ and divergence for $|x|>1$. At $x=1$ it is harmonic and diverges; at $x=-1$ it is alternating harmonic and converges conditionally. The interval is $[-1,1)$, not an automatically closed radius interval.

sections.title: The center shifts everything
sections.text: For $\sum a_{n}(x-c)^n$, the radius measures distance from $c$. A radius can be zero or infinite. Partial sums are polynomials; their limit is defined only on the convergence set, and may behave differently at its boundary.

exercise.prompt: Find the interval of convergence of $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(x-2)^n/(n\,3^n)$.
exercise.hint: Use $|x-2|<3$, then inspect both endpoints.
exercise.solution: The radius is 3 about 2. At $x=-1$ the series is alternating harmonic and converges; at $x=5$ it is harmonic and diverges. The interval is $[-1,5)$.
rubric: Shift the radius interval around the correct center.
Test each endpoint independently.

sections.title: Operate inside the radius
sections.text: A power series may be differentiated or integrated term by term inside its radius, and the new series has the same radius. Endpoint convergence can change. The theorem relies on uniform control on each smaller closed interval and is imported here, rather than proved by formal symbol manipulation.

sections.title: Derive a logarithmic series
sections.text: Integrating $\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n=1/(1-x)$ from $0$ to $x$ gives $\sum_{n=1}^\infty x^n/n=-\ln(1-x)$ for $|x|<1$. The integration constant is fixed by the zero value at $x=0$. At $x=-1$ an additional endpoint argument is needed; interior validity alone does not prove it.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x^n/n$ inside its radius. What happens at $x=-1$?
exercise.hint: The differentiated coefficients lose the factor $1/n$.
exercise.solution: The derivative series is $\sum_{n=1}^\infty x^{n-1}=1/(1-x)$ for $|x|<1$. At $x=-1$ its terms alternate $\pm 1$ and do not tend to zero, so it diverges although the original series converges there.
rubric: State the open interval of termwise validity.
Recheck endpoints after differentiation.

contentBlocks.title: Taylor’s finite remainder theorem (imported)
contentBlocks.statement: For $x$ near $a$, $f(x)=P_n(x)+f^{(n+1)}(\xi)(x-a)^{n+1}/(n+1)!$ for some $\xi$ between $a$ and $x$.
hypotheses: $f$ has $n+1$ continuous derivatives on an interval containing $a$ and $x$.
prerequisites: Mean value theorem and repeated differentiation

sections.title: A polynomial is not automatically an infinite expansion
sections.text: Taylor’s polynomial uses derivatives at one center. Taylor’s theorem supplies a finite remainder under sufficient differentiability; equality with the infinite Taylor series additionally requires that remainder to tend to zero. Smoothness alone does not ensure that.

sections.title: A smooth counterexample
sections.text: Define $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=\exp(-1/x^{2})$ for $x\ne 0$. Every derivative at zero vanishes (exponential decay dominates each inverse power), so its Taylor series is zero, yet $f(x)>0$ away from zero. For $e^x$ on a bounded interval, by contrast, the factorial remainder bound tends to zero.

sections.title: Choose a nonzero center and certify a degree
sections.text: Center $\log x$ at $a=1$: $P_n(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^{k+1}(x-1)^k/k$. For $x=1.2$, $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\leq n!$ on $[1,1.2]$, so Taylor's finite remainder obeys $|R_{n}|\leq0.2^{n+1}/(n+1)$. Degree 2 gives only a 0.00267 guarantee; degree 3 gives $0.0004<0.001$ and $P_{3}(1.2)=0.182666…$. This finite accuracy claim follows from the derivative bound. Equality with an infinite series is a separate limit claim requiring $R_{n}\to 0$.

exercise.prompt: Use a Taylor polynomial centered at $a=1$ to approximate $\log(1.2)$ with certified error below $0.001$. Choose a degree from a remainder bound; state separately what would justify equality with the infinite Taylor series.
exercise.hint: On [1,1.2], |$\frac{d^{n+1}}{dx^{n+1}}\log x|\leq n$!, hence $|R_{n}|\leq0.2^{n+1}/(n+1)$. Compare degrees 2 and 3.
exercise.solution: Degree 3 suffices: $P_{3}(1.2)=0.2-0.2^{2}/2+0.2^{3}/3\approx 0.182667$ and $|R_{3}|\leq 0.2^{4}/4=0.0004$. The degree-2 bound is $0.2^{3}/3\approx 0.00267$, so it does not certify the target. The infinite representation additionally needs proof that $R_{n}\to 0$ (which this bound provides at $x=1.2$)..
rubric: Center at 1 and compute the degree-3 polynomial.
Use a derivative bound to certify the requested error; do not infer it from a decimal approximation.
Separate finite accuracy from equality to the infinite series.

sections.title: Coefficients and termination
sections.text: The coefficient of $x^n$ in $(1+x)^\alpha$ is $\alpha(\alpha-1)\cdots(\alpha-n+1)/n!$, with constant term $1$. For nonnegative integer $\alpha$ the series terminates as a polynomial. Otherwise its expansion is valid for $|x|<1$ and endpoints need separate analysis.

sections.title: A concrete expansion
sections.text: For $\alpha =1/2$ the first terms are $1+x/2-x^{2}/8+x^{3}/16$. This approximates $\sqrt{1+x}$ near zero. For $\alpha =-1$ the coefficients alternate and recover $1/(1+x)=1-x+x^{2}-…$ inside the radius.

exercise.prompt: Find the quadratic Taylor approximation of $(1+x)^{-2}$ at zero.
exercise.hint: Use $\alpha =-2$ in the coefficient formula.
exercise.solution: The first terms are $1-2x+3x^{2}$, with remainder of order $x^{3}$ near zero. The infinite nonterminating series has radius 1.
rubric: Divide the second falling product by 2!.
Do not treat the approximation as exact.

sections.title: Expand far enough to survive cancellation
sections.text: For $(\sin x-x)/x^3$, use $\sin x=x-x^3/6+O(x^5)$. After cancellation and division, the expression is $-1/6+O(x^2)$, so the limit is $-1/6$. Stopping at $\sin x\approx x$ would discard the decisive term.

sections.title: Meaning of error symbols
sections.text: $R(x)=O(x^k)$ means $|R(x)|\le C|x|^k$ in a sufficiently small neighborhood for some fixed $C$. $R(x)=o(x^k)$ means its ratio to $x^k$ tends to zero. Dividing an expansion by $x^m$ also divides its error; retain enough orders to make the resulting error vanish.

exercise.hint: Keep the cubic term and a controlled higher-order remainder.
exercise.solution: Taylor gives numerator $x^{3}/6+O(x^{4})$, so the quotient is $1/6+O(x)$ and tends to $1/6$.
rubric: Retain the first uncancelled term.
Track the remainder after division.

sections.title: Separate points and displacements
sections.text: Points describe locations; their difference is a displacement vector. For $A=(1,-1,2)$, $B=(3,2,2)$, $B-A=(2,3,0)$ has length $\sqrt{13}$. The dot product $u\cdot v=|u||v|\cos \theta$ measures alignment; normalization $v/|v|$ requires $v\ne 0$.

sections.title: Projection is a signed component
sections.text: The scalar component of $v$ along a unit vector $e$ is $v\cdot e$, and the vector projection is $(v\cdot e)e$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|u\cdot v|\leq |u||v|$, the estimate later used for gradient bounds. Orthogonal vectors have dot product zero; the zero vector has no direction.

exercise.prompt: Project $v=(3,4,0)$ onto the direction $(1,1,0)$.
exercise.hint: Normalize the direction first.
exercise.solution: The unit direction is $e=(1,1,0)/\sqrt{2}$. The scalar component is $7/\sqrt{2}$ and vector projection is $(7/2,7/2,0)$. The residual $(-1/2,1/2,0)$ is perpendicular to $e$.
rubric: Normalize a nonzero vector.
Distinguish scalar component from vector projection.
Check the residual dot product.

sections.title: One trace, several clocks
sections.text: The circle $r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$ traces once for $0\le t\le2\pi$ and twice for $0\le t\le4\pi$. The image set is unchanged, but traversal-sensitive integrals count both passes. Reversing $t$ reverses orientation; a positive increasing change of clock preserves it.

sections.title: Speed enters length
sections.text: For $r(t)=(\cos2t,\sin2t)$, speed is $2$. On $[0,\pi]$ the length is $\int_0^\pi2\,dt=2\pi$, one traversal. The unit-speed parameter is arc length, not every parameter called $t$.

exercise.prompt: Compare the lengths of $r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$ on $[0,2\pi]$ and $[0,4\pi]$.
exercise.hint: Length integrates speed over the actual parameter interval.
exercise.solution: The lengths are $2\pi$ and $4\pi$. The geometric image is the same circle, but the second curve traverses it twice.
rubric: Use the interval as part of the parametrized curve.
Do not confuse image length with traversal length.

sections.title: Use the defining constraint
sections.text: A line from $A$ to $B$ is $A+t(B-A)$, $0\le t\le1$. An ellipse $x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2=1$ is $(a\cos t,b\sin t)$. For an intersection with $z=x^2+y^2$, substitute a planar parametrization into $z$ to satisfy both equations.

sections.title: Check coverage and orientation
sections.text: The intersection $x^2+y^2=1$ and $z=x+y$ can be written $(\cos t,\sin t,\cos t+\sin t)$, $0\le t\le2\pi$. It traverses once counterclockwise in $xy$ projection. Substitution verifies membership; the full parameter interval verifies coverage.

exercise.prompt: Parametrize the line segment from $(1,0,2)$ to $(0,3,1)$.
exercise.hint: Add $t$ times the endpoint difference.
exercise.solution: $r(t)=(1-t,3t,2-t)$, $0\leq t\leq 1$. At 0 and 1 it gives the assigned endpoints, with orientation from the first to the second.
rubric: Supply the parameter interval.
Check both endpoints and direction.

sections.title: Regularity belongs to the parametrization
sections.text: A regular curve has nonzero velocity. The map $r(t)=(t^{3},0)$ stops at zero but its image is a straight line, so a singular parameter need not mean singular geometry. The cusp $(t^{2},t^{3})$ has zero velocity at zero and requires a separate local analysis.

sections.title: Length and reparametrization
sections.text: For a piecewise continuously differentiable curve, length is $\int |r'(t)|dt$ over its pieces. A regular change of parameter preserves length after the speed factor and bounds are transformed. Unit tangent $r\prime/|r\prime|$ is defined only where speed is nonzero.

exercise.prompt: For $r(t)=(t,t^2)$, find speed and unit tangent at $t=1$.
exercise.hint: Differentiate components before taking the norm.
exercise.solution: $r'(1)=(1,2)$, speed $\sqrt{5}$, and unit tangent $(1,2)/\sqrt{5}$. The tangent line is $(1,1)+s(1,2)$.
rubric: Keep the selected point distinct from its velocity.
Normalize by speed.

contentBlocks.title: Intersect every input restriction
contentBlocks.text: For a real-valued expression in two variables, impose every operation's real-input condition at once. A square root in a denominator requires a strictly positive radicand, rather than merely a nonnegative one.

contentBlocks.title: Find the domain before drawing the graph
contentBlocks.strategy: Intersect the real square-root condition with the nonzero-denominator condition.
contentBlocks.setup: For the Lecture 01 expression $f(x,y)=x/\sqrt{y^{2}-x}$, find every allowed input.

steps.label: Require a real denominator
steps.text: A real square root needs $y^{2}-x\ge0$, but a denominator may not equal zero. Combine the conditions as $y^{2}-x>0$.

steps.label: State the planar region
steps.text: The natural domain is all points strictly to the left of the parabola $x=y^{2}$; points on that curve are excluded.

contentBlocks.result: The domain is $D=\{(x,y):x<y^{2}\}$, even where the numerator also vanishes.
contentBlocks.verification: At $(0,0)$ the denominator is zero, so a zero numerator cannot make that boundary input valid.

contentBlocks.title: Keep the domain and attainable heights
contentBlocks.text: A level set is the preimage $\{(x,y)\in D:f(x,y)=k\}$, so an equation found by squaring must be checked against the original square root and its domain. A contour at the maximum height may collapse to one point.

contentBlocks.title: A contour is a horizontal slice
contentBlocks.strategy: Set the height equal to the requested level, then solve for the planar radius without losing the domain.

steps.label: Keep the height range
steps.text: The square root is nonnegative, so only $0\le k\le6$ can occur. Squaring $f(x,y)=k$ now preserves equivalence.

steps.label: Read each level
steps.text: For $0\le k<6$ the contour is a circle of radius $\sqrt{36-k^2}$. The $k=0$ contour is the disk boundary; the $k=6$ contour is the single point $(0,0)$, not a circle of positive radius.

contentBlocks.result: Increasing the level shrinks the concentric contours toward the top of the hemisphere.
contentBlocks.verification: Substituting the radius into the original square root gives $\sqrt{k^2}=k$ because $k\ge0$.

exercises.outcome: Combine a logarithm restriction with a denominator square-root restriction.
exercises.prompt: Find and describe the natural domain of $g(x,y)=\log(y-x^2)/\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}$. Are either boundary curves included?
exercises.hint: The logarithm argument must be strictly positive; the denominator square root must be strictly positive too.
exercises.solution: Both conditions must hold: $y>x^2$ and $x^2+y^2<4$. Their intersection is the domain. Neither the parabola $y=x^2$ nor the circle $x^2+y^2=4$ is included, even where the other condition holds.
rubric: Use a strict inequality for the logarithm argument.
Exclude zero from the denominator radicand.
Intersect both restrictions and identify excluded boundaries.

exercises.outcome: Convert specified heights on a new hemisphere into planar contours, including a degenerate top level.
exercises.prompt: For $h(x,y)=\sqrt{25-x^2-y^2}$ on its natural domain, describe the level sets $h=3$, $h=4$, and $h=5$. Why is $h=-3$ empty?
exercises.hint: First restrict heights to $[0,5]$, then solve $x^2+y^2=25-k^2$.
exercises.solution: The levels 3 and 4 are circles centered at the origin with radii 4 and 3. Level 5 is the singleton $(0,0)$. Level $-3$ is empty because a real square root is nonnegative.
rubric: Check the attainable height range before squaring.
Give the two nondegenerate radii and the singleton top level.
Reject the negative level using the original expression.

sections.title: Graph, level set, parametrization
sections.text: A graph $z=f(x,y)$ has one height for each allowed planar input. A level set $F(x,y,z)=c$ may fail to be a graph in a chosen direction. A sphere has two $z$ values over most of its disk projection and needs upper and lower branches or surface charts.

sections.title: Read slices deliberately
sections.text: For $z=x^{2}-y^{2}$, fixing $y$ gives upward parabolas and fixing $x$ gives downward parabolas. Level zero is the pair $y=\pm x$; positive and negative levels give differently oriented hyperbolas. Distinguish a horizontal contour from a vertical slice.

exercise.prompt: Why is $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ not globally a graph $z=f(x,y)$?
exercise.hint: Inspect the two points above $(0,0)$.
exercise.solution: Both $(0,0,1)$ and $(0,0,-1)$ lie on the sphere. A single-valued graph cannot assign both heights; separate hemisphere graphs are possible over appropriate domains.
rubric: Use an explicit repeated planar input.
Distinguish local representation from global representation.
exercise.solutionTex: (0,0,1),(0,0,-1)\in S\implies S\text{ is not a single }z\text{-graph}

contentBlocks.title: Openness and closedness are separate tests
contentBlocks.text: In $\mathbb R^2$, openness requires an interior ball around every member. Closedness requires every limit point to belong. One included boundary point can refute openness, and one excluded limit point can refute closedness.

contentBlocks.title: Classify with an interior ball and a missing limit point
contentBlocks.strategy: Test openness at an included boundary and closedness at an excluded accumulation point.
contentBlocks.setup: Consider $S=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:0<x^2+y^2\le4\}$ in the ambient plane.

steps.label: Test an included edge
steps.text: $(2,0)\in S$, but every open ball centered there contains points of radius greater than 2. Thus $S$ is not open.

steps.label: Test a missing limit point
steps.text: $(1/n,0)\in S$ for $n\ge1$ and tends to $(0,0)\notin S$. Thus $S$ is not closed.

contentBlocks.result: $S$ is neither open nor closed in $\mathbb R^2$.
contentBlocks.verification: The verdict uses the ambient Euclidean plane and treats openness and closedness as separate questions.

exercises.outcome: Give separate witnesses for openness and closedness in the plane.
exercises.prompt: In $\mathbb R^2$, classify $H=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le4,\ y>0\}$ as open, closed, both, or neither. Give a witness for each failed property.
exercises.hint: Inspect a point on the included circular arc and a sequence tending to the excluded diameter.
exercises.solution: It is neither. The point $(0,2)$ belongs to $H$ but no open ball around it stays inside the disk, so $H$ is not open. The points $(0,1/n)$ belong to $H$ and tend to $(0,0)$, which is excluded by $y>0$, so $H$ is not closed.
exercises.solutionTex: (0,2)\in H\text{ has no interior ball};\quad(0,1/n)\in H\to(0,0)\notin H
rubric: Use an included boundary point to refute openness.
Use an excluded limit point to refute closedness.
State the ambient space.

sections.title: Open balls encode all directions
sections.text: A ball $B(a,r)$ consists of points with distance less than $r$; its boundary sphere is excluded. A set is open when each member has some ball contained in it, and closed when it contains its limit points. A set can be neither open nor closed.

sections.title: Boundary depends on ambient space
sections.text: The disk $x^{2}+y^{2}<1$ is open in the plane, but the same disk embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ has no three-dimensional interior. For limits on a restricted domain, only points belonging to that domain are admissible approaches.

exercise.prompt: Classify the annulus $1<\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\le 2$ as open, closed, or neither in $\mathbb R^2$.
exercise.hint: Test the included outer boundary and excluded inner boundary.
exercise.solution: It is neither: at an outer-circle point every ball leaves the set, while a sequence approaching the inner circle has a limit outside the set.
rubric: Name a witness against openness.
Name a missing limit point against closedness.

sections.title: One radius must cover every approach
sections.text: For a multivariable limit, every domain point with $0<|x-a|<\delta$ must meet the output tolerance. A separate $\delta$ for each ray is insufficient unless one common positive radius works uniformly.

sections.title: Use norm inequalities
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=2x-3y$ at zero, $|2x-3y|\leq \sqrt{13}\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. Choosing $\delta =\varepsilon /\sqrt{13}$ proves the limit zero over every approach, including curved paths.

exercise.prompt: Prove $x^2+y^2$ tends to zero at the origin with an explicit $\delta$.
exercise.hint: Write the function in terms of the Euclidean radius $r$.
