supplementalBlocks.title: Solve the positive box equations
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check regularity and domain, solve the constraint system, then justify the global conclusion separately.

steps.label: System
steps.text: $yz=\lambda(y+2z)$, $xz=\lambda(x+2z)$, and $xy=2\lambda(x+y)$.

steps.label: Eliminate
steps.text: Positivity implies $\lambda>0$. Multiply the first two equations by $x$ and $y$ to get $x(y+2z)=y(x+2z)$, hence $x=y$. Compare with the third equation to get $x=2z$.

supplementalBlocks.result: The only positive multiplier candidate is $(2,2,1)$; its global status still needs proof.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Physical pages 15–16 give this candidate; all divisions use positive quantities.

supplementalBlocks.title: A global bound without compactness
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check regularity and domain, solve the constraint system, then justify the global conclusion separately.
supplementalBlocks.setup: For every positive feasible box with $xy+2xz+2yz=12$, bound $V=xyz$.

steps.label: Equality
steps.text: $V\le4$. Equality requires $xy=2xz=2yz=4$, giving uniquely $x=y=2$, $z=1$.

supplementalBlocks.result: $V$ has global maximum $4$ at the unique box $(2,2,1)$ despite the noncompact feasible set.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Physical pages 16–17 show nonclosed/unbounded witnesses and this AM–GM certificate.

exercises.outcome: Transfer open-box modeling and global certification.
exercises.prompt: An open-top box has base-material cost $1$ per unit area and side-material cost $3/2$ per unit area. With budget $18$, maximize its volume over positive dimensions. Use multipliers for candidates, then a separate global certificate.
exercises.hint: The budget is $A=xy+3xz+3yz=18$. Solve the positive multiplier equations; then apply AM–GM to $xy$, $3xz$, $3yz$.
exercises.solution: $\nabla A=(y+3z,x+3z,3x+3y)$ is nonzero on the positive domain. The positive multiplier equations are $yz=\lambda(y+3z)$, $xz=\lambda(x+3z)$, and $xy=3\lambda(x+y)$. Multiplying the first two by $x$ and $y$ gives $x=y$; then the third gives $\lambda=x/6$, and the first gives $x=3z$. Thus $3x^2=18$ and the candidate is $(x,y,z)=(\sqrt6,\sqrt6,\sqrt6/3)$. For every feasible box, $(9V^2)^{1/3}=((xy)(3xz)(3yz))^{1/3}\le18/3=6$, hence $V\le2\sqrt6$. Equality requires $xy=3xz=3yz=6$, reached uniquely at that candidate.
rubric: Model the higher side-material cost correctly.
Check regularity and solve every positive candidate.
Use equality in AM–GM to certify the global maximum.

sections.title: Independence matters
sections.text:
For two constraints $g=c$ and $h=d$ in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, independent gradients give a tangent direction $
abla g	imes 
abla h$. At a constrained extremum, $
abla f$ lies in their span: $
abla f=\lambda 
abla g+\mu 
abla h$. Dependent gradients invalidate this regular argument.

sections.title: Reduce when possible
sections.text: On $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=1$ and $z=0$, maximizing $x+y$ reduces to the unit circle in the xy-plane. The two gradients $(2x,2y,0)$ and $(0,0,1)$ are independent everywhere on the feasible circle, so the multiplier method is legitimate.

sections.title: Two gradients must have rank two
sections.text:
For two equality constraints in $\mathbb R^3$, the regular theorem needs $
abla g$ and $
abla h$ linearly independent at the feasible extremum. Physical page 18 states only a nonzero-gradient pair; that is insufficient. If the gradients are dependent, inspect the feasible geometry directly before using $
abla f=\lambda
abla g+\mu
abla h$.

sections.title: The source gives a prompt only
sections.text: Physical page 19 asks for extrema of $x^2+y^2+z^2$ on the cone $z^2=x^2+y^2$ intersected with $x+y-z+1=0$. Physical pages 20–23 carry continuation headings but no readable worked solution. The calculation below is an independent derivation, not a transcription of source answers.

exercise.prompt: Find extrema of $x$ on $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ with $y=z$.
exercise.hint: Either use two multipliers or observe the feasible circle contains $(\pm 1,0,0)$.
exercise.solution: Since $|x|\leq 1$ on the sphere and both $(\pm 1,0,0)$ satisfy $y=z$, extrema are $\pm 1$ at those points. The constraint gradients are independent throughout the intersection.
rubric: Check feasibility of equality cases.
Identify the regularity assumption when using multipliers.

supplementalBlocks.title: Nonzero gradients can still be dependent
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check regularity and domain, solve the constraint system, then justify the global conclusion separately.

steps.label: Feasible set
steps.text: $x=0$ and $y^2+z^2=0$ leave only the origin, so $f$ has both a constrained minimum and maximum there.

steps.label: Rank failure
steps.text:
At the origin, $
abla g=
abla h=(1,0,0)$: both are nonzero but dependent. $
abla f=(0,1,0)$ is not in their span.

supplementalBlocks.result: The source page’s nonzero condition cannot imply the two-multiplier conclusion; rank two is required.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Independent counterexample to the insufficient condition printed on physical page 18.

supplementalBlocks.title: Derive the cone-plane answer independently
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Check regularity and domain, solve the constraint system, then justify the global conclusion separately.

steps.label: Reduce
steps.text: Put $u=x+1$, $v=y+1$. Eliminating $z=x+y+1=u+v-1$ gives $uv=1/2$ and $f=2(u+v-1)^2$.

steps.label: Compare branches
steps.text: $u,v$ have the same sign. On the positive branch, $u+v\ge\sqrt2$, with equality at $u=v=1/\sqrt2$. On the negative branch, $u+v\le-\sqrt2$, giving larger $|z|$.

steps.label: Global verdict
steps.text: The minimum is $2(\sqrt2-1)^2$ at $x=y=1/\sqrt2-1$, $z=\sqrt2-1$. As $u\to\infty$ with $v=1/(2u)$, $f\to\infty$, so no maximum exists.

steps.label: Regularity
steps.text: For $g=z^2-x^2-y^2$ and $h=x+y-z+1$, dependent $\nabla g$ and $\nabla h$ on the cone would force the apex $(0,0,0)$, which is not on the plane; rank two holds on this feasible set.

supplementalBlocks.result: The source prompt has a unique global minimum and no maximum; this solution is derived here, because source pages 20–23 show none.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Checked algebra and feasible points independently against the page 19 prompt; no source solution claimed.

exercises.outcome: Decide whether nonzero constraint gradients justify two multipliers.
exercises.prompt: At the origin, take $g=x$, $h=2x+y^2+z^2$, and $f=z$, with $g=h=0$. Does the two-multiplier necessary condition apply?
exercises.hint: Find the feasible set and compare the two constraint gradients at the origin.
exercises.solution:
The feasible set is only the origin, so it is a constrained extremum of $f$. Yet $
abla g=(1,0,0)$ and $
abla h=(2,0,0)$ are nonzero but dependent; $
abla f=(0,0,1)$ lies outside their span. The regular two-multiplier theorem does not apply.
rubric: Check linear independence, not mere nonzero status.
Show the feasible geometry and failed span conclusion.

exercises.outcome: Solve a regular two-constraint problem independently.
exercises.prompt: Find both extrema of $f=z$ on $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ and $x+y=0$, checking regularity.
exercises.hint: Use $x=-y$ and $z^2=1-2x^2$; check the two constraint gradients are independent on the feasible circle.
exercises.solution: $-1\le z\le1$, with maximum $1$ at $(0,0,1)$ and minimum $-1$ at $(0,0,-1)$. The gradients $(2x,2y,2z)$ and $(1,1,0)$ cannot be parallel on the feasible set: parallelism plus $x+y=0$ would force $x=y=z=0$, contradicting the sphere.
rubric: Identify both feasible equality points.
Justify rank two on the full feasible set.

sections.title: Cells contribute value times area
sections.text: Over a rectangle, a double Riemann sum adds $f(\text{sample})\Delta x\Delta y$. Both widths are essential. Integrability requires independence of increasingly fine tagged partitions; a single sampled mesh is a numerical approximation.

sections.title: Signed volume versus physical volume
sections.text: If $f\geq 0$, the integral is volume under its graph. If $f$ takes both signs, it is signed accumulation. For $f=x$ on $[-1,1]\times [0,1]$, the integral is zero while the volume between graph and plane is $\int |x|=1$.

exercise.prompt: Compute the double integral of constant 3 over $[0,2]\times [0,4]$.
exercise.hint: Every cell contributes three times its area.
exercise.solution: The rectangle area is 8, so the integral is 24. With density units $kg/m^{2}$ and coordinates in metres, the result is kilograms.
rubric: Include both dimensions of area.
Interpret the units of the integrand.

sections.title: A sufficient computational framework
sections.text: For a bounded region with a boundary of area zero and a function continuous on its closure, the double integral can be defined by extending the function by zero to a containing rectangle. The extension may jump at the region boundary but remains Riemann integrable under these sufficient assumptions.

sections.title: Name the stronger theorem
sections.text: The criterion that a bounded function on a rectangle is Riemann integrable when its discontinuity set has area zero is imported here. Lebesgue integration extends beyond Jordan regions and is an optional advanced framework, not a prerequisite silently hidden inside the elementary continuous-rectangle theorem.

exercise.prompt: Why can a continuous density on a disk be extended by zero for integration on a containing square?
exercise.hint: Where can new discontinuities occur?
exercise.solution: Only the circular boundary can acquire jumps. That boundary has area zero, so the bounded zero extension is Riemann integrable by the stated criterion. Its integral equals the disk integral.
rubric: Identify the possible discontinuity set.
Invoke the appropriate extension theorem.

sections.title: Order is a theorem, not typography
sections.text: A continuous function on a closed rectangle has equal double and iterated integrals. For zero extensions over ordinary piecewise smooth regions, a stronger integrability version is required because the extension may have boundary jumps.

sections.title: A sufficient extension for calculations
sections.text: For a bounded Riemann-integrable function whose slices are integrable apart from finitely many exceptional outer values, the iterated integrals agree with the double integral; changing bounded values on those exceptional slices does not affect it. In the Lebesgue setting, absolute integrability permits Fubini and nonnegativity permits Tonelli, but those are separate imported results.

exercise.prompt: Compute $\int_0^1\int_0^2(x+y)\,dy\,dx$ in both orders.
exercise.hint: The rectangle and continuous polynomial satisfy the elementary theorem.
exercise.solution: Integrating in $y$ gives $2x+2$, then total 3. Reversing gives $\int_0^2(1/2+y)\,dy=3$. The domain remains the same rectangle.
rubric: State why the swap is valid.
Keep each variable’s interval attached to it.

sections.title: Bounds describe a set
sections.text: The region $0\leq x\leq 1$, $x^{2}\leq y\leq x$ lies between a parabola and a line. For horizontal slices, $0\leq y\leq 1$ and $y\leq x\leq \sqrt{y}$. Derive these inequalities before changing the integration order.

sections.title: Split when one slice formula fails
sections.text: A region may need several Type I or Type II pieces. Splitting along an internal boundary does not duplicate area if pieces overlap only on boundaries of area zero. Draw or solve each boundary intersection and determine which curve actually limits a slice.

exercise.prompt: Reverse $\int_0^1\int_{x^2}^x f(x,y)\,dy\,dx$.
exercise.hint: Solve $y\geq x^{2}$ and $y\leq x$ in the nonnegative quadrant.
exercise.solution: The reversed integral is $\int_0^1\int_y^{\sqrt{y}}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy$. The conditions give $x\leq \sqrt{y}$ and $x\geq y$.
rubric: Derive both horizontal bounds.
Preserve the region and integrand.

sections.title: Linearity concerns values
sections.text: For integrable $f$,$g$, $\int (af+bg)=a\int f+b\int g$. It does not assert that $\int fg=(\int f)(\int g)$. A product separates only under additional structure, such as independent factors on a product rectangle.

sections.title: Additivity concerns regions
sections.text: If a region is split into pieces overlapping only on negligible boundaries, add their integrals. For signed accumulation, negative contributions remain negative. Overlapping pieces with positive area require subtracting the overlap to avoid double counting.

exercise.prompt: If $\iint_D f\,dA=2$ and $\iint_D g\,dA=-1$, find $\iint_D(3f-2g)\,dA$. Can you infer $\iint_D fg\,dA$?
exercise.hint: Apply linearity only to the linear combination.
exercise.solution: The first integral is $3\cdot 2-2\cdot (-1)=8$. The product integral cannot be determined from these two numbers alone.
rubric: Handle the negative coefficient.
Do not invent multiplicativity.

sections.title: Derive the factor geometrically
sections.text: A polar cell has radial thickness $dr$ and transverse length approximately $r\,d\theta$, so area is approximately $r\,dr\,d\theta$. The derivative columns of $(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ have determinant $r$, confirming the local scale for $r\ge0$.

sections.title: A coordinate singularity is not a hole
sections.text: At $r=0$ all angles describe one point and the determinant vanishes. For standard disk integrals this point has area zero and can be handled by a limiting argument. Angular endpoints also represent the same ray when using a full $2\pi$ interval.

exercise.prompt: Compute the area of the annular sector $1\le r\le 2$, $0\le \theta\le \pi/3$.
exercise.hint: Integrate the Jacobian $r$, not 1.
exercise.solution: The area is $\int_0^{\pi/3}\int_1^2r\,dr\,d\theta=(\pi /3)(3/2)=\pi /2$.
rubric: Include the radial factor.
Distinguish parameter-rectangle area from physical area.

sections.title: Derive the shifted disk
sections.text: For $(x-1)^2+y^2\le1$, substitute polar coordinates to get $r^2-2r\cos\theta\le0$. With $r\ge0$ and $r>0$ this gives $0<r\le2\cos\theta$, so $\cos\theta\ge0$. Choose $-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2$, with $r=0$ included separately.

sections.title: Verify the area
sections.text: The integral is $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\int_0^{2\cos\theta}r\,dr\,d\theta=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}2\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\pi$. This matches a disk of radius one. A centered fixed-radius sector would represent a different region.

exercise.prompt: Write polar bounds for $(x-2)^2+y^2\le 4$.
exercise.hint: Repeat the algebra with center and radius 2.
exercise.solution: The bounds are $-\pi /2\leq \theta \leq \pi /2$ and $0\leq r\leq 4cos \theta$. The area is $4\pi$, matching the disk radius 2.
rubric: Derive the angular range from nonnegative radius.
Handle the origin without dividing by zero.

sections.title: Volume cells need three widths
sections.text: A triple sum adds $f(\text{sample})\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z$. For $f=1$ it approximates volume; for mass density it approximates mass. A display containing only a few columns is a schematic, not a complete three-dimensional partition.

sections.title: Check a separable box
sections.text: For $f=xyz$ on $[0,1]\times [0,2]\times [0,3]$, continuity allows repeated integration and the product structure separates the result into $(1/2)\cdot 2\cdot (9/2)=9$. This separation depends on both the factorized integrand and rectangular domain.

exercise.prompt: Integrate constant density 5 on a box with side lengths 2,3,4.
exercise.hint: Multiply density by the volume.
exercise.solution: The integral is $5\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot 4=120$. If density is $kg/m^{3}$, this is mass in kg.
rubric: Include all three dimensions.
Interpret the measure and units.

sections.title: Project before setting height bounds
sections.text: The tetrahedron $x,y,z\geq 0$ with $x+y+z\leq 1$ projects onto $x,y\geq 0$, $x+y\leq 1$. Thus $0\leq x\leq 1$, $0\leq y\leq 1-x$, $0\leq z\leq 1-x-y$. The inner bounds depend only on outer variables.

sections.title: Each order describes the same solid
sections.text: A different outer coordinate requires a different projection. Writing all upper limits as 1 would replace the tetrahedron by a cube. Integrating 1 over the correct bounds gives volume $1/6$.

exercise.prompt: Write bounds with $x$ innermost for the same tetrahedron.
exercise.hint: Project onto the yz-plane.
exercise.solution: Use $0\leq z\leq 1$, $0\leq y\leq 1-z$, $0\leq x\leq 1-y-z$. Integrating 1 again yields $1/6$.
rubric: Derive the outer projection.
Keep an inner bound free of its own integration variable.

sections.title: A planar polar map plus height
sections.text: Cylindrical coordinates are $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$, $z=z$ with $r\ge0$. The volume Jacobian is $r$. The angle is measured around the $z$-axis; it does not tilt toward that axis.

sections.title: Identify surfaces by equations
sections.text: $r=2$ is a cylinder, $z=2$ a horizontal plane, and $z=r$ a cone above the plane. The $z$-axis has $r=0$ and nonunique $\theta$; this coordinate singularity does not remove the axis from a solid.

exercise.prompt: Convert $x^2+y^2\le 4$ and $1\le z\le 3$ into cylindrical bounds.
exercise.hint: The planar projection is a full disk.
exercise.solution: $0\leq r\leq 2$, $0\leq \theta \leq 2\pi$, $1\leq z\leq 3$, with volume element $r$ dr $d\theta$ dz in a compatible chosen order.
rubric: Include the full angular range.
Use the factor $r$ for volume.

sections.title: Transform bounds and integrand
sections.text: Between $z=r^{2}$ and $z=4$, the surfaces meet at $r=2$. Volume is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2\int_{r^2}^4 r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=8\pi$. An integrand $x^{2}+y^{2}$ becomes $r^{2}$, creating $r^{3}$ after multiplication by the Jacobian.

sections.title: Do not count the Jacobian twice
sections.text: The measure $r$ dr $d\theta$ dz already accounts for geometric stretching. If the physical density is itself $r$, the total factor $r^{2}$ has two different origins: density and volume measure. Label them separately.

exercise.prompt: Find the integral of $x^2+y^2$ over the cylinder of radius 1 and height 2.
exercise.hint: Use density $r^{2}$ and measure $r$.
exercise.solution: The result is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1\int_0^2r^3\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=\pi$.
rubric: Transform the scalar field.
Multiply by one volume Jacobian.

sections.title: Fix the angle convention
sections.text: Use $\rho\ge0$, azimuth $\theta$ around the $z$-axis, and polar angle $\varphi$ down from the positive $z$-axis: $x=\rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta$, $y=\rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta$, $z=\rho\cos\varphi$. Standard ranges are $0\le\theta<2\pi$ and $0\le\varphi\le\pi$.

sections.title: Distinguish coordinate singularities
sections.text: At $\rho =0$ every angle pair represents the origin. At $\varphi =0$ or $\pi$ the azimuth is nonunique. These failures of coordinates do not imply the sphere or solid is geometrically singular.

exercise.prompt: What spherical coordinates describe $(0,0,-2)$?
exercise.hint: The point lies on the negative polar axis.
exercise.solution: $\rho =2$ and $\varphi =\pi$; any $\theta$ represents the same point. The nonunique azimuth is expected.
rubric: State the polar-angle convention.
Allow nonunique coordinates on the axis.

contentBlocks.title: A sphere centered away from the origin
contentBlocks.strategy: Convert each surface separately, then intersect the allowed angle and radial intervals before integrating.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $E$ lie above $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and inside $x^2+y^2+z^2=z$, as posed in MH2100 Lecture 07, physical page 50. Derive its bounds before evaluating the volume.

steps.label: Cone selects directions
steps.text: For $\rho\ge0$, the cone inequality becomes $\rho\cos\varphi\ge\rho\sin\varphi$. Except at the origin this gives $0\le\varphi\le\pi/4$; rotational symmetry gives $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.

steps.label: Sphere sets a variable radial ceiling
steps.text: The sphere inequality is $\rho^2\le\rho\cos\varphi$. The origin is included, and for positive radius the upper bound is $\cos\varphi$, not a constant.

steps.label: Integrate the actual solid
steps.text: Use density $1$ and exactly one spherical volume factor $\rho^2\sin\varphi$. Integrating first in radius gives $\cos^3\varphi/3$.

contentBlocks.result: The exact volume is $\pi/8$; replacing $\cos\varphi$ by a fixed sphere radius changes the region.
contentBlocks.verification: At $\varphi=0$ the radial ceiling is $1$; at $\varphi=\pi/4$ it is $1/\sqrt2$. The sphere is centered at $(0,0,1/2)$ with radius $1/2$, so a constant radial ceiling about the origin cannot describe it.

sections.title: Three scale factors
sections.text: A small spherical cell has lengths approximately $d\rho$, $\rho\,d\varphi$ and $\rho\sin\varphi\,d\theta$. Its volume factor is $\rho^2\sin\varphi$. The signed determinant depends on coordinate order; scalar volume uses its absolute value.

sections.title: Cone and sphere bounds
sections.text: Inside a sphere of radius $R$ and above the cone $\varphi =\pi /4$, use $0\leq \rho \leq R$, $0\leq \varphi \leq \pi /4$, $0\leq \theta \leq 2\pi$. Volume is $(2\pi R^{3}/3)(1-1/\sqrt{2})$, not a cylinder sector.

sections.title: Shifted spheres need variable radial bounds
sections.text: For a sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=cz$ with $c>0$, the interior is $0\leq\rho\leq c\cos\varphi$ where $\cos\varphi\ge0$. An intersecting cone $z\geq\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ restricts directions to $0\leq\varphi\leq\pi/4$. These inequalities specify the same physical solid before any Jacobian is applied.

exercise.prompt: Integrate $x^2+y^2+z^2$ over the ball of radius $R$.
exercise.hint: The integrand is $\rho^2$ and the measure adds another $\rho^2\sin\varphi$.
exercise.solution: The integral is $(R^{5}/5)\cdot 2\cdot 2\pi =4\pi R^{5}/5$. For $R=1$ it is $4\pi /5$.
rubric: Use the full polar range.
Separate the integrand from the Jacobian.

exercises.outcome: Derive a variable spherical radial bound and transform a nonconstant density independently of the Jacobian.
exercises.prompt: Let $D$ lie above $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and inside $x^2+y^2+z^2=2z$. Set spherical bounds and compute $\iiint_D z\,dV$.
exercises.hint: The cone still limits $\varphi$ to $[0,\pi/4]$. Divide the sphere inequality by positive $\rho$, then keep the density $z=\rho\cos\varphi$ separate from $dV$.
exercises.solution: The sphere gives $0\le\rho\le2\cos\varphi$, while $0\le\varphi\le\pi/4$ and $0\le\theta\le2\pi$. The density times the volume factor is $\rho^3\cos\varphi\sin\varphi$. Radial integration gives $4\cos^5\varphi\sin\varphi$, so the integral is $8\pi(1-(1/\sqrt2)^6)/6=7\pi/6$.
rubric: Derive the radial bound from the shifted sphere, not a constant-radius ball.
Use the cone for the polar angle and all azimuths.
Transform the density and include the volume factor once.

sections.title: Columns are transformed edges
sections.text: For $A=[[2,1],[0,3]]$, the unit square edges map to $(2,0)$ and $(1,3)$. Their parallelogram area is |det $A|=6$. Every cell has the same area scale because the map is linear.

sections.title: Orientation and collapse
sections.text: A negative determinant reverses orientation while keeping positive area scale. A zero determinant collapses the plane into a line or point, so a two-dimensional inverse does not exist. The determinant is a number; the derivative matrix is a different object.

exercise.prompt: Find signed and unsigned area factors for $T(u,v)=(u,-2v)$.
exercise.hint: Use the diagonal derivative matrix.
exercise.solution: The signed determinant is $-2$ and area scale is 2. The map reverses orientation.
rubric: Keep sign for orientation.
Use absolute value for scalar area.

sections.title: A nonlinear map with variable scale
sections.text: Let $T(u,v)=(u,(1+u)v)$, $0\leq u,v\leq 1$. Its derivative columns are $(1,v)$ and $(0,1+u)$, so det $DT=1+u$. The image is $0\leq x\leq 1$, $0\leq y\leq 1+x$: a trapezoid with area $3/2$.

sections.title: Finite cells versus infinitesimal cells
sections.text: For $T(u,v)=(u,(1+u)v)$, the exact image area of $[u,u+h]\times [v,v+k]$ is $hk(1+u+h/2)$. Its finite scale approaches $1+u$ as $h\to 0$. The separate shrinking-cell experiment uses $T(u,v)=(u,v+uv^{2})$. Its exact ratio is $1+2(u+h/2)(v+k/2)$, while det $DT=1+2uv$. With $k$ fixed and $h\to 0$, bias uk remains: the cell diameter does not vanish. Shrinking $h$ and $k$ together makes diameter $\sqrt{h^{2}+k^{2}}$ tend to zero and recovers the local determinant.

exercise.prompt: Compute $\iint_R y\,dA$ over that trapezoid using $T$.
exercise.hint: Replace $y$ by $(1+u)v$ and also include the Jacobian.
exercise.solution: The transformed integrand is $(1+u)^{2}v$. Integrating $v$ from 0 to 1 gives $(1+u)^{2}/2$, and integrating $u$ gives $7/6$.
rubric: Transform the field as well as the measure.
Distinguish finite-cell scale from the derivative.

sections.title: Volume is a triple product
sections.text: For $T(u,v,w)$, the signed determinant of its three derivative columns measures oriented volume scale. Scalar volume uses its absolute value. Swapping two parameter columns reverses the sign without changing the physical volume.

sections.title: Order in spherical coordinates
sections.text: With columns ordered $(\rho,\varphi,\theta)$ for $x=\rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta$, $y=\rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta$, $z=\rho\cos\varphi$, the determinant is $\rho^2\sin\varphi$. The order $(\rho,\theta,\varphi)$ has its negative. Both give the same positive volume factor on the standard interior range.

exercise.prompt: Find the volume scale for $T(u,v,w)=(2u,-3v,4w)$.
exercise.hint: Multiply the diagonal entries.
exercise.solution: The signed determinant is $-24$ and the volume scale is 24. The negative sign records orientation reversal.
rubric: State the coordinate order.
Use absolute value for volume.

sections.title: State the map’s scope
sections.text: A sufficient change-of-variables setting is a one-to-one $C^1$ map on a neighborhood of a region with nonzero determinant, plus an integrable transformed field and ordinary negligible boundaries. The transformed integral uses $f(T(u))|\det DT(u)|$.

sections.title: Local invertibility is not global injectivity
sections.text: The map $(u,v)\mapsto(e^u\cos v,e^u\sin v)$ has nonzero determinant $e^{2u}$, but repeats whenever $v$ increases by $2\pi$. Integrating over two full angle turns counts the image twice. Restrict the parameter range or explicitly account for multiplicity.

exercise.prompt: Why does a polar integral over $\theta\in [0,4\pi]$ double-count a disk?
exercise.hint: Compare points at $\theta$ and $\theta +2\pi$.
exercise.solution: They have identical physical coordinates for each positive $r$, so almost every disk point is covered twice. Using the usual $r$ Jacobian over that interval computes twice the disk integral.
rubric: Check global coverage, not only the determinant.
Explain multiplicity away from negligible seams.

sections.title: Invert at corresponding points
sections.text: For an invertible differentiable map $S=T^{-1}$, $DS(T(u))DT(u)=I$. Thus $\det DS(T(u))=1/\det DT(u)$. The locations matter: reciprocal determinants are evaluated at points related by the map.

sections.title: A nonlinear example
sections.text: For $u=x$ and $v=y/(1+x)$, with $x>-1$, the forward determinant is $1/(1+x)$. The inverse is $x=u,y=(1+u)v$ and its determinant is $1+u$. When integrating in $u$,$v$, use the latter absolute factor.

exercise.prompt: For $u=2x$ and $v=3y$, what factor converts $du dv$ to $dx dy$?
exercise.hint: Compute the inverse map, or reciprocate the nonzero determinant.
exercise.solution: The inverse is $x=u/2,y=v/3$, so dx $dy=(1/6)du$ dv.
rubric: Identify the direction of substitution.
Do not insert the forward determinant 6.

sections.title: Density accumulates with length
sections.text: For a parametrized curve $r(t)$, $\int_C f\,ds=\int f(r(t))|r'(t)|\,dt$. Reversing orientation preserves the value because speed is nonnegative. Repeated traversal repeats the accumulation.

sections.title: Non-unit speed is visible
sections.text: For $r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t)$, speed is $2$. With density $f=3$, one traversal has integral $\int_0^{2\pi}6\,dt=12\pi$. Using $dt$ alone would underestimate by a factor of two.

exercise.prompt: Integrate density $f(x,y)=x$ along $r(t)=(t,2t)$, $0\le t\le 1$.
exercise.hint: The speed is constant $\sqrt{5}$.
exercise.solution: The integral is $\sqrt{5}\int_0^1t\,dt =\sqrt{5}/2$. Reversing the traversal leaves the scalar line integral unchanged.
rubric: Evaluate density along the curve.
Include the speed factor.

sections.title: Components depend on position
sections.text: A vector field $F$ assigns a vector to each point of its domain. For $F=(-y,x)$, arrows are tangential to circles about zero; for $F=(x,y)$, arrows are radial. Arrow normalization improves legibility but hides magnitude unless a scale or readout supplies it.

sections.title: Domain is part of the field
sections.text: The field $(-y/(x^{2}+y^{2}),x/(x^{2}+y^{2}))$ excludes the origin. A plot that omits one arrow does not repair the missing domain point; theorem hypotheses must respect that puncture.

exercise.prompt: At $(1,0)$, compare radial $F=(x,y)$ and rotational $G=(-y,x)$.
exercise.hint: Substitute the point into each component.
exercise.solution: $F=(1,0)$ points outward and $G=(0,1)$ is tangent counterclockwise. Their dot product is zero.
rubric: Evaluate the field at the point.
Distinguish field vector from position vector when they differ.

sections.title: Work uses a signed component
sections.text: Work is $\int F(r(t))\cdot r'(t)dt$. Parallel force and velocity contribute positively, opposed ones negatively, and perpendicular components contribute zero. Unlike a scalar length integral, reversing traversal reverses the sign.

sections.title: A transverse component contributes nothing
sections.text: On $r(t)=(t,0)$, $0\leq t\leq 1$, $F=(1,5)$ has dot product 1 with $r'=(1,0)$. Work is 1 despite the large vertical force component. For $F=(-1,5)$, work is $-1$.

exercise.prompt: Find the work of $F=(2,3)$ along the segment from $(0,0)$ to $(1,2)$.
exercise.hint: Use $r(t)=(t,2t)$.
exercise.solution: The dot product $(2,3)\cdot (1,2)=8$ is constant, so work is 8. The reverse path gives $-8$.
rubric: Use velocity rather than unit tangent alone.
Retain orientation and sign.

sections.title: Three differentials are one dot product
sections.text: The expression $P$ $dx+Q dy+R$ dz becomes $[P(r)x'+Q(r)y'+R(r)z']dt$. Each differential follows the same parameter interval; none is an independent integration variable.

sections.title: Check terms individually
sections.text: Along $r(t)=(t,t^{2})$, $0\leq t\leq 1$, $\int y dx+x$ dy becomes $\int (t^{2}+2t^{2})dt=1$. The form is $d(xy)$, so endpoints independently give $1-0=1$.

exercise.prompt: Evaluate $\oint(x\,dy-y\,dx)$ around the unit circle counterclockwise.
exercise.hint: Use $x=\cos t$, $y=\sin t$ and differentiate both.
exercise.solution: The integrand becomes $\cos^{2}t+\sin^{2}t=1$, giving $2\pi$ over $[0,2\pi ]$. Reversing orientation gives $-2\pi$.
rubric: Differentiate both coordinates.
Carry the minus sign in dx.

sections.title: Each piece gets its own parameter
sections.text: For a path from A to $B$ to $C$, parametrize both oriented segments and add their integrals. Shared endpoints contribute no interval length. Reversing a piece changes its vector line integral sign but not a scalar length integral.

sections.title: Compare different paths
sections.text: For $F=(y,0)$, from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$, traveling horizontally then vertically gives work 0. Traveling vertically then horizontally gives work 1. The same endpoints do not imply the same work without conservativeness.

exercise.prompt: Compute $\int y\,dx$ along $(0,0)\to(1,0)\to(1,1)$.
exercise.hint: On the first segment $y=0$; on the second $dx=0$.
exercise.solution: Both pieces contribute zero, so the integral is zero. The alternative path through $(0,1)$ gives 1.
rubric: Respect the order and direction of pieces.
Avoid inferring endpoint-only dependence.

sections.title: Circulation is work on a closed traversal
sections.text: For $F=(-y,x)$ and the unit circle counterclockwise, $F(r)=r'$ and the dot product is 1, giving circulation $2\pi$. For the radial field $(x,y)$, it is zero because field and velocity are perpendicular.

sections.title: A field can change the sign around a path
sections.text: For constant $F=(1,0)$ on a circle, local work density is $-\sin t$. Some arcs contribute positively and others negatively, with total zero. Zero net work does not mean every local contribution vanishes.

exercise.prompt: Find circulation of $F=(-2y,2x)$ around a radius-$R$ circle counterclockwise.
exercise.hint: Both field and velocity scale with $R$.
exercise.solution: The dot product is $2R^{2}$, giving circulation $4\pi R^{2}$. Clockwise traversal changes the sign.
rubric: Track both radius factors.
State the orientation.

sections.title: Apply chain rule along the curve
sections.text: If $F=\nabla \varphi$ on a domain containing the entire piecewise smooth path, then $F(r)\cdot r'=(\varphi \circ r)'$. Integrating gives $\varphi(\text{end})-\varphi(\text{start})$. A closed path then has zero work.

sections.title: Construct a potential with a missing function
sections.text: For $F=(2xy,x^{2}+2y)$, integrate the first component in $x$ to get $\varphi =x^{2}y+C(y)$. Differentiating in $y$ and matching the second component gives $C'=2y$, hence $\varphi =x^{2}y+y^{2}+\text{constant}$.

exercise.prompt: Find work of that field from $(0,0)$ to $(1,2)$.
exercise.hint: Evaluate the potential at endpoints.
exercise.solution: $\varphi (1,2)=2+4=6$ and $\varphi (0,0)=0$, so work is 6 along every admissible path in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.
rubric: Verify both partials of the potential.
Subtract in endpoint order.

sections.title: Curl-free needs a domain theorem
sections.text: A $C^1$ field on a simply connected open domain with zero curl is conservative. On an arbitrary domain, zero curl is only a local condition. A potential always forces zero curl when mixed derivatives may be interchanged.

sections.title: The punctured-plane counterexample
sections.text: $F=(-y/r^{2},x/r^{2})$ has zero scalar curl away from zero, yet its circulation around the unit circle is $2\pi$. The loop surrounds an excluded point, so no global single-valued potential exists on the punctured plane. On a suitable cut domain an angle potential is possible.

exercise.prompt: Can Green’s theorem on the full disk justify zero circulation for this vortex?
exercise.hint: Is the field defined on a neighborhood of the whole disk?
exercise.solution: No. It is undefined at the center, violating the theorem’s domain hypothesis. Direct circulation is $2\pi$; an annulus would have both outer and inner boundaries.
rubric: Check the interior as well as the curve.
Account for an inner boundary when using an annulus.

sections.title: Orient the whole boundary
sections.text: For a positively oriented simple closed piecewise smooth curve bounding a suitable planar region, with $P$,$Q$ continuously differentiable on a neighborhood, $\oint P dx+Q dy=\int \int (Q_{x}-P_{y})dA$. Positive orientation keeps the region on the left; inner boundaries of holes therefore run clockwise.

sections.title: Why internal edges disappear
sections.text: Partitioning a region into smaller pieces gives two traversals of every shared edge with opposite directions. Their line integrals cancel, leaving the outer and hole boundaries. This motivates the theorem; a full proof requires controlling the partition and regularity.

exercise.prompt: Find $\oint(-y\,dx+x\,dy)$ around the unit circle counterclockwise using Green.
exercise.hint: Compute $Q_{x}-P_{y}$.
exercise.solution: The scalar curl is $1-(-1)=2$. The disk area is $\pi$, so circulation is $2\pi$.
rubric: Check the field on the entire disk.
Use the assigned boundary orientation.

sections.title: Choose a field whose curl is one
sections.text: The forms $x\,dy$, $-y\,dx$, and $(x\,dy-y\,dx)/2$ all integrate to area on a positively oriented simple boundary because each corresponding scalar curl equals 1. Reverse orientation and the signed result changes sign.

sections.title: A polygon reduces to endpoint data
sections.text: On a straight edge from $(x_i,y_i)$ to $(x_j,y_j)$, the symmetric form contributes $(x_i y_j-x_j y_i)/2$. Summing edges gives the shoelace formula. Self-intersecting traversals produce signed multiplicity-weighted area rather than automatically the union’s geometric area.

exercise.prompt: Use boundary data to find the area of triangle $(0,0)$, $(3,0)$, $(0,2)$ in that order.
exercise.hint: Sum the three cross-products and divide by two.
exercise.solution: Only the edge $(3,0)\to (0,2)$ contributes 6 before halving. The area is 3 and the ordering is counterclockwise.
rubric: Close the polygon.
Check sign and orientation.

sections.title: Two parameters trace a surface
sections.text: A chart $r(u,v)$ maps a planar parameter region into space. Regularity requires $r_{u}\times r_{v}\ne 0$. To integrate without multiplicity, also check coverage: a regular map can cover the same physical patch more than once.

sections.title: Seams are coordinate artifacts
sections.text: A sphere chart $r(\varphi,\theta)=(\sin\varphi\cos\theta,\sin\varphi\sin\theta,\cos\varphi)$ repeats at the angular seam and degenerates at the poles. Multiple charts or exclusion of negligible boundary sets can handle these defects; they do not make the sphere itself nonsmooth.

exercise.prompt: Parametrize the cylinder $x^2+y^2=4$ for $0\le z\le 3$.
exercise.hint: Use angle and height as independent parameters.
exercise.solution: $r(\theta ,z)=(2cos \theta ,2sin \theta ,z)$, $0\leq \theta \leq 2\pi ,0\leq z\leq 3$. It covers the side once apart from the repeated seam.
rubric: Specify the parameter rectangle.
Explain seam duplication and distinguish the cylinder caps.

sections.title: Differentiate one parameter at a time
sections.text: For $r(u,v)=(u,v,u^{2}+v^{2})$, the tangent vectors are $r_{u}=(1,0,2u)$ and $r_{v}=(0,1,2v)$. Their cross product is $(-2u,-2v,1)$, a nonzero upward normal.

sections.title: Tangent plane versus the curved patch
sections.text: At $(u,v)=(1,1)$, the surface point is $(1,1,2)$ and normal ($-2$,$-2$,1), yielding $z=2x+2y-2$. The plane is the affine first-order approximation, not the whole surface.

exercise.prompt: Find tangent vectors and a normal for $r(u,v)=(u,v,uv)$ at $(1,2)$.
exercise.hint: Evaluate derivatives at the parameter pair, not at the 3D point.
rubric: Distinguish parameter pair from physical point.
Verify the normal is perpendicular to both tangents.

sections.title: A local parallelogram supplies area
sections.text: The parameter cell du dv maps approximately to edges $r_u\,du$ and $r_v\,dv$, giving $dS=|r_u\times r_v|\,du\,dv$. The norm removes orientation but retains stretch; using a unit normal here would lose the area factor.

sections.title: Graphs are a special case
sections.text: For $z=f(x,y)$, $r=(x,y,f)$ gives $dS=\sqrt{1+f_{x}^{2}+f_{y}^{2}}dx$ dy. On the plane $z=x+2y$ over a unit square, the factor is $\sqrt{6}$ and the area is $\sqrt{6}$.

exercise.prompt: Find the area of $z=3x$ over $0\le x\le 2$, $0\le y\le 1$.
exercise.hint: The graph area factor is constant.
exercise.solution: The factor is $\sqrt{1+9}=\sqrt{10}$. Multiplying by projected area 2 gives $2\sqrt{10}$.
rubric: Use surface area rather than projected area.
Keep the factor under the square root.

sections.title: Density times area
sections.text: The scalar surface integral is $\int \int f(r(u,v))|r_{u}\times r_{v}|du$ dv. It is unaffected by reversing orientation, although repeating coverage repeats the integral.

sections.title: A plane with variable density
sections.text: On $z=x+y$ over the unit square, density $f=z$ becomes $u+v$ and area factor $\sqrt{3}$. The integral is $\sqrt{3}\int_0^1\int_0^1(u+v)\,du\,dv =\sqrt{3}$. Using only the projected measure would miss the slope factor.

exercise.prompt: Integrate constant density 2 over a sphere of radius $R$.
exercise.hint: Multiply density by surface area.
exercise.solution: The result is $8\pi R^{2}$. It does not change if inward rather than outward orientation is named, because this is a scalar area integral.
rubric: Distinguish scalar integration from flux.
Use area, not enclosed volume.

sections.title: Orientation is a continuous choice
sections.text: An orientation chooses one of the two unit normal directions continuously across a regular surface. Reversing parameter order reverses $r_{u}\times r_{v}$. A closed bounding surface usually uses outward normals; open surfaces need an explicit convention.

sections.title: A Möbius strip has no global side
sections.text: Following a local normal around a $M$öbius strip returns it reversed. Thus one global continuous normal cannot be chosen. Local charts and scalar area still make sense; a globally oriented flux or ordinary oriented Stokes surface requires more care.

exercise.prompt: For the graph $z=x^2+y^2$, which cross-product sign gives downward orientation?
exercise.hint: The standard $(x,y)$ order produces a positive $z$ component.
exercise.solution: The upward area vector is $(-2x,-2y,1)$dx dy. Downward uses its negative, $(2x,2y,-1)$dx dy.
rubric: Choose sign from the requested direction.
Do not discard the area magnitude when integrating flux.

sections.title: Flux retains the normal sign
sections.text: Flux is $\int \int F\cdot n$ dS, or $\int \int F(r)\cdot (r_{u}\times r_{v})du$ dv with a compatible parameter orientation. The dot product measures only the normal component; reversing the normal reverses flux.

sections.title: Oblique fields and cancellation
sections.text: For constant $F=(1,0,0)$ on an outward unit sphere, local flux is positive on the right hemisphere and negative on the left, giving total zero. This differs from the radial field $F=(x,y,z)$, which is outward everywhere and has flux $4\pi$.

exercise.prompt: Find upward flux of $F=(1,2,3)$ through the unit square in $z=0$.
exercise.hint: The upward unit normal is $(0,0,1)$.
exercise.solution: The dot product is 3, so flux is 3. Horizontal components contribute zero. Downward orientation gives $-3$.
rubric: Choose the normal.
Multiply normal component by area.

sections.title: Curl measures oriented circulation density
sections.text: In three dimensions curl $F$ has components $(R_{y}-Q_z,P_z-R_{x},Q_{x}-P_{y})$. Its dot product with a chosen unit normal measures infinitesimal circulation per area in that plane, under smoothness hypotheses.

sections.title: Curved arrows alone are misleading
sections.text: The field $(-y,x,0)$ has curl $(0,0,2)$, while $(-y/r^{2},x/r^{2},0)$ has zero curl away from the $z$-axis despite circular arrows. The latter has an excluded singular axis, so its global circulation behavior needs the domain.

exercise.prompt: Find curl of $F=(0,0,xy)$.
exercise.hint: Only derivatives of the third component are nonzero.
exercise.solution: Curl $F=(x,-y,0)$. At $(1,2,0)$ it is $(1,-2,0)$, describing oriented circulation in corresponding coordinate planes.
rubric: Use the correct component order.
Distinguish curl from the field itself.

sections.title: Divergence is a signed scalar
sections.text: For $F=(P,Q,R)$, divergence is $P_{x}+Q_{y}+R_z$. Positive divergence means local net outward flux density, not necessarily arrows pointing directly away from the origin.

sections.title: A non-radial example
sections.text: For $F=(x,-y,0)$, divergence is zero: expansion in the $x$ direction balances contraction in $y$. For $F=(x,y,z)$, divergence is 3. Arrow length and direction alone do not supply the derivative balance.

exercise.prompt: Compute divergence of $F=(x^2,yz,z^2)$. Where is it zero?
exercise.hint: Differentiate each component in its matching coordinate.
exercise.solution: Divergence is $2x+z+2z=2x+3z$, zero on the plane $2x+3z=0$.
rubric: Use matching partial derivatives.
Do not add the components without differentiating.

sections.title: Write the cancellations
sections.text: For a $C^2$ scalar $\varphi$, $\operatorname{curl}(\nabla\varphi)=0$ because each component is a difference of equal mixed partials. For a $C^2$ vector field, $\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}F)=0$ by the same pairwise cancellations.

sections.title: Converse statements need separate conditions
sections.text: Curl-free does not always mean a global gradient on a punctured domain. Divergence-free does not automatically provide a globally defined vector potential on every domain. These identities are necessary structural checks, not universal converse theorems.

exercise.prompt: Could $F=(x,y,z)$ be the curl of a $C^2$ vector field on an open ball?
exercise.hint: Compute its divergence.
exercise.solution: No: div $F=3$, whereas the divergence of the curl of a $C^{2}$ field must be zero.
rubric: State the smoothness setting.
Use the identity as a necessary condition.

sections.title: Boundary and normal are paired
sections.text: Stokes relates $\oint_{\partial S}F\cdot d\mathbf r$ to $\iint_S(\nabla\times F)\cdot n\,dS$ for a suitable oriented piecewise smooth surface and $C^1$ field on a neighborhood. Point the right thumb along the chosen normal: curled fingers give the induced boundary direction. For a surface with an upward normal and a simple projected boundary, this is counterclockwise when viewed from above. Across glued patches, shared edges cancel.

sections.title: Choose the easier surface lawfully
sections.text: For $F=(-y/2,x/2,0)$, curl is $(0,0,1)$. Around a unit horizontal circle counterclockwise, the flat disk gives flux $\pi$. Another admissible spanning surface with the same induced boundary has the same curl flux, provided the field remains smooth near it.

sections.title: A replacement surface needs the same edge
sections.text: A tilted loop can bound its tilted planar disk. Before replacing a curved spanning surface, check that the new surface has exactly the same oriented boundary and that $F$ is smooth on a neighborhood of the whole replacement surface. If the requested traversal is opposite to the disk’s induced direction, reverse the normal or negate the resulting integral.

exercise.prompt: Find circulation of $F=(-y,x,0)$ around the unit circle viewed clockwise from above.
exercise.hint: Use a downward-oriented disk.
exercise.solution: Curl $F=(0,0,2)$. With downward normal, flux is $-2$ times the disk area, giving $-2\pi$.
rubric: Match the boundary to the surface normal.
Check the field on a neighborhood of the spanning surface.

contentBlocks.title: A tilted boundary and a lawful flat spanning disk
contentBlocks.strategy: Identify the boundary, choose the planar disk it encloses, check the field and orientation, then integrate curl on that disk.
contentBlocks.setup: MH2100 Lecture 11, physical pages 24–26: $C$ is $x^2+y^2=1$ in the plane $y+z=2$, counterclockwise when viewed from above; $F=(-y^2,x,z^2)$ is defined on $\mathbb R^3$. Evaluate $\oint_C F\cdot d\mathbf r$.

steps.label: Choose an admissible surface
steps.text: The tilted planar disk $S=\{(x,y,2-y):x^2+y^2\le1\}$ is smooth with the required edge $C$. The polynomial field is smooth on a neighborhood of the entire disk; Stokes therefore applies.

steps.label: Match the boundary orientation
steps.text: The parameter order $(x,y)$ gives $\mathbf r_x\times\mathbf r_y=(0,1,1)$, whose vertical component is positive. Seen from above, its induced boundary is counterclockwise, as requested.

steps.label: Integrate the actual curl
steps.text: Here $\nabla\times F=(0,0,1+2y)$. The vertical component of the oriented area vector is $1$, and the $2y$ term integrates to zero by symmetry of the unit disk.

contentBlocks.result: The circulation is $\pi$. A tilted boundary need not use a horizontal disk: the disk must actually have edge $C$.
contentBlocks.verification: Directly, $\mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,2-\sin t)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$ gives $F\cdot\mathbf r'(t)=\sin^3 t+\cos^2 t-(2-\sin t)^2\cos t$; only $\cos^2 t$ has nonzero integral, again $\pi$.

exercises.outcome: Choose a lawful tilted spanning disk and match its induced boundary orientation before using Stokes.
exercises.prompt: Let $C$ be $x^2+y^2=4$ in the plane $z=1+x$, traversed clockwise when viewed from above, and let $F=(-y,x,z^2)$ on $\mathbb R^3$. Decide whether its tilted planar disk is an admissible Stokes surface; choose its normal orientation and evaluate $\oint_C F\cdot d\mathbf r$. Explain why the horizontal disk $z=1$ cannot simply be substituted.
exercises.hint: Parametrize the tilted disk by $\mathbf r(x,y)=(x,y,1+x)$ over $x^2+y^2\le4$. Determine the upward cross product, then reverse it for the requested traversal. Check the field on the whole disk.
exercises.solution: The tilted disk has edge $C$ and the polynomial field is smooth on all of $\mathbb R^3$. Its upward area vector is $(-1,0,1)\,dx\,dy$, inducing counterclockwise travel viewed from above; use $(1,0,-1)$ for the requested clockwise direction. Since $\nabla\times F=(0,0,2)$, the flux is $-2$ times the disk area $4\pi$, hence $-8\pi$. The horizontal disk has a different boundary, so Stokes does not equate its flux directly with this circulation.
rubric: Verify the replacement disk has exactly the given edge and that the field is smooth on it.
Relate the upward area vector to counterclockwise travel and reverse for clockwise travel.
Use the actual curl and account for the disk area; reject the horizontal disk as a different boundary.

sections.title: The surface must close the region
sections.text: For a suitable bounded solid $V$ with outward-oriented boundary and $C^1$ field near its closure, total flux equals $\iiint_V\operatorname{div}F\,dV$. An open cap or side surface needs its missing pieces included and then subtracted.

sections.title: Singularities and holes
sections.text: The field $r/|r|^{3}$ is singular at zero, so the theorem cannot be applied to a ball containing zero despite vanishing divergence away from it. On a shell the inner boundary points toward the center as an outward normal from the shell, and its flux cancels the outer contribution.

exercise.prompt: Find outward flux of $F=(x,y,z)$ through a sphere of radius $R$.
exercise.hint: Use divergence 3 and the enclosed volume.
exercise.solution: The flux is $3\cdot (4\pi R^{3}/3)=4\pi R^{3}$. Directly, $F\cdot n=R$ and surface area is $4\pi R^{2}$, giving the same answer.
rubric: Use outward orientation on a closed surface.
Check with the direct area calculation.

sections.title: Keep the original review data
sections.text: The two Stokes tasks use outward curl flux for $F=(y,-x,z)$ on the cone $z=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$, $0\leq z\leq 1$, joined to the cylinder $x^{2}+y^{2}=1$, $1\leq z\leq 4$; and upward curl flux for $F=(x+y^{2},y+z^{2},z+x^{2})$ on the first-octant triangle $x+y+z=3$. The original Green task from Lecture 12, physical page 7, asks for clockwise circulation of $P\,dx+Q\,dy$ around the triangle $(0,0)$,$(0,12)$,$(3,0)$, where $P=y\cos x-xy\sin x$ and $Q=xy+x\cos x$. The original potential task on physical page 10 gives $(2xy+e^{-x^2})\,dx+(x^2+y\cos(\pi y^2/2))\,dy$ along the oriented curve whose parametrization $r(t)=(e^{t^2-t}-\cos(2\pi t),2\sin(\pi t^2/2)-t^9)$, $0\leq t\leq 1$, runs opposite to the requested orientation. These original tasks are distinct from the simplified scaffolds below.

sections.title: Work the Stokes setups
sections.text: For the cone and cylinder, the top boundary is clockwise under the outward side orientation; $r=(\cos t,-\sin t,4)$ gives integrand 1 and answer $2\pi$. Excluding a tiny cone-tip cap and taking its limit handles the apex. For the first-octant triangle, $\operatorname{curl}F=(-2z,-2x,-2y)$; its dot product with the upward area vector $(1,1,1)$ is $-6$, so the flux is $-27$. Check the induced boundary orientation before using Stokes instead.

sections.title: Original Green task: cancellation before integration
sections.text: Differentiate both components of the original field: $Q_x=y+\cos x-x\sin x$, while $P_y=\cos x-x\sin x$. Thus $Q_{x}-P_{y}=y$; the trigonometric terms cancel only after the full source field has been used. The triangle has $0\leq x\leq 3$ and $0\leq y\leq 12-4x$. Green’s theorem with clockwise orientation gives $-\int_0^3\int_0^{12-4x}y\,dy\,dx=-72$. As a simpler, separately labelled scaffold, $F=(0,xy)$ on the same triangle has the same curl and answer but does not teach that derivative cancellation.

sections.title: Original potential task: endpoints and reversed orientation
sections.text: The original field has potential $\varphi (x,y)=x^{2}y+\int_0^xe^{-s^2}\,ds +\sin(\pi y^{2}/2)/\pi$. Its derivatives reproduce both field components. The supplied complicated parametrization has $r(0)=(0,0)$ and $r(1)=(0,1)$, opposite to the requested curve orientation. Hence the requested integral is $\varphi (0,0)-\varphi (0,1)=-1/\pi$; no elementary antiderivative of $e^{-x^2}$ or direct path integration is needed. The straight segment $r(t)=(0,1-t)$, $0\leq t\leq 1$, is a separately labelled scaffold with the desired direction, not the original parametrization.

exercise.prompt: For the original Green field $P=y\cos x-xy\sin x$, $Q=xy+x\cos x$, reverse the triangle direction and compute the new circulation by Green’s theorem.
exercise.hint: Differentiate the full $P$ and $Q$ before cancelling terms; reversing clockwise orientation changes the sign.
exercise.solution: $Q_x=y+\cos x-x\sin x$ and $P_y=\cos x-x\sin x$, so $Q_{x}-P_{y}=y$. Counterclockwise circulation is $\int_0^3\int_0^{12-4x}y\,dy\,dx=72$. The simplified scaffold $F=(0,xy)$ gives the same result, but skips the cancellation in the original field.
rubric: Use both components of the original source field.
Match orientation before integrating.
Show the curl cancellation and bounds.

sections.title: Map every boundary
sections.text: For the first-quadrant region bounded by $y=x^{3},y=2x^{3},xy=1,xy=3$, take $u=y/x^{3}$ and $v=xy$. The new rectangle is $1\leq u\leq 2,1\leq v\leq 3$. The inverse $x=(v/u)^{1/4}$, $y=u^{1/4}v^{3/4}$ maps its four edges to the actual curved boundaries.

sections.title: Check sign, scale, and bounds
sections.text: The inverse determinant is $-1/(4u)$, so scalar area uses $1/(4u)$. Integrating gives $(\ln 2)/2$. Since the factor lies between $1/8$ and $1/4$ on a rectangle of area 2, the result must lie between $1/4$ and $1/2$; this catches a mistaken forward determinant.

exercise.prompt: Compute $\iint_D xy\,dA$ over the same region.
exercise.hint: The integrand xy becomes $v$.
exercise.solution: The integral is $\int_1^2\int_1^3\frac{v}{4u}\,dv\,du=(ln2)/4\cdot 4=ln2$.
rubric: Transform both region and field.
Use the absolute inverse determinant.
Compare with the area-scaled bounds.

sections.title: Why the box is centered
sections.text: For an axis-aligned box whose eight vertices lie on $2x^{2}+72y^{2}+18z^{2}=288$, compare vertices differing in only one coordinate. Their squared endpoints must agree, so a nondegenerate box has opposite coordinate pairs. Its positive half-lengths $x$,$y$,$z$ give volume 8xyz.

sections.title: Global bound without multipliers
sections.text: Set $X=x/12,Y=y/2,Z=z/4$. The constraint becomes $X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}=1$. AM–GM gives $X^{2}Y^{2}Z^{2}\leq 1/27$, so $XYZ\leq 1/(3\sqrt{3})$. Since $8xyz=768XYZ$, maximum volume is $256/\sqrt{3}$, attained at $X=Y=Z=1/\sqrt{3}$. Boundary boxes have zero volume.

exercise.prompt: For an ellipsoid $x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2+z^2/c^2=1$ with $a,b,c>0$, find the largest axis-aligned inscribed box.
exercise.hint: Normalize coordinates and maximize the product.
exercise.solution: The half-lengths are $a/\sqrt{3},b/\sqrt{3},c/\sqrt{3}$, so volume is $8abc/(3\sqrt{3})$. Positivity and AM–GM establish the global maximum, while degenerate boundary volumes vanish.
rubric: Distinguish half-lengths from side lengths.
State positive semiaxes.
Prove a global bound and its equality case.

sections.title: Enumerate rather than sample
sections.text: For $f=x^{4}-2x^{2}+y^{3}-3y$, stationarity gives $x\in {-1,0,1}$ and $y\in {-1,1}$, producing six points. The Hessian is diagonal with entries $12x^{2}-4$ and 6y, so its signs classify every candidate.

sections.title: Keep all values and types
sections.text: At $(\pm 1,1)$, both entries are positive: strict local minima of value $-3$. At $(0,-1)$, both are negative: strict local maximum of value 2. At $(\pm 1,-1)$ the signs differ: saddles of value 1; $(0,1)$ is a saddle of value $-2$. The cubic $y$ term makes the full surface unbounded in both directions, so none is a global extremum.

exercise.prompt: At $(0,1)$, show directly that the value $-2$ is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum.
exercise.hint: Compare small displacements along $x$ and along $y$.
exercise.solution: Along $(h,1)$, $f+2=h^{4}-2h^{2}<0$ for small nonzero $h$. Along $(0,1+k)$, $f+2=3k^{2}+k^{3}>0$ for small nonzero $k$. Both signs occur arbitrarily close.
rubric: Keep the base value in the comparison.
Use sufficiently small nonzero displacements.

supplementalBlocks.title: Use the exact inline pair
supplementalBlocks.text: The inline controls compare two distinct review functions with their own candidate planes and normalized residuals. The sampled meshes show shape, while the $r^2$ bound for the first function and the positive-diagonal obstruction for the second decide the claims. The generic side scene is a related illustration, not either exact proof.

exercises.outcome: Transfer the full-radius remainder method to a new function without relying on sampled paths.
exercises.prompt: Let $u(x,y)=x^2y^2/\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ away from zero and $u(0,0)=0$. Prove total differentiability at zero and give a sufficient $\delta(\varepsilon)$ for the normalized error.
exercises.hint: Use $2|xy|\le x^2+y^2=r^2$ to bound $x^2y^2$.
exercises.solution: Both partials are zero, so $L=0$. Since $x^{2}y^{2}\leq r^{4}/4$, $|u|/r=x^{2}y^{2}/r^{2}\le r^{2}/4\to 0$. Given $\varepsilon >0$, choosing $\delta =2\sqrt{\varepsilon }$ makes the normalized error $<\varepsilon$ whenever $0<r<\delta$.
rubric: Identify the candidate linear map from the axis restrictions.
Give an inequality valid for all directions.
State $\delta$ as a function of $\varepsilon$ with the puncture.

sections.title: A successful all-direction estimate
sections.text: For $f=(x^{4}+y^{4})/r$ away from zero and $f(0)=0$, both coordinate partials are zero. Since $x^{4}+y^{4}\leq r^{4}$, $|f|/r\leq r^{2}\to 0$. Thus the derivative is the zero map, with $\delta =\sqrt{\varepsilon }$ supplying an explicit normalized-error guarantee.

sections.title: A continuous failure
sections.text: For $g=(x^{3}-xy^{2})/(x^{2}+y^{2})$ with $g(0)=0$, the candidate derivative is $L(x,y)=x$. The remainder is $-2xy^{2}/(x^{2}+y^{2})$. Along $(t,t)$, its normalized magnitude is $1/\sqrt{2}$, so differentiability fails. Nevertheless $|g|\leq r$ proves continuity. A graph of a canonical bowl cannot establish either result.

exercise.prompt: Explain why testing just the two coordinate axes would wrongly suggest differentiability of $g$.
exercise.hint: Evaluate $g-L$ on each axis.
exercise.solution: On both coordinate axes the remainder is zero, so those tests see no error. Along the diagonal the normalized error stays $1/\sqrt{2}$. Total differentiability needs one estimate for all small vectors, not only coordinate directions.
rubric: Identify the unique candidate map from the partials.
